questions.topic: Settling fraud-related fund recoveries between financial institutions
questions.stem: Two banks disagree about the amount recoverable after a fraudulent payment, with one treating a provisional customer credit as the final interbank settlement. Select TWO distinctions necessary for defensible reconciliation.
options: Close the matter without reconciling returned sums because an account was blocked.
Maintain transaction references, recovery communications, and agreed settlement records to support the interbank position.
Net all victim complaints together without identifying individual transaction amounts.
Reconcile the customer's provisional credit with its own fraud ledger while not confirming what the receiving bank actually returned.
Separate customer reimbursement or provisional credit from funds actually returned by the recipient institution.
questions.explanation: The guide describes recovery settlement as a coordinated and documented process. Customer credits and recovered funds are different events; reliable reconciliation needs traceable transaction and settlement records. The strongest competing approach falls short because the institution's provisional customer credit is not evidence of an interbank return of the same funds.

options: Report the confirmed cash amount and suspect identity while maintaining the control bypass and response timeline only in informal emails.
The report cannot reliably support investigation, management accountability, control remediation, or lessons learned without a reconstructable incident narrative.
The incident becomes legally harmless when the amount is small.
A concise loss total is always sufficient for operational and regulatory review.
questions.explanation: The guide treats incident reporting as documentation and analysis, not only loss enumeration. A reproducible chronology and control assessment help prevent recurrence and inform oversight. The strongest competing approach falls short because a report without integrated incident chronology cannot reliably be used to learn from the control failure.

questions.stem: A financial institution operates in several jurisdictions and uses a single US incident-reporting checklist for all customers. What is the principal weakness in this approach?
options: Adopt one internal policy based on the strictest single jurisdiction without validating whether other local duties differ in substance.
Fraud reporting, privacy, payment treatment, and evidence duties can differ by jurisdiction and must be mapped to the actual product and incident.
An internal checklist automatically overrides every regulator's requirements.
Local variation matters only after a company is convicted of fraud.
questions.explanation: The guide stresses that anti-fraud rules are region-specific, not universally interchangeable. A control framework needs local legal mapping and updates rather than assuming one country's obligations cover all activities. The strongest competing approach falls short because a strict policy from one country can still overlook different reporting, privacy, and payment duties elsewhere.

options: Revert every additional authentication step because any decline in conversion outweighs all prevented fraud.
Consider customer complaints irrelevant because increased friction always represents stronger fraud protection.
Assess loss prevention alongside false positives, approval outcomes, customer friction and the opportunity to target controls more selectively.
Use alert volume as the only numerator in the effectiveness calculation and avoid measuring payment approvals.
questions.explanation: The guide explicitly addresses balancing fraud reduction with client experience and monitoring both positive and negative interactions.

Both approaches are identical names for the same sequence of automated case-management controls.
The Reid approach prohibits evaluating the interviewee’s behavior and relies exclusively on documentary exhibits.
The Reid method emphasizes behavioral assessment and admissions, whereas PEACE provides a structured, non-coercive investigative interview framework.

questions.topic: Leveraging data from technology platforms for fraud detection
questions.stem: A fraud model uses app activity but ignores call-centre interactions, device changes, and customer complaints. Select TWO steps that better leverage technology-platform data.
options: Discard contact-centre data because it is partly unstructured.
Integrate cross-channel events under usable customer and account identifiers with consistent timestamps.
Use only device model numbers and never consider account-level activity.
Merge device and app activity but exclude contact-centre reports because their event times may be less standardized.
Establish normal behavior from available history and compare new events with that baseline for suspicious deviations.
questions.explanation: The guide emphasizes combining technology-platform sources to understand expected behavior. Linking complementary events and a baseline improves anomaly detection; an isolated signal should not be treated as proof. questions.topic: Bias and fairness in fraud detection models and algorithms
questions.stem: Fraud losses fall after a model is deployed, but one customer segment experiences an unusually high rate of legitimate transaction blocks. The product team proposes ignoring the disparity because total fraud savings are positive. Select TWO measures or conclusions that address the evidence most defensibly.
options: Use the historical training distribution as proof of fairness even when operating data shows materially different error rates.
Test disparate outcomes across relevant groups and apply appropriate fairness and performance controls without abandoning fraud mitigation.
Automatically exempt the affected segment from fraud detection without checking whether alternative safeguards are available.
Exclude all performance reporting by customer segment because aggregate improvement proves every segment is treated fairly.
Assess whether disparate impacts arise from biased training data, feature choices or thresholds and document mitigation.
questions.explanation: The guide discusses sources of algorithmic bias and techniques such as fairness constraints, representative data and monitoring. Assess whether disparate impacts arise from biased training data, feature choices or thresholds and document mitigation.

options: Change records to remove details inconsistent with the preferred conclusion.
Interview appropriate parties and analyze competing explanations in the context of the evidence.
Skip evidence gathering once a payment is recalled.
Gather relevant documentation, access logs, and transaction histories and preserve their provenance.
Base the investigative outcome mainly on the alert rationale, using interviews only to confirm a preselected hypothesis.
questions.explanation: The guide describes an investigative process of evidence gathering, interviews, and analysis. Alert generation and payment intervention may occur early, but they do not replace a reasoned evidential conclusion. Give fraud operations complete ownership of a large incident and involve legal and communications only after public scrutiny begins.
Put all operational and legal responsibilities on a single junior analyst.
Set escalation and coordination points so teams share verified information and avoid conflicting actions.

options: Authorization-time monitoring enables immediate interdiction, while batch analysis can investigate patterns across completed transactions; they serve complementary purposes.
Batch analysis is suitable for immediate authorization decisions because all daily payments are reviewed together.
A real-time engine has no value once a transaction settles, while a batch process cannot identify coordinated activity.
Both operate on an identical decision timeline and differ primarily in which technology vendor supplies them.

Assume effective controls for one product establish adequate protection for all channels.

Apply retail transaction thresholds without testing whether they fit treasury activity.

Implement a new preventive control based on an audit finding but defer its operating test until the next annual risk assessment.
Omit operating tests because the risk assessment has already been completed.
Set controls before identifying the process in which fraud can occur.
questions.explanation: The guide describes assessment-led control design and subsequent validation. A product purchase is not equivalent to a tested reduction in the identified risk. Discard all unusual observations because extreme values always indicate malicious rather than erroneous activity.
Apply completeness, format, range and consistency checks with traceable corrections before analysis or scoring.
Move the errors to the reporting layer so the model can use uncorrected inputs for training and production.

Use the test team’s commercial contract as sufficient authority to bypass all customer privacy and data-security rules.
Permit unrestricted attack attempts because identifying a weakness is inherently lawful when the stated purpose is fraud prevention.

Improve data coverage where appropriate, consider fairness-aware model methods, and continue measuring differential outcomes.
Discard the underrepresented group’s transactions from model evaluation to restore the historic aggregate accuracy.
Treat all group-level error differences as evidence that the transactions were fraudulent in that segment.

options: Design a risk-based use case with measurable mitigation and customer objectives, involve IT and other impacted functions, and assess build-versus-buy and integration needs.
Purchase a limited license immediately and define responsibilities after deployment to avoid delaying a promising control.
Use the vendor’s accuracy demonstration as the decision metric and defer financial or legal review to contracting.
Prioritize the option with the lowest subscription fee because integration choices are operational concerns outside fraud risk management.
questions.explanation: The guide calls for clear use cases and outcomes, return-on-investment evaluation, stakeholder involvement and attention to integration and in-house-versus-vendor options before making portfolio decisions.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS Study Guide v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program · Best practices for setting up an anti-fraud technology portfolio
questions.sourceSection: Best practices for setting up an anti-fraud technology portfolio

questions.topic: Fraud risk management program review process
questions.stem: A program has completed its annual fraud review, but emerging scams, investigative findings, and control failures are not reflected in the action plan. Select TWO necessary follow-up steps.
options: Use only training attendance as proof of enterprise risk reduction.
Feed new threat intelligence and incident root causes into reassessed risks and revised control priorities.
Exclude failed controls from the report to keep assurance ratings stable.
Conduct another annual review but leave newly identified control failures outside the approved roadmap until the next cycle.
Track accountable remediation, milestones, and performance after the review rather than treating its publication as completion.
questions.explanation: The guide expects regular program review to incorporate performance, emerging threats, and compliance changes. Findings must cause measured action; a static annual report does not demonstrate improvement. The strongest competing approach falls short because ignoring new findings until the next cycle undermines the guide's emphasis on continuous adjustment.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS Study Guide v1.03 · Domain 1 · Fraud risk management program review process
questions.sourceSection: Fraud risk management program review process

questions.topic: Card-not-present fraud (Case example: Missed delivery text scam)
questions.stem: Susan enters debit-card details after a convincing missed-delivery text and later suffers remote unauthorized purchases. Select TWO points that distinguish this CNP scam from a genuine parcel interaction.
options: A customer who followed the message must have intended the subsequent purchases.
The resulting remote card transactions can occur without the physical card, so authorization evidence should be assessed separately from the message.
The message exploits delivery urgency to harvest payment credentials rather than simply confirm shipment details.
The absence of a physical card means the later payments cannot be fraudulent.
Focus on validating the delivery text rather than independently examining authorization evidence for the later card transactions.
questions.explanation: The guide's missed-delivery case combines smishing and card-not-present misuse. Plausible messaging and victim participation in a preliminary interaction do not validate later unauthorized card transactions. The strongest competing approach falls short because the original phishing text and subsequent unauthorized card purchases require distinct evidence and control assessment.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS Study Guide v1.03 · Domain 3 · Card-not-present fraud (Case example: Missed delivery text scam)
questions.sourceSection: Card-not-present fraud (Case example: Missed delivery text scam)

questions.stem: A bank updates a fraud rule after a confirmed scam and then sees fewer claims. Investigators still report new variants, while legitimate customer declines are rising. Management wants to declare the corrective action complete. What should the feedback loop require?
options: Increase the rule’s coverage universally without measuring false positives, customer impact or new scam patterns.
Leave the rule unchanged because the original targeted scam has declined, regardless of emerging fraud variants.
Use only a one-time post-incident presentation, as continuous evidence collection would contradict case closure.
Feed confirmed outcomes and operational effects back into risk assessment and detection controls, with measured revisions to the rule.
questions.explanation: The guide positions investigation findings and fraud outcomes as inputs to continuing control and process improvement.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS Study Guide v1.03 · Domain 3 · Fraud feedback loop
questions.sourceSection: Fraud feedback loop

questions.topic: Legal and ethical considerations in fraud investigations
questions.stem: An investigator is offered confidential account records by an external institution without any stated authority for the disclosure. Select TWO appropriate ethical and legal safeguards.
options: Alter original evidence to conceal how it was obtained.
Verify the legal basis, permissions, and necessity for receiving and using the material.
Publish the records to crowdsource a suspect's identity.
Preserve provenance and restrict access to relevant authorized investigators while recording evidential handling.
Use externally supplied confidential data immediately but investigate whether the disclosure was lawful only when the case closes.
questions.explanation: The guide stresses lawful, objective investigations and proper management of external information. Evidence may be relevant but cannot be used indiscriminately without authority, provenance, and confidentiality controls. The strongest competing approach falls short because the relevance of information does not override requirements for lawful acquisition and controlled handling.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS Study Guide v1.03 · Domain 3 · Legal and ethical considerations in fraud investigations
questions.sourceSection: Legal and ethical considerations in fraud investigations
questions.questionObjective: unt records by an external institution without any stated authority for the disclosure. Select TWO appropriate ethical and legal safeguards.

questions.stem: An investigator becomes convinced the customer fabricated a claim after noticing one inconsistent timestamp, and stops seeking evidence that could support an account compromise. Select TWO behaviors that better reflect an investigative mindset.
options: Seek additional material supporting the initial fraud allegation while excluding contradictory authentication or witness evidence.
Discard information inconsistent with the preferred explanation.
Adopt a confrontational interview solely to secure agreement with the working hypothesis.
Document contradictions, limitations, and why the accumulated evidence supports the final disposition.
Maintain healthy skepticism and test alternative hypotheses against independently obtained records.
questions.explanation: The guide describes curiosity, analytical thinking, and systematic evidence evaluation. A single discrepancy should prompt corroboration rather than confirmation bias; defensible closure explains both supporting and contrary evidence. The strongest competing approach falls short because selectively collecting only confirming material makes an apparently complete conclusion unreliable.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS Study Guide v1.03 · Domain 3 · Implementing a fraud investigative mindset
questions.sourceSection: Implementing a fraud investigative mindset
questions.questionObjective: amp, and stops seeking evidence that could support an account compromise. Select TWO behaviors that better reflect an investigative mindset.

questions.stem: Three separate investigations reveal that fraudsters exploited the same beneficiary-amendment weakness, although each customer was reimbursed and each case was administratively closed. The fraud team shares a spreadsheet of incidents with analytics and risk management, but six months later the weakness persists. Which TWO changes would most effectively complete the fraud feedback loop?
options: Convert recurring case findings into owned control changes with measurable expected outcomes and review dates.
Have analytics, investigations and risk teams share results and test whether the changes reduce the observed problem.
Circulate the completed case spreadsheet more widely and consider the exercise finished once all recipients acknowledge it.
Use the number of closed cases as evidence that the preventive control now operates effectively.
Defer the control update until a single incident causes enough loss to exceed the organization’s annual threshold.
questions.explanation: The guide describes feedback pillars translating case evidence into defined, measurable corrective improvements, with ongoing evaluation by analytics, investigations and risk management.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS Study Guide v1.03 · Fraud Investigations · Fraud feedback loop

questions.topic: Challenges and limitations of fraud detection techniques
questions.stem: A small institution cannot afford every detection technology, and its static rules are missing a fast-changing new scam. Which response best addresses the guide's limitations of fraud detection?
options: Buy every new analytics product without examining affordability or integration.
Keep current rules unchanged because modifying them might affect historical performance comparisons.
Prioritize controls for material risk, supplement static rules with appropriate monitoring or intelligence, and periodically evaluate evolving patterns and resource trade-offs.
Prioritize a more sophisticated detection vendor without assessing cost, existing controls, and the threat's demonstrated evolution.
questions.explanation: The guide identifies cost, resources, and evolving tactics as limitations. A risk-based combination of feasible tools and ongoing reassessment is stronger than abandonment, uncontrolled spending, or a permanently frozen system. The strongest competing approach falls short because technology complexity is not evidence of better cost-effective risk mitigation against the institution's evolving threats.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS Study Guide v1.03 · Domain 2 · Challenges and limitations of fraud detection techniques

questions.topic: Using identity proofing as a key fraud control (Case example: SoFi)
questions.stem: A fintech expands its online account-opening volume rapidly. Its identity proofing permits accounts to be opened using insufficiently verified information and the business cites growth as proof of success. Select TWO measures or conclusions that address the evidence most defensibly.
options: Identity verification quality needs effective controls, testing and ongoing monitoring; growth or throughput cannot substitute for reliable proofing.
Account-opening anomalies should be treated only as marketing data because post-onboarding transaction monitoring can replace identity verification.
A successful onboarding completion rate establishes that the applicant is genuine without further identification or verification checks.
Weak customer identification is acceptable if the institution promises to review suspicious accounts after their first loss event.
Apply quality assurance and audit to account-opening controls rather than treating conversion metrics as evidence of compliance.
questions.explanation: The guide’s SoFi example describes weaknesses in identity proofing and a regulatory penalty, emphasizing preventive verification and monitoring. Apply quality assurance and audit to account-opening controls rather than treating conversion metrics as evidence of compliance.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS Study Guide v1.03 · Domain 2 · Using identity proofing as a key fraud control (Case example: SoFi)

title: Fraud Risk Strategy & Detection Challenges · Form D
name: Fraud Risk Strategy & Detection Challenges · Form D
subtitle: Advanced cross-domain · Form D

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The committee pack contains three competing indicators: a flat historical fraud-loss series, a material increase in external industry warnings, and a decline in digital customer complaints that management interpreted as improved satisfaction. Nobody tested whether complaints were being coded consistently. The proposed biometric tool has impressive vendor benchmarks but no institution-specific pilot, and operational resilience is already an active board concern.

A regional bank historically experiences almost no mobile-account takeover losses. Its head of fraud presents intelligence about coordinated smishing campaigns in neighboring institutions and asks for a major biometric investment immediately. Finance points to a committed core-banking upgrade and the chief executive says there is no evidence the bank has been targeted. A week later, a limited test reveals previously unrecognized mule-linked instant payments. The fraud head wants approval before another attack; IT warns that deploying the proposed product without integration testing may itself disrupt payments. The board asks what should have governed the competing investment decisions before any incident became public. Which response best accords with the study guide?
options: Temporarily suspend the exposed channel until fraud losses demonstrate the precise investment requirement.
Authorize the proposed control now on the basis of external threat intelligence, then retrospectively document budget impacts.
Replace the enterprise assessment with a vendor-provided peer benchmark to accelerate approval.
Reassess enterprise fraud exposure, residual risks, and priorities, then choose proportionate controls with implementation testing.
questions.explanation: The guide’s smishing case favors reevaluating budget priorities on the basis of a refreshed enterprise-wide risk assessment, not automatic spending, blanket product withdrawal, or vendor delegation.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Introduction to Fraud Risk Management
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Introduction to Fraud Risk Management

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The fraud taxonomy used by the payments department was written before synthetic identities became prominent. Analysts have been allocating cases based primarily on whose account carried the payment rather than who provided the information or knowingly participated. Several individual transactions touch more than one participant, and the dispute team wants a scheme label that is stable even after a recovery outcome changes.

An investigator is reviewing four superficially similar events after the quarter-end fraud committee questions inconsistencies in loss reporting. A borrower uses genuine identification but falsifies income and plans never to repay; a separate borrower uses a fabricated persona combining genuine and invented identifiers; a legitimate account owner knowingly receives stolen funds on another person’s instructions for a commission; and an unrelated hacker steals a customer’s credentials and initiates withdrawals. The committee suggests categorizing every event involving a bank account as third-party fraud because the institution is the ultimate loser. Under the guide’s expressly stated fraud categories, which statements are supported? Select THREE.
options: The knowingly participating account owner exemplifies second-party fraud.
The unrelated hacker’s account takeover exemplifies third-party fraud.
The synthetic identity must be classified only as third-party fraud because some identity data are invented.
A real-account mule is necessarily an innocent third-party victim.
The borrower intentionally misrepresenting earnings exemplifies first-party fraud.
questions.explanation: The guide categorizes deliberate misrepresentation and synthetic fraud as first-party, knowing collaboration/muling as second-party, and unrelated account takeover as third-party. Classification turns on participation and relationship, not merely which account moves money.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Types of Fraud, pp. 13–15
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Types of Fraud, pp. 13–15

questions.stem: A senior procurement employee receives threatening debt collection calls, controls supplier master data, and explains a questionable vendor payment by saying, “I was merely borrowing what the company owed me for years of unpaid overtime.” Internal audit finds that the employee was allowed to add new vendors and authorize disbursements without an independent check. The company wants to modify one component of the fraud triangle through a direct control intervention, while acknowledging that psychological drivers may persist. What is the MOST direct effect of implementing independent vendor verification and separate payment approval?
options: Reduce rationalization primarily by requiring an annual fraud-code attestation before vendors are created.
Reduce pressure by referring the employee to a voluntary financial-wellness assistance program.
Reduce opportunity only if the approval changes are accompanied by a criminal conviction.
Reduce opportunity by limiting unilateral access and decision rights.
questions.explanation: Segregation and independent verification primarily reduce the opportunity element. Debt relates to pressure; self-justification is rationalization. A control change alone does not prove intent.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Fraud Triangle, p. 9
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Fraud Triangle, p. 9

questions.stem: The fraud strategy unit owns production rules and produces weekly detection performance packs. Compliance challenges whether loss appetite has been exceeded, creates the fraud policy and reviews regulatory implications. Internal audit independently selects alert cases, verifies whether investigators followed approved procedures and recommends corrective actions. An executive argues that audit should own daily rule tuning because it detected problems; the strategy team argues that compliance should independently approve every transaction. Which assignment is MOST consistent with the guide, allowing for variation in local organizational structures?
options: First line operates detection and response; second line oversees policy/risk; third line independently assures.
First line audits its own monitoring; second line processes suspicious payments; third line drafts operating procedures.
Second line must own all frontline rule-tuning; first line exclusively conducts independent assurance.
Third line performs day-to-day case resolution while the other two lines only attend governance committees.
questions.explanation: The guide places fraud operations, analytics, and strategy commonly in the first line, oversight/policy in the second, and independent assurance in the third, while recognizing organizational variation.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Fraud Risk Management Framework, pp. 32–38
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Fraud Risk Management Framework, pp. 32–38

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The previous assessment reports were produced ahead of regulatory examinations and never updated after new services launched. Separate AML and fraud assessments apply different definitions of a mule, while the payments division has no documented owner for emerging channel risks. A recent consumer-complaint review suggests that the recorded loss series may understate potential exposure to manipulated authorized payments.

A multinational payments institution prepares its annual fraud assessment by copying last year’s retail risks and drawing a heat map exclusively from actual confirmed fraud losses. It omits the recently launched business payments product, a supplier with privileged IT access, customer complaints about manipulation, and potential collusion between staff and vendors. The assessment is signed by the product owner alone, because internal audit has never detected fraud in that division. The board asks what should be strengthened to make the exercise enterprise-wide, defensible and responsive to changing exposure. Select THREE.
options: Limit scope to previously confirmed losses because prospective scenarios cannot be evidenced.
Obtain inputs from different functions and lines of defense, with appropriate independent validation and board involvement.
Assume no relevant risk exists in any unit that passed a prior financial statement audit.
Include inherent risk, effectiveness of controls, and residual exposure across relevant fraud taxonomies.
Use feedback from emerging typologies, complaints, new products, and risks involving insiders or vendors.
questions.explanation: An effective assessment covers risks before and after mitigation, relevant internal and external channels, stakeholder participation, independent audit validation, and ongoing feedback; past loss alone is insufficient.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Risk Assessment, pp. 39–43
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Risk Assessment, pp. 39–43

questions.stem: A fintech experiences one low-value confirmed merchant impersonation loss after implementing proportionate preventative controls. It remains below its documented fraud loss appetite, but the first-line manager says residual risk therefore requires no further monitoring, reporting or review until a breach of appetite is recorded. This conclusion is aligned with the guide’s risk-based approach.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Staying within appetite is not permission to stop monitoring or learning. The framework calls for ongoing control testing, reporting, updated assessments, and response to emerging threats.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Framework and Continuous Improvement
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Framework and Continuous Improvement

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The override was introduced as a temporary business-continuity exception six months earlier and has since become routine practice. Two recent reconciliations found unapproved disbursement adjustments, but neither has yet been established as criminal. The business line owner objects that upgrading the maker-checker workflow would reduce loan turnaround time, and finance can fund only one material remediation during the quarter.

A consumer lender’s RCSA identifies four risks: a likely low-impact clerical refund error; a moderately likely, high-impact internal disbursement override; an extremely unlikely website cosmetic glitch; and a previously mitigated chargeback issue with only minor residual exposure. A manager argues the team should address whichever risk has produced the most alerts, regardless of severity or effectiveness of controls. Staff have supplied credible workflow evidence showing the disbursement override can circumvent dual authorization. Which risk-based decision should come first?
options: Prioritize the most common minor refund failure first because frequency always outweighs financial severity.
Treat the override as mitigated by general KYE checks unless a loss is already confirmed.
Prioritize the low-probability website issue solely because uncertain probabilities are difficult to quantify.
Record and prioritize the override based on likelihood, impact, controls and residual exposure, with a tracked action plan.
questions.explanation: RCSA evaluates likelihood, impact, existing-control effectiveness and critical residual exposure, then plans actions with ownership and timelines.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Line of Business RCSA, pp. 42–43
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Line of Business RCSA, pp. 42–43

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The policy document received the highest mark in a desktop compliance assessment. Yet the test population was selected from routine invoices, not the urgent changes that occurred on the incident date. Both approvers completed annual ethics training, and the vendor portal displayed a “verified” badge despite no independent confirmation of the altered account. Management now must distinguish a control existing on paper from functioning against realistic abuse.

Following a vendor-payment diversion, executives proudly present evidence that their policy requires two signatories and automated validation against the vendor master record. The investigation finds both signatories approved a last-minute bank-detail change without independent confirmation; the automated rule did not flag small changes; and a senior employee was permitted to override the alert with no second-level review. The chief risk officer needs control assurance beyond a screenshot of the policy manual. Which approaches appropriately test or repair the weaknesses? Select THREE.
options: Apply independent third-party validation and strengthen controls based on test failures.
Remove transaction monitoring because preventive approval is sufficient.
Treat documented approval rules as proof that the controls worked in all actual transactions.
Simulate manipulated invoices and vendor bank-detail changes to test detection and approvals.
Test exception and override paths, including collusion scenarios and small discrepancies.
questions.explanation: The guide’s mystery-shopper-style control test specifically probes minor discrepancies, bypass/collusion and dual approvals; failed tests require multilayer improvements and independent validation.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Fraud Control Tests, pp. 66–67
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Fraud Control Tests, pp. 66–67

questions.stem: An insurance company discovers that an external repair vendor intentionally inflated invoices. A staff adjuster approved those bills while secretly receiving payments from the vendor. The vendor supplied falsified work orders, and the staff member used insider permissions to waive discrepancies. At a governance meeting, a director argues this is solely external fraud because the vendor created the invoices. Another says it is exclusively first-party fraud because the company processed the payments. What assessment best recognizes the actual threat?
options: Only accidental operational loss because the vendor was contractually approved.
Only first-party customer fraud because the company was the payer.
An external fraud with a possible internal collusion/insider fraud component requiring both vendor and employee controls.
A case that must be excluded from fraud reporting until criminal charges are secured.
questions.explanation: Fraud can involve an external vendor and an insider in collusion. Investigating vendor integrity, employee permissions, conflicts and failed approvals addresses both risk sources.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Internal vs External Fraud, pp. 10–12
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Internal vs External Fraud, pp. 10–12

questions.stem: A digital bank invests in sophisticated document validation and identity checks when customers open accounts, then never reviews profile changes. Fraud teams observe successful takeover attempts shortly after phone-number resets and new-beneficiary creation; several former accounts closed for confirmed fraud are later reopened under the same identity. The bank’s onboarding model nevertheless retains a high accuracy score. The board wants the single most complete improvement, rather than another opening-stage check. Which approach is strongest?
options: Apply risk-based controls at onboarding, during account maintenance and payment activity, and when exiting and restricting reentry.
Rely on origination scoring because a verified document remains reliable throughout account life.
Eliminate exit controls to avoid customer-service friction.
Conduct identity validation only after a confirmed payment loss.
questions.explanation: Fraud mitigation follows the entire relationship, from origination through transaction and profile-change monitoring to exit/reentry protections.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Fraud Mitigation Life Cycle, pp. 57–58
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Fraud Mitigation Life Cycle, pp. 57–58

questions.stem: A firm experiences losses from an employee deliberately modifying vendor details for personal gain and losses from a power outage that interrupts payments. Its risk report labels both incidents as operational risks, but separates the intentional deception as operational fraud risk. Under the guide, this distinction is conceptually appropriate even though both incidents can disrupt operations.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Fraud risk belongs within operational risk, but requires intentional deception; an accidental outage is not itself fraud.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Operational Processes Fraud Risk, pp. 16, 46
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Operational Processes Fraud Risk, pp. 16, 46

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The loan origination team has legitimate evidence that the borrower passed identity proofing at application. Collections notes show no hardship notice before the sudden default. Customer-service records also show an otherwise ordinary sequence of limit requests. A prior review incorrectly treated every unpaid balance as fraud, so the investigator has been instructed to distinguish subsequent inability to pay from a preconceived intention not to repay.

A borrower submits genuine identification and verifiable employment documents, initially uses a small credit limit, and makes timely repayments for nine months. Following a series of requested limit increases, they rapidly exhaust multiple lines and cease all payments. Archived messages obtained later show this pattern was planned at onboarding. The fraud analyst initially classifies it as account takeover because the loss was abrupt and authentication had been successful. Which category BEST explains the scheme?
options: Third-party account takeover because limits increased rapidly.
Unintentional money muling because repayments established good faith.
First-party bust-out within origination/transaction fraud despite genuine identifying information.
Only credit risk, since no one fabricated a document or stole credentials.
questions.explanation: Bust-out uses one’s own identity, builds apparently good payment history and then exhausts credit without intent to repay. Lack of identity theft does not exclude first-party fraud.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Origination Fraud, pp. 45–48
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Origination Fraud, pp. 45–48

questions.stem: The fraud team is assessing a newly introduced international peer-to-peer transfer service. Some users are mismatched against their purported residence jurisdictions; other users make unusually rapid, high-value transfers using unfamiliar devices; and the service is accessible through web, telephone and mobile channels. A senior analyst proposes classifying everything under a single “customer risk” heading to simplify management reports. Which distinct risk dimensions should remain visible? Select FOUR.
options: Product risk arising from the payment instrument and how it can be abused.
Customer risk arising from intentional customer misuse or misrepresentation.
Jurisdiction risk where documents and activity do not align with claimed residence or operation.
Channel risk arising from different entry points and their specific attack surfaces.
Only the institution’s stock-price volatility, because fraud is merely an investment risk.
questions.explanation: The guide identifies the four transaction-fraud dimensions as customer, jurisdiction, product and channel. Each informs targeted control design.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Transactional Fraud Risk, pp. 44–45
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Transactional Fraud Risk, pp. 44–45

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The outsourced provider handles both production support and a weekly export of account reconciliation files. Procurement regards corporate registration as the critical onboarding requirement, while information security focuses on privileged access. Human resources previously identified no concern during the employee’s hiring checks. The risk committee wants to know whether the original process and the subsequent relationship monitoring adequately address different but potentially interacting sources of risk.

A payments processor onboards an outsourced IT provider with access to sensitive infrastructure. Due diligence checks the vendor’s corporate registration and sanctions only; it does not verify personnel, data security, or conflicts with staff. Months later the processor learns that an employee has an unusually close relationship with the vendor’s director and the vendor’s subcontractor has copied client data. The vendor argues that its initial legal registration automatically satisfies anti-fraud expectations. Which corrective program best follows the guide?
options: Transfer all compliance responsibilities to procurement without consulting IT or fraud teams.
Treat licensing as sufficient and investigate only the individual employee if loss is proven.
Combine ongoing KYE/KYV due diligence, screening relevant principals/personnel, cybersecurity checks and monitoring throughout the relationship.
Screen only customers because employee and vendor risk is unrelated to financial crime.
questions.explanation: KYE and KYV extend past onboarding and include relevant checks on staff, directors, cyber access, conflicts and relationship monitoring.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Know Your Employee and Vendor, p. 61
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Know Your Employee and Vendor, p. 61

questions.stem: A retailer’s online sales triple during a holiday promotion. To protect checkout conversion, the fraud director suspends all high-velocity alerts for the entire period without testing any alternative or monitoring claim trends. The director states that the guide recommends reducing detection sensitivity whenever legitimate seasonal volume rises sharply.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The guide cautions that relaxing rules during seasonal peaks can cause more fraud; targeted, adaptive mitigation should balance security with service quality.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Seasonal Fraud Risk, p. 47
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Seasonal Fraud Risk, p. 47

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The payments business reports that losses fell most sharply among new customers, but its measure of successful checkout considers only attempts that progressed beyond the new-device check. Product staff calculate a different conversion measure including customers who abandoned checkout at the challenge stage. The fraud team also finds that several false-positive appeals were approved only after merchants lost the sale. Neither the loss figure nor the complaint count alone captures all effects.

A credit card issuer implements an aggressive rule rejecting every first purchase on a new device. Confirmed fraud losses fall but genuine customer declines surge; call-center wait times double, and many longtime cardholders stop using the card. The fraud strategy lead proposes removing the rule entirely; the operations lead proposes keeping it indefinitely because loss is lower. The board wants an intervention supported by the guide’s view of effectiveness. Which decision is best?
options: Replace new-device checks with a single static amount threshold to improve consistency.
Retune thresholds and add appropriate authentication or step-up review, measuring both residual fraud and legitimate-customer friction.
Retain the rule until confirmed fraud losses return to baseline, then address legitimate declines separately.
Exclude abandoned transactions from the customer-impact metric because those payments were not completed.
questions.explanation: Fraud controls must be monitored for overrestriction and underrestriction. Excessive false positives and customer impact must be weighed against losses.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Developing Fraud Controls, pp. 58–59
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Developing Fraud Controls, pp. 58–59

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The dashboard's author explains that the data warehouse contains gross losses, attempted values and claims in different feeds. Some fraud cases were recovered after initial booking, and the customer-service team measures attrition separately. The audit remediation tracker resides outside the fraud reporting environment. The board does not ask that every raw transaction be reproduced; it asks for an intelligible risk picture with reconciled definitions and explicit changes in controls.

A board risk committee receives a monthly dashboard showing only total gross fraud loss. The chair asks why customer reimbursements are rising, whether new merchant fraud is confined to one channel, why a suspicious rule was deactivated, and whether an audit finding is closed. Fraud operations says these details are “too operational” for the governance pack. Which enhancements are consistent with fraud-program oversight? Select THREE.
options: Include customer effects, retention/reimbursement indicators and emerging risks where material.
Report fraud exposure, confirmed losses, trends and meaningful channel or product breakdowns.
Show control quality, audit gaps, remediation status and changes to the risk landscape.
Suppress material control weaknesses until an external regulator requests them.
Treat reporting as a substitute for independent control testing.
questions.explanation: The guide emphasizes transparent governance, fraud KPIs, audit remediation and communication of material trends to leadership, including customer effects.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Governance and Reporting, pp. 63–65
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Governance and Reporting, pp. 63–65

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The demonstration dataset resembles a large overseas issuer rather than the bank’s own customer mix. Fraud investigators have not agreed how scores map to holds, recalls or manual investigation. The vendor promises quick integration through an API but has not shared performance dependencies. A governance reviewer also notes that a biometric flag that is not accessible until after authorization may add little preventive value, even if its offline prediction score is strong.

A vendor demonstrates a powerful AI monitoring engine that produces visually convincing risk scores. A bank wants it in production within 10 days, but no one has defined the use case, how alerts will be actioned, data access needs, expected customer benefits, or whether legacy payment systems support interdiction. Finance assumes the annual subscription price proves return on investment; legal has not reviewed location-data consent. What should fraud leadership do BEFORE committing to the platform?
options: Procure the platform on condition that full device-location consent and legal analysis are completed before renewal.
Run a limited live pilot immediately and develop the business case after reviewing its production fraud score.
Use the vendor’s independent certification as a substitute for assessing local architecture and workflow.
Construct a use case, benefits/ROI and implementation requirements with IT, legal, finance, operations, compliance and relevant vendor assessment.
questions.explanation: Technology selection should be driven by a documented use case, ROI, stakeholder coordination, integration considerations and vendor due diligence.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Anti-Fraud Technology Portfolio, pp. 72–73
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Anti-Fraud Technology Portfolio, pp. 72–73

questions.stem:
Case-file context. Call-center agents are already receiving inconsistent guidance about whether affected customers should reset credentials or wait for the technical incident team. The payments processor and the outsourced notification vendor each claim that the other should contact the bank. Meanwhile, a routine logging job is approaching its overwrite window. Executives want rapid containment but recognize that evidence and communications must remain credible for later regulatory and internal review.

A small bank detects a large-volume overnight credential compromise. Fraud operations has hundreds of alerts; media calls are arriving; some accounts may require restrictions; and technical staff fear that altering the environment will overwrite evidence. A manager proposes having each department respond informally via personal messages, explaining that written protocols slow containment. Under the guide, which incident-response features are important? Select THREE.
options: Clear internal and external communication chains coordinated through assigned leadership.
Automatic public disclosure of every unverified suspect’s name without legal review.
Postponement of all documentation until the crisis has fully ended.
Defined triggers, task owners, time frames and protected evidence-handling actions.
Cross-functional actions involving fraud, cybersecurity, IT, legal, communications and other relevant teams.
questions.explanation: The response plan establishes responsibilities, timing, communications, evidence preservation and a coordinated cross-functional response, rather than untracked improvisation.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Fraud Response Plan, pp. 88–92
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Fraud Response Plan, pp. 88–92

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The customer paid from a registered mobile phone at their ordinary home location. Device intelligence therefore rated the login low risk, and the ordinary transaction authentication recorded no anomaly. The beneficiary account, however, had been added shortly before the request, and the supplier later produced its genuine invoice showing different account details. The review team must consider whether normal authentication answers the distinct question of deceptive persuasion.

A customer receives an apparently authentic message from a long-standing supplier instructing payment to changed bank details. The customer logs into the genuine banking app, passes strong authentication and deliberately authorizes the transfer. The customer later discovers the supplier was impersonated. An investigator argues that because authentication was successful there was no fraud and the case should be closed. Which interpretation is most accurate under the guide?
options: It cannot be investigated unless the bank’s application itself has been breached.
This can be authorized push payment fraud: the genuine user authorized a transfer under deception, requiring a different control strategy from unauthorized takeover.
It is always unauthorized account takeover because the beneficiary is fraudulent.
This is necessarily first-party chargeback abuse because the user entered a password.
questions.explanation: APP scams induce a real customer to authorize a payment; strong authentication alone does not prevent manipulation. Behavioral tools and customer education can be more relevant.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Fraud Risk Management Process, pp. 36–37
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Fraud Risk Management Process, pp. 36–37

questions.stem: A global institution uses one fraud-case closure deadline for every country and disregards local consumer-protection timelines. It argues that consistency with a stricter internal standard in its home market is necessarily sufficient to meet all local reporting, provisional credit and closure obligations. This is an appropriate interpretation of the guide.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The guide expressly cautions that case resolution, reimbursement, reporting and closure requirements vary by jurisdiction and circumstances.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Fraud Remediation, pp. 93–94
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Fraud Remediation, pp. 93–94

questions.stem: Internal assurance runs a controlled vendor-invoice test: an authorized employee substitutes an account number that differs in just two digits, signs off with a second approver, and sends the payment through the normal workflow. The automated rule does not flag the difference; the payment reaches the wrong account. Operations argues dual authorization worked because there were two logins, so the test passed. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The only remediation is to increase payment thresholds so fewer invoices are checked.
The exercise is not a control test because it used a synthetic invoice rather than a genuine customer payment.
The control failed substantively; authorization count alone does not show that bank-detail discrepancies were identified or challenged.
The test passed because any second approval eliminates the possibility of collusion or error.
questions.explanation: The guide’s example explicitly treats failure to detect minor invoice discrepancies as a failed test despite a dual-approval control.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Fraud Control Tests, pp. 66–67
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Fraud Control Tests, pp. 66–67

questions.stem:
Case-file context. Operations had a service-level target to close 95% of disputes within two working days. Cases with no immediate recovery prospect were moved into a simplified closure stream. The case-management tool allowed free-text conclusions without attaching evidence or recording the customer interview. The audit sample includes cases from different investigators, suggesting that the issue may lie in the process rather than one individual’s judgment.

After a fraudulent transaction dispute, a bank’s fraud analyst identifies the recipient account but fails to preserve customer communications, interview the account holder or document whether an identity change preceded the payment. The case is closed as “unable to recover.” A later audit discovers the same vulnerability in several cases, and the bank argues recovery failure meant the investigation had no learning value. Which activities support the guide’s investigative purpose? Select THREE.
options: Gather transaction records, communications and relevant internal account data promptly.
Interview appropriate parties and analyze evidence to determine what happened.
Record the control failures and use lessons learned to strengthen prevention and detection.
Assume that inability to recover funds proves no fraud occurred.
Exclude investigation files from quality and audit review once any customer is reimbursed.
questions.explanation: Fraud investigations establish whether fraud occurred and identify improvements. Evidence collection, interviews, analysis, root cause and auditability matter even without recovery.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Conducting Investigations, pp. 77–83
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Conducting Investigations, pp. 77–83

questions.stem: A customer reports electronic payment fraud and the institution grants provisional credit while investigating. Additional forensic evidence eventually shows the transaction was genuinely authorized for a legitimate purchase, after which the customer receives a reasoned explanation. Another manager claims any provisional credit automatically becomes permanent and cannot be reconsidered. According to the guide’s description of remediation, what may the bank appropriately do, subject to applicable law and policy?
options: Automatically treat the claim as criminal fraud irrespective of the evidence.
Communicate the case result and potentially reverse the provisional credit if the finding is not in the customer’s favor.
Avoid issuing a decision because provisional credit replaces investigation closure.
Extend the case indefinitely to avoid challenging the claim.
questions.explanation: The guide describes converting provisional credit to permanent when a claim succeeds, or re-debiting when a finding is adverse, with customer communication and applicable timeframes.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Fraud Case Closure, pp. 93–94
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Fraud Case Closure, pp. 93–94

questions.stem: A bank wants to improve detection of identity fraud using employee notes, customer photographs, device location, public social media, and a commercial data aggregator. A colleague proposes copying all customer files onto personal USB drives and transferring them across borders, arguing that fraud prevention overrides ordinary privacy conditions. The chief risk officer asks for the safeguards that follow the guide. Select THREE.
options: Apply need-to-know access, approved storage and appropriate retention/destruction policies.
Use relevant and reliable sources, corroborate investigative data, and follow ethical collection rules.
Assume every publicly searchable item is suitable for unrestricted republishing.
Consider consent and lawful gateways for location, sensitive data access and cross-border transfers.
Retain copied personal data indefinitely in unmanaged files to maximize future model training.
questions.explanation: Data collection for anti-fraud work remains subject to privacy, authorized access, retention, cross-border safeguards and lawful/ethical use of external sources.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Data Security and Investigation Sources, pp. 22, 79–80
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Data Security and Investigation Sources, pp. 22, 79–80

questions.stem: Three fraud-risk changes compete for budget. Risk A is frequent with minor, recoverable losses; Risk B is less frequent but could cause irreversible high-value payments and regulatory harm; Risk C has a large number of alerts but almost all are well-documented false positives. The board asks for a ranking that transparently accounts for more than raw volumes. Which approach is most defensible?
options: Assess likelihood, severity, detectability, customer harm, regulatory urgency, existing controls and risk appetite before prioritizing.
Automatically rank the risk with the highest number of complaints irrespective of impact.
Focus only on the risk that is easiest to automate because ease of delivery establishes materiality.
Rank A, then C, then B using alert frequency alone.
questions.explanation: The guide’s criteria include likelihood, frequency, loss severity, detectability, mandates, customer impact and the controls/risk-appetite context.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Fraud Risk Prioritization, pp. 65–66
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Fraud Risk Prioritization, pp. 65–66

questions.stem: A bank’s CEO is trusted and has personally signed the fraud policy. Risk management therefore exempts the CEO’s wire approvals from transaction limits and independent checks, asserting that executive accountability is an effective compensating control. Under the guide’s lessons from the Heartland Tri-State Bank case, this exemption is justified.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The guide stresses that anti-fraud policies and controls must apply to leadership too; trust and seniority do not replace controls.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Financial Stability Case Example, pp. 19–20
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Financial Stability Case Example, pp. 19–20

questions.stem: Following a costly claims-fraud incident, the CRO authorizes remedial actions. Operations reports that the new rules were installed, but there is no evidence of control testing, no owner for measuring impact, no assessment of new false positives and no periodic feedback to the risk committee. Audit plans a follow-up. Which components are necessary to establish genuine continuous improvement? Select THREE.
options: Measure control outcomes and fraud KPIs against predefined targets and risk appetite.
Declare effectiveness proven solely by implementation of a new system.
Complete independent assurance/testing and track corrective actions with accountable owners.
Close the action plan before determining whether new rules adversely affect customers.
Use fraud-incident analysis and new typologies to update risk assessments and control priorities.
questions.explanation: Implementation is not the same as effectiveness. The guide requires KPIs, assurance, feedback, lessons learned and risk-based adjustment.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Continuous Improvement, pp. 101–107
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Continuous Improvement, pp. 101–107

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The customer supplied a copy of the fraudulent invoice, a transfer confirmation and correspondence apparently from a longstanding trading partner. The recipient account is maintained in another jurisdiction and the funds may already have moved. The caller is worried about liquidity and demands an exact compensation date. Front-office staff have authority to register cases but not to decide complex cross-border reimbursement claims.

A customer approved a supplier invoice sent by a criminal, and funds travelled to a bank overseas. A branch employee promises the victim a full refund within an hour because the transfer is “clearly fraud.” The transfer may be difficult to recall and the bank has not yet established whether any reimbursement duty applies. In line with the guide’s goldsmith case, what is the most appropriate FIRST institutional action?
options: Escalate through the fraud department so investigators can establish facts, guide recovery efforts and apply legal/policy requirements.
Offer a conditional refund before establishing the factual or regulatory position to preserve confidence.
Direct the customer to law enforcement first, then open an internal case once a formal crime number exists.
Contact the overseas receiving institution directly before recording the incident in the fraud system.
questions.explanation: The goldsmith scenario says the relationship manager should initially involve the fraud department, rather than promise a refund or make unilateral external demands.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Fraud Response and Remediation, pp. 85–86
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Fraud Response and Remediation, pp. 85–86

questions.stem: A fraud ring tests stolen payment cards with tiny merchant transactions and then shifts to higher-value online transfers from linked accounts. The card team sees low-value anomalies; the banking team sees new beneficiaries; neither reports material aggregate loss. A director concludes there is no actionable fraud because each product remains below its individual trigger. How can the organization improve detection? Select THREE.
options: Centralize and correlate information from multiple products, channels and relevant teams.
Incorporate appropriate continuous monitoring and adapt rules to revealed fraud tactics.
Remove low-value test transactions from analytics because their monetary impact is immaterial.
Use analytics to identify relationships, anomalies and linked activity across product boundaries.
Require each product to investigate only its own isolated alerts, never sharing relevant observations.
questions.explanation: The guide advocates orchestrated cross-product data, correlation analysis, collaboration and continuously updated detection models.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Detecting Patterns Across Products, pp. 74–75
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Detecting Patterns Across Products, pp. 74–75

questions.stem: A firm operates mortgages, instant payments and wealth management. It maintains only a single enterprise label, “fraud,” and cannot explain which typologies drive losses or whether controls address different products. The risk committee proposes a more granular fraud taxonomy aligned with business offerings and geographic exposure. The guide regards this as a meaningful part of an effective risk framework.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. A tailored fraud taxonomy helps categorize exposures and match controls to fraud types, products, industries and geographies.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Framework, pp. 32–33
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Framework, pp. 32–33

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The payment service provider operates subsidiaries with different client agreements and case-management deadlines. Its incident dashboard identifies payments as either customer-initiated or technically unauthorized, but the taxonomy lacks a specific APP field. The legal team cautions that reimbursement and reporting obligations may turn on the location, type of payment, governing regime and facts, not simply the appearance of successful authentication.

A bank with UK and EU payment customers copies an American electronic-transfer policy into both markets. A UK customer manipulated into approving a fraudulent push payment complains that the team assessed only whether the transaction passed authentication. The legal adviser warns that the case may fall into a distinct APP reimbursement regime, not merely unauthorized payment rules. Which governance correction is best grounded in the guide?
options: Treat every authenticated payment as ineligible for any fraud review in every jurisdiction.
Use corporate preference rather than jurisdiction to determine all potential reimbursement obligations.
Assume a single global anti-fraud law displaces local payment regulations.
Map the fraud event to relevant regional payment and consumer rules and distinguish APP from unauthorized transaction cases.
questions.explanation: The guide distinguishes local frameworks and recognizes UK APP reimbursement requirements separately from unauthorized transaction reimbursement rules.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · UK Regulations, pp. 26–27
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · UK Regulations, pp. 26–27

questions.topic: Defining fraud risk appetite and loss
questions.stem: An institution’s loss appetite is expressed as a monetary threshold. During a fraud spike, gross attempted loss is high, most attempts are stopped, but confirmed net loss is relatively low. Meanwhile, customer complaints and reputational exposure increase sharply. A risk manager proposes reporting only net confirmed loss and ignoring attempted fraud and customer impact. Which statements align with the guide? Select THREE.
options: Because prevented attempts caused no net loss, they must never be monitored or reported.
Loss appetite is one important threshold but should be assessed alongside other risk indicators and customer consequences.
Prevention performance, fraud losses, and control effectiveness provide useful governance information.
The framework can track potential exposure, confirmed incidents, and organizational impact distinctly.
Compliance obligations disappear whenever the monetary loss appetite is not breached.
questions.explanation: The guide describes potential fraud, confirmed incidents, impacts, fraud appetite, risk indicators, and controls/KPIs; net loss alone cannot tell the whole risk story.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Fraud Framework and Governance, pp. 32–33, 63–65
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Fraud Framework and Governance, pp. 32–33, 63–65

questions.stem: A payroll analyst privately reports that a director appears to have approved repeated payments to a relative’s consultancy. The fraud team proposes emailing the complaint and reporter’s identity to everyone in the department to “invite perspectives.” The director offers to conduct the investigation personally because they understand the arrangements. No allegation is yet proven. Which response best protects both the process and the reporting program?
options: Place the director on an automatic prohibited-person list before evidence is tested.
Circulate the allegation to a limited group of reporting-line managers, including the subject, for immediate verification.
Ask the implicated director to provide a management-certified account before deciding whether independent review is needed.
Use protected whistleblower escalation and an impartial, confidential investigation with evidence-based conclusions.
questions.explanation: The guide emphasizes reporting channels, whistleblower protection, confidentiality and independent, fair review of suspected insider fraud.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Fraud Policies and Insider Risk, pp. 32–33, 62–63
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Fraud Policies and Insider Risk, pp. 32–33, 62–63

questions.stem: A large institution needs to understand an improbable but catastrophic payments-platform compromise, a recurring cluster of unusual beneficiary networks, and weaknesses in the end-to-end loan disbursement workflow. Management suggests using one annual employee survey for all three because it is inexpensive. What combinations of tools would be well matched to the questions? Select THREE.
options: Exclusively a customer satisfaction survey, because process and fraud vulnerabilities are identical.
Only historic total confirmed losses, because prospective techniques are speculative.
Process mapping for control handoffs, vulnerabilities and workflow weaknesses.
Scenario analysis for low-probability, high-severity events.
Data analytics or relationship analysis for recurring abnormal transactions and networks.
questions.explanation: The guide names scenario analysis, data analytics and process mapping for these different objectives; one tool rarely addresses all exposures.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Fraud Assessment Tools, pp. 41–42
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Fraud Assessment Tools, pp. 41–42

questions.stem: A bank outsources identity proofing to a reputable vendor. Three months later the vendor silently updates its algorithm; approvals rise but downstream synthetic identity losses increase. Procurement says the outsourcing contract shifts control responsibility entirely away from the bank. Fraud analytics wants to review the change log and recalibrate verification steps. Which approach best reflects the guide?
options: Eliminate onboarding due diligence because new models are always more accurate.
Restrict all assessments to the annual financial-statement audit.
Maintain vendor-performance oversight, assess technology changes against risk and strengthen controls when new products or risks emerge.
Accept the supplier’s assurances because vendor technology is beyond internal monitoring.
questions.explanation: Fraud vendor management covers performance monitoring and response to vendor changes, while the institution must evaluate its actual risk and control results.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Best Practices for Fraud Management, p. 35
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Best Practices for Fraud Management, p. 35

questions.stem: After a customer makes three unusual withdrawals, an investigator classifies them as confirmed intentional fraud without speaking to the customer or checking activity context, because rule-based alerts are proof of criminal deception. The guide supports using a detection alert alone as conclusive evidence of fraud.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Alerts indicate suspicion and require examination; investigations evaluate evidence, interview parties and analyze context before reaching a conclusion.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Investigations, pp. 77–78
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Investigations, pp. 77–78

questions.stem: A diversified banking group has identified 18 fraud-control weaknesses. IT wants to implement the easiest fixes first; finance favors the lowest-cost initiatives; and risk management worries about three issues with high residual loss potential. Some fixes require policy changes, vendor coordination and staff retraining. Which roadmap design is strongest?
options: Schedule by whichever department has spare staff without identifying risk priorities.
Set a risk-based, sequenced plan tied to impact, likelihood, appetite, stakeholders, resources, ownership and measurable remediation.
Execute every item on the same date to avoid perceived favoritism.
Delay all preventive work until the bank records one more loss in each category.
questions.explanation: The guide connects action planning and implementation to residual risk, business priorities, resources and execution accountability.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Implementation Plan, pp. 106–109
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Implementation Plan, pp. 106–109

questions.stem: Several customers receive urgent texts apparently sent by their bank, followed by phone calls where callers ask for one-time authentication information. Other customers are manipulated into paying a “safe account” despite having no credential compromise. The head of service argues that all cases are solved by a one-time password reminder posted on a website annually. Which interventions provide a stronger education program? Select THREE.
options: Issue timely, scheme-specific alerts through channels customers use and explain safe verification behavior.
Instruct customers to share passwords with a bank caller if the caller knows their address.
Train customer-facing personnel to recognize and respond to evolving attack patterns and offer individual guidance.
Explain how PII, emotional pressure and purported banking messages are abused, including customers authorizing fraudulent payments.
End customer education after onboarding because alerts remain effective for life.
questions.explanation: Ongoing education, targeted alerts, responsive staff and clear guidance on phishing/social engineering are emphasized in the guide.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Customer Awareness, pp. 69–70
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Customer Awareness, pp. 69–70

questions.stem: A bank’s head of lending has authority to originate, approve and disburse loans, as well as suppress audit exceptions. The bank’s internal audit previously tested only aggregate portfolio reporting. A later review identifies fictitious borrowers and disbursements into controlled external accounts. Senior management argues that a highly experienced employee required no independent oversight because productivity was exceptional. What correction MOST directly addresses the design weakness?
options: Defer remediation until the current branch manager retires.
Keep approvals unchanged and increase only the employee’s annual training hours.
Segregate incompatible duties, restrict overrides, investigate/report appropriately and test individual transaction controls.
Permit repayment of the missing funds without reporting to protect the employee’s reputation.
questions.explanation: The guide’s trusted-employee case highlights segregation, timely reporting and substantive control review; reputation and experience are not control substitutes.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 1 · Fraud Risk Management Framework case, pp. 29–30
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 1 · Fraud Risk Management Framework case, pp. 29–30

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The attacker's first payment was a nominal test transfer, which a transaction-value dashboard ignored. The account normally uses a domestic salary and utilities profile, and the beneficiary was created minutes before the outbound transfers. The legitimate business user in the comparison group operates cross-border weekly transfers from preapproved devices. The fraud committee now wants detection logic that can recognize disparate normal behaviors without assuming the same monetary threshold defines anomaly for everyone.

An international bank has long relied on a single alert whenever a retail customer sends more than a fixed currency amount overseas. A fraudster takes over a low-activity account, logs in at an unusual hour from an unrecognized device, adds a beneficiary and sends a series of transfers individually below that amount. The system produces no alert. At the same time, a legitimate business customer often exceeds the threshold and is repeatedly interrupted. Analysts have adequate historical account behavior, device information and beneficiary-change records. Which change most directly addresses the two weaknesses?
options: Apply identical step-up authentication to every new beneficiary transaction irrespective of risk context.
Replace the amount trigger with a device blacklist and disregard beneficiary timing.
Add behavior-aware features combining deviations in device, time, recipient and velocity with transaction context.
Lower the uniform amount threshold and add manual exemptions for established large-value customers.
questions.explanation: Behavioral analytics combines context and deviations from historical patterns, improving detection beyond rigid monetary limits while reducing needless friction for legitimate patterns.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Fraudulent Behavioral Patterns, pp. 12–17
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Fraudulent Behavioral Patterns, pp. 12–17

questions.stem: A fraud ring initially phones a call center to gather account-recovery information, later uses a phishing site to collect verification codes, and finally uses mobile banking to add beneficiaries and send funds. Three separate business units investigate isolated alerts. The head of analytics says the activity belongs to one channel and its history alone is sufficient. Under the guide’s view of fraud channel switching, which data or actions would improve detection? Select THREE.
options: Link identity, device, session and account events across telephone, web and mobile touchpoints.
Analyze behavioral sequences showing movement from information collection to account control and payments.
Classify a legitimate mobile login as proof that earlier phishing reports are immaterial.
Discard call-center events once the final payment took place in mobile banking.
Coordinate intelligence and monitoring across channel teams rather than treating each event as unrelated.
questions.explanation: Fraud can migrate between touchpoints, so integrated data and cross-channel behavior patterns reveal the connected campaign.
