questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Fraud Origination and Switching Channels, pp. 21–25
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Fraud Origination and Switching Channels, pp. 21–25

questions.stem: A lender studies suspected application fraud. Its analysts have application amounts, dates, addresses and transaction records in structured tables. They also possess free-text call-center notes, customer emails, recorded interview summaries and document images. Management proposes dropping the latter material because it cannot fit directly into a conventional numeric column. The team wants a defensible, complete initial threat assessment while respecting privacy requirements. What is the best response?
options: Use only numerical transaction fields because qualitative and unstructured information never has evidential value.
Prepare, organize and analyze relevant structured and unstructured inputs, extracting useful signals and corroborating patterns.
Assume that adding raw free text to a model automatically ensures unbiased and accurate conclusions.
Replace all historical data with social-media screenshots because text is inherently more reliable.
questions.explanation: The data preparation and analytic process can use diverse internal and external sources; structured and unstructured material should be cleaned, transformed and assessed for relevance.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Data Collection and Preparation, pp. 29–45
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Data Collection and Preparation, pp. 29–45

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The back-test report includes a dense set of overall performance graphs, but no separate count of true positives, false negatives or alerts generated. Product leaders also want to compare this model against a simpler rule engine, which historically catches some confirmed chargebacks with a manageable investigation load. An analyst points out that the large legitimate population can dominate a headline average while the bank’s actual objective is detecting rare events.

A transaction model is evaluated against 20,000 historical payments, only 200 of which were confirmed fraudulent. It labels every transaction legitimate. The product team celebrates 99% accuracy and requests deployment because the metric exceeds last year’s 96% benchmark. The fraud director asks whether the model actually identifies any fraud. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The classifier may have high specificity, which is sufficient to establish acceptable fraud recall.
Accuracy is sufficient if the testing population contains more than a thousand confirmed legitimate transactions.
High accuracy in this imbalanced dataset can conceal failure to detect the positive fraud class.
The skew can be ignored if the test and training periods cover different calendar quarters.
questions.explanation: An all-legitimate classifier gets 19,800/20,000 predictions correct (99%) yet has zero recall for fraud; metrics appropriate to rare fraud are needed.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Model Selection and Evaluation Metrics, pp. 76–77
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Model Selection and Evaluation Metrics, pp. 76–77

questions.stem: Two candidate card-fraud models are assessed on the same labeled validation population. Model X identifies more genuine fraud cases but places many more legitimate purchases into manual review. Model Y produces fewer false alerts but misses an additional group of fraudulent purchases. The merchant complaints team is concerned about customer friction, while fraud loss specialists are concerned about undetected transactions. Which metrics illuminate the competing decisions? Select THREE.
options: A confusion matrix to see true/false positive and negative outcomes.
Precision to examine the fraction of fraud predictions that actually are fraud.
Recall or sensitivity to examine how many actual fraud cases are detected.
Number of database columns, because larger datasets prove better classification.
Headline accuracy alone, because class imbalance never distorts it.
questions.explanation: Recall measures detected true fraud, precision measures correct positive predictions, and the confusion matrix makes the underlying error types visible.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Model Selection and Evaluation Metrics, pp. 76–77
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Model Selection and Evaluation Metrics, pp. 76–77

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The operations manager highlights that the current alert queue requires additional investigators and occasionally delays genuine merchant settlements. The fraud prevention manager replies that missed attacks can still impose meaningful losses. Before discussing threshold changes, they agree to calculate separate measures for alert trustworthiness and the ability to detect all actual fraud cases, using the same adjudicated sample.

A high-risk card-payment rule is tested against independently reviewed transactions. It generates 120 alerts: 48 are confirmed fraudulent, while the other 72 concern legitimate customers. In addition, the retrospective sample contains 32 confirmed fraud cases that did not alert. The business wants to measure how trustworthy a positive fraud alert is, not what proportion of all fraud was detected. Management reports 60% and calls it precision. Which answer correctly identifies precision?
options: 60%, calculated from the number of legitimate alerts divided by the total number of alerts.
60%, calculated from the number of detected frauds divided by all confirmed frauds in the reviewed population.
75%, calculated from the proportion of alerts not included in the missed-fraud set.
40%, because 48 of 120 flagged payments were confirmed fraud.
questions.explanation: Precision = true positives / (true positives + false positives) = 48/120 = 40%. The 48/80 measure is recall, not precision.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Evaluation Metrics, pp. 76–77
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Evaluation Metrics, pp. 76–77

questions.stem:
Case-file context. Several missed cases were later identified through customer complaints rather than algorithm alerts, and the second-line model team has confirmed their fraud labels. Operations points to the long queue of legitimate transactions as evidence that any change to the threshold must examine the customer-impact cost. The requested metric is deliberately narrower: how complete was detection among all genuinely fraudulent cases in the sample?

A fraud model identifies 75 out of 100 transactions eventually confirmed as fraud. Another 25 actual frauds pass through without an alert. The alerts also include 125 legitimate payments, causing long queues. The CRO wants one metric specifically to describe the percentage of actual fraud the model found, while reserving a separate metric for alert quality. Which figure and concept should be reported?
options: Precision of 75%, because 25 frauds were missed.
Recall of 75%, because 75 of the 100 actual frauds were identified.
Specificity of 75%, because true negatives are not provided.
Recall of 37.5%, because 75 of 200 alerts were fraudulent.
questions.explanation: Recall = TP/(TP+FN) = 75/(75+25) = 75%. Precision would be 75/(75+125) = 37.5%.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Evaluation Metrics, pp. 76–77
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Evaluation Metrics, pp. 76–77

questions.stem: A fraud analyst says: “Precision measures the proportion of real fraud incidents we managed to catch, while recall measures the percentage of alerts that turned out to be fraudulent.” The bank operates a model with significant false positives and false negatives, so the distinction would affect its tuning decisions. This statement accurately uses the terminology set out in the study guide.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The analyst has reversed the terms. Recall concerns detected share of actual fraud; precision concerns correctness among predicted frauds.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Evaluation Metrics, pp. 76–77
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Evaluation Metrics, pp. 76–77

questions.stem: A bank is consolidating branch, card and mobile fraud data into a detection environment. Card timestamps use UTC, branch timestamps use local time, account identifiers have different formatting, and some payment records include empty recipient fields. A developer suggests concatenating every file directly into the training dataset because the analytics algorithm will discover the inconsistencies by itself. What should be done first?
options: Apply appropriate extraction, cleansing, normalization, transformation and loading steps with data-quality checks.
Delete all branch records to avoid time-zone conversion.
Relabel any record with an empty field as fraud so the model learns missingness.
Train the final model on raw data before any reconciliation, and clean only after launch.
questions.explanation: The data preparation process addresses missing/invalid values, common formats and consistent transformation before dependable mining or modeling.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Data Preparation and ETL, pp. 39–43
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Data Preparation and ETL, pp. 39–43

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The vendor’s development environment merges online authorization logs with a later case-management extract. Many older records have final investigation results because claims were adjudicated weeks afterward. The candidate model is intended to stop an attempted transaction in milliseconds. A technically correct historical join therefore risks making the test seem predictive when it actually uses knowledge unavailable to the decision system at the time.

An analytics unit wants to predict fraud at payment authorization. Candidate features include the customer’s prior 30-day transaction velocity, change in device fingerprint, time since beneficiary creation, and the fraud-investigation outcome recorded three weeks AFTER payment. During testing, the last variable nearly guarantees perfect separation, and a junior analyst recommends retaining it for production. Which steps best reflect sound feature engineering? Select THREE.
options: Assume that all variables must be retained to prevent bias, even if they leak future information.
Construct relevant behavior and transaction-derived features that exist when authorization decisions must occur.
Retain the future investigation outcome because high back-test accuracy is proof of deployable skill.
Exclude features unavailable at decision time because they can create misleading training success.
Apply selection, standardization or dimensionality reduction where appropriate and assess performance on unseen data.
questions.explanation: Feature engineering should create meaningful available-at-decision signals and prevent overfitting/misleading performance, with evaluation on unseen data.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Feature Engineering, p. 78
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Feature Engineering, p. 78

questions.stem: A payments processor has years of carefully labeled card-not-present chargeback outcomes but has recently encountered an unfamiliar rapid-movement pattern among newly opened accounts for which there are almost no labels. A manager proposes building just one supervised model and assumes it can learn the new behavior directly from categories absent from the training records. Which combined strategy is most defensible?
options: Use a supervised model alone and add the new pattern to the target label by assuming flagged accounts are fraudulent.
Treat the unsupervised output as confirmed fraud only if it is generated from more than one cluster.
Use unsupervised clustering alone because labeled historical data cannot improve known-pattern detection.
Apply supervised detection to known labeled typologies and unsupervised anomaly techniques to help surface emerging patterns.
questions.explanation: Supervised models learn from known labels, while unsupervised approaches can highlight previously unrecognized clusters/anomalies requiring review.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Supervised versus Unsupervised Learning, pp. 65–67
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Supervised versus Unsupervised Learning, pp. 65–67

questions.stem: A model review describes three proposals. Proposal Alpha trains multiple models on random bootstrap samples and aggregates predictions. Proposal Beta builds a sequence in which later learners focus on mistakes by earlier learners. Proposal Gamma trains distinct base models and then teaches a higher-level model how to combine their outputs. The sponsor says all three proposals are identical and any one term can describe all of them. Which mappings are correct? Select THREE.
options: Gamma illustrates stacking.
Alpha illustrates stacking because its subsets are drawn randomly.
Alpha illustrates bagging.
Beta illustrates boosting.
Beta illustrates bagging because each model is fitted sequentially.
questions.explanation: Bagging uses sampled parallel models; boosting sequentially corrects error; stacking uses a meta-model to combine base predictions.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Ensemble Methods, p. 79
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Ensemble Methods, p. 79

questions.stem: An online lender uses unlabeled transaction data to identify a small network of accounts sharing devices and unusual payment flows. An unsupervised model clusters them together, but none has yet been confirmed fraudulent. The compliance director wants an immediate adverse final disposition for every account because the model is “objective.” What should the analytics team recommend?
options: Suppress the network because unlabelled methods are appropriate only for technical anomaly detection, not financial fraud.
Treat the cluster as a lead for investigation and corroboration rather than conclusive proof.
Treat cluster membership as sufficient evidence if the algorithmic confidence score is high.
Assign temporary confirmed-fraud labels to enable supervised training, then retract labels only if complaints arise.
questions.explanation: Unsupervised outputs flag unusual patterns but are not labels establishing criminal fraud. Review and feedback improve their practical use.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Unsupervised Learning and Fraud Analytics, pp. 65–67
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Unsupervised Learning and Fraud Analytics, pp. 65–67

questions.stem: A fraud data scientist uses the training set to fit the algorithm, the validation set to choose hyperparameters and decision thresholds, and a separately held-out test set to evaluate generalization. The scientist refuses to keep tuning after examining the test performance, because repeatedly optimizing against that set would compromise its independence. This separation follows the model evaluation approach described in the study guide.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Training, validation and testing serve separate functions, helping avoid overfitting and preserving an unbiased estimate of generalization.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Model Evaluation, p. 82
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Model Evaluation, p. 82

questions.stem:
Case-file context. A development review shows that the original team repeatedly tuned its parameters after reviewing its only test extract. The model has excellent discrimination among merchant IDs present in that extract, but newer merchant populations behave differently. The bank has no documented independent validation sample. Management must separate genuine external changes in fraud patterns from an overly optimistic development and evaluation process.

A bank’s new fraud model detects 98% of the records used for training, but on a fresh month of activity it misses many attacks and produces a surge of false positives. The model had hundreds of derived variables, was tuned repeatedly on the same sample, and was never cross-validated. The model owner insists that the training score proves accuracy and the population must have suddenly changed. What should reviewers assess first?
options: Whether to release every blocked transaction permanently to improve conversion.
Fraud investigator performance only, because training metrics establish the model’s quality conclusively.
Only the average transaction value; model complexity and unseen performance are irrelevant.
Overfitting and weak generalization, using cross-validation, held-out evaluation and appropriate feature/complexity adjustments.
questions.explanation: The guide identifies overfitting as high training but poor unseen performance; model review should include independent testing, cross-validation and tuning.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Training and Tuning, pp. 81–82
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Training and Tuning, pp. 81–82

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The card and real-time payments teams use the same model, but each has different operational loss tolerances and customer-contact capabilities. Recent complaints show more declined legitimate transactions among newly onboarded merchants. The model developer proposes using a test population selected from only its highest-scoring alerts, while assurance asks for a representative baseline and records of approval decisions.

An institution uses a supervised fraud model built before a new real-time payment product was introduced. Fraud patterns change, confirmed false negatives rise, and a development team proposes changing production thresholds without recording the rationale or testing customer impacts. Compliance warns that the model now covers a different risk environment, and the board requests a sustainable response. Which measures best comply with the guide? Select THREE.
options: Maintain documented review, approval, monitoring and model governance of significant modifications.
Validate changes using relevant metrics and monitor impacts on fraud and legitimate transactions.
Refresh labeled data and retrain or adjust the model where analysis supports it.
Assume that the original training score remains sufficient despite emerging fraud typologies.
Apply threshold changes without documenting them because greater recall is always costless.
questions.explanation: Ongoing monitoring, new-data retraining, threshold review and model governance are essential as attack patterns and business conditions change.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Training, Tuning and Governance, pp. 81, 85–86
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Training, Tuning and Governance, pp. 81, 85–86

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The current review committee receives monthly fraud-loss totals but not comparative false-decline rates across customer groups. Some additional challenges are imposed by a variable derived from incomplete address records. Customer service reports that people affected often abandon transactions before filing a complaint. Managers need to assess whether the feature is informative, whether the sample is representative and whether a less intrusive treatment can manage equivalent risk.

A card issuer’s risk model disproportionately challenges transactions in a particular customer segment, even though investigators find relatively few confirmed fraud cases there. The model heavily weights a coarse geographic proxy and training data underrepresent the segment. Fraud managers argue that any algorithmic score is necessarily impartial and that reducing challenges would sacrifice safety. Which remediation best reflects the guide?
options: Apply an identical low score to every customer in the affected segment without examining observed risk.
Make all model inputs public at record level to allow affected customers to verify statistical fairness.
Investigate dataset representation and feature bias, test fairness and model performance, and adjust controls without abandoning fraud-risk management.
Preserve the model and alter customer communications because the model’s inputs are numerical rather than subjective.
questions.explanation: The guide addresses bias and fairness as model governance challenges requiring evaluation of data, features, performance and customer outcomes.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Bias and Fairness, pp. 98–100
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Bias and Fairness, pp. 98–100

questions.stem: A treasury assistant receives a voice call appearing to be from the CFO demanding an urgent transfer, followed by a video clip matching the executive’s face and speech. The payment instructions differ from the established approval workflow and the beneficiary is new. The assistant says the apparent likeness overrides the usual controls. The security team suspects generative AI impersonation. What is the strongest safeguard?
options: Treat matching voice and video as sufficient confirmation when they are consistent with the executive’s established communication style.
Execute the payment after one additional check that the caller knows a confidential but potentially compromised project detail.
Replace manual secondary verification with a trained staff member’s subjective recognition of the speaker.
Enforce independent payment verification and approval workflows, supported where appropriate by deepfake detection and risk signals.
questions.explanation: AI-generated voice/video impersonation can undermine trust in apparent identity; robust verification and independent authorization remain critical.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · AI Used to Defraud and Deepfake, pp. 18–20
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · AI Used to Defraud and Deepfake, pp. 18–20

questions.stem: A digital payments operator investigates attacks that begin on trusted devices after prolonged user sessions. Its threat team wants to fuse payment activity with device, location and behavioral signals. Privacy officers warn that intrusive data gathering may be unlawful or weaken customer trust. Which decisions are appropriate under the guide? Select THREE.
options: Treat any atypical touch pattern as proof that the account holder is an impostor.
Use analytics and authentication to identify deviations while tracking the effect on customers.
Apply lawful data collection, consent where required and proportionate controls consistent with privacy obligations.
Assess device and session signals alongside transaction patterns rather than assuming any one identifies fraud conclusively.
Collect continuous precise location for all customers regardless of policy or consent.
questions.explanation: Behavioral/device intelligence can improve detection but signals require context, proper governance and privacy-aware collection.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Biometric Analytics and Fraud Detection Systems, pp. 69–71, 95–98
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Biometric Analytics and Fraud Detection Systems, pp. 69–71, 95–98

questions.stem: An anti-fraud manager compares a candidate detection model with random selection of the same number of transactions for review. The candidate identifies substantially more fraud than random selection. The manager calls that comparative improvement “lift” and uses it as one performance consideration, not as a substitute for all other metrics. This characterization is consistent with the guide.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Lift describes improvement versus a random baseline; other metrics remain relevant for fraud rarity, errors and cost.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Selection and Evaluation Metrics, p. 76
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Selection and Evaluation Metrics, p. 76

questions.stem: A merchant-acquiring bank investigates a rise in disputes. One analytic output groups last quarter’s losses by channel, week and merchant to explain where the problem occurred. Another model estimates the likelihood that a pending transaction is fraudulent before it is approved. A committee member calls both outputs predictive because they involve numbers. Which distinction is correct?
options: A risk model is only descriptive if it uses machine learning rather than rules.
Historic summaries are descriptive analytics; forward-looking estimation of fraud likelihood is predictive analytics.
Historic summaries are predictive analytics because the data are numerical.
Both are qualitative interviewing methods because transaction data involve human behavior.
questions.explanation: Descriptive analytics summarizes historical patterns; predictive analytics uses existing patterns to estimate likely future or new events.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Descriptive and Predictive Analytics, pp. 55, 59
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Descriptive and Predictive Analytics, pp. 55, 59

questions.stem: Fraud investigators complain that monthly model recall figures are volatile. Review finds inconsistent labels from different teams, missing outcome updates, and mixed transaction timestamps across data feeds. Another division wants to publish a performance score based only on cases investigators confirmed, excluding unreviewed alerts and missed fraud later reported through claims. Which actions improve interpretability and validity? Select THREE.
options: Reconcile definitions and validate the quality of labels and outcomes.
Conclude that any positive lift resolves labeling errors.
Exclude every customer claim that did not originate from a model alert.
Evaluate representative false positives and false negatives rather than only readily confirmed alert cases.
Review extraction, transformation and timestamp handling for consistent inputs.
questions.explanation: Reliable analytics requires sound data preparation and outcome labels, alongside representative evaluation including missed and incorrectly flagged transactions.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Data Quality and Model Evaluation, pp. 39–45, 76–82
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Data Quality and Model Evaluation, pp. 39–45, 76–82

questions.stem: A payment provider proposes lowering its fraud threshold. The head of fraud worries that changing authorization logic immediately could disrupt a major client. The analytics lead suggests reviewing transactions that the existing model did not flag, comparing potential missed fraud against confirmed outcomes without altering the live production decision. Which technique best characterizes this interim check?
options: Below-the-line testing of false-negative activity without affecting live operating decisions.
Mandatory production hard decline of all sampled transactions.
A replacement for all future validation and outcome monitoring.
A mystery shopper test of branch employees using fraudulent invoices.
questions.explanation: The guide explicitly describes below-the-line testing as a way to study false negatives without impacting the operating model.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Model Selection and Evaluation Metrics, p. 76
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Model Selection and Evaluation Metrics, p. 76

questions.stem: A claims-fraud analyst sees several apparently unrelated insurance policies, each with modest loss amounts. A graph analysis uncovers repeated links among the same repair shop, telephone number, claimant devices and payment beneficiary, with overlapping dates. No individual claim is large enough to exceed the ordinary threshold. What is the best interpretation of this graph finding?
options: It is a relationship-based indicator that warrants a coordinated investigation of possible organized fraud.
It is irrelevant because claims must be evaluated only by standalone payment size.
It conclusively proves every claimant committed fraud, without requiring further evidence.
It can be interpreted only after deleting the shared merchant and beneficiary identifiers.
questions.explanation: Social network analysis exposes hidden connections that single-transaction rules can miss; it provides investigative signals rather than automatic guilt.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Social Network Analysis and Fraud Graphs, pp. 56–58
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Social Network Analysis and Fraud Graphs, pp. 56–58

questions.stem: A fraud training dataset contains transaction amounts ranging into six figures, normalized counts of recent device changes, and dozens of correlated historical behavior attributes. A developer fears the model is dominated by the amount feature and training is unnecessarily slow. The team discusses standardization, principal component analysis and feature selection. Which conclusions are consistent with the guide? Select THREE.
options: PCA can reduce dimensionality using principal components that retain important variation.
Standardization can place differently scaled features on a comparable basis.
PCA guarantees that every transformed component directly explains a specific fraud offense.
Retaining all correlated variables unchanged necessarily eliminates overfitting.
Feature selection can discard less useful predictors and may improve generalization.
questions.explanation: The guide describes standardization, PCA and feature selection as complementary ways to improve training, reduce dimensionality and control overfitting.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Feature Engineering, p. 78
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Feature Engineering, p. 78

questions.topic: Rules review and changing fraud patterns
questions.stem: An institution’s geographic velocity rule catches sudden card use in distant places. Attackers begin making fraudulent payments from devices near customers’ usual locations and distribute transfers across multiple channels. A quarterly review finds falling true-positive alerts for the original rule, but an operations manager insists its historic effectiveness justifies no changes. What is the strongest response?
options: Keep the rule unchanged because a rule that worked historically remains valid until a criminal conviction.
Review the rule against updated typologies, labeled outcomes and customer behavior, adapting the detection strategy as needed.
Evaluate the rule exclusively on alert counts, not the outcomes of cases.
Disable all geographic analysis forever because one evasion pattern exists.
questions.explanation: Fraud rules and models must be reviewed and tuned as threats evolve; historical success alone is not enough.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Fraud Detection Rules Review, p. 91
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Fraud Detection Rules Review, p. 91

questions.stem: An authentication model flags many low-risk legitimate users and imposes repeated biometric challenges, reducing completed purchases. Its administrator concludes that an increase in interrupted legitimate transactions is irrelevant to fraud-system performance because only fraud loss reduction should determine whether a model remains deployed. The guide supports this conclusion.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The guide explicitly balances false-positive friction, operating burden, customer experience and fraud risk in model design and tuning.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Customer Experience and Fraud Detection, pp. 96–98
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Customer Experience and Fraud Detection, pp. 96–98

questions.stem: After testing two detection engines, a bank chooses the one that scores highest on a historical dataset. It plans to go live without identifying which teams will own alerts, how the system interfaces with card authorization, what the review process will be for suspect decisions, or how to measure performance in production. The sponsor says model selection is the entire implementation task. What is the most appropriate next action?
options: Skip alert-response design until customers complain, because analysts can invent workflows later.
Establish governance, integration, operating workflows, accountability, monitoring and model feedback before controlled deployment.
Publish the performance benchmark and permanently cease further validation.
Require the vendor to classify every alert as confirmed fraud so metrics remain high.
questions.explanation: Effective implementation goes beyond algorithm selection to operating integration, responsibilities, control testing, feedback and risk/customer impact monitoring.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Implementing a Fraud Detection System, pp. 85–101
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Implementing a Fraud Detection System, pp. 85–101

questions.stem: An online merchant repeatedly experiences late-November card testing followed by January return and chargeback abuse. A newly introduced loyalty product also changes purchasing behavior, complicating anomaly detection. The fraud strategy group wants a year-round rule fixed at the lowest threshold and believes monitoring external developments has no incremental value. Which improvements are better supported by the guide? Select THREE.
options: Monitor emerging tactics, industry signals and new products for detection gaps.
Suspend monitoring for the entire holiday period because most transactions are legitimate.
Use historic seasonal patterns to anticipate changes and plan proportionate model/rule adjustments.
Use the same untested threshold in every channel regardless of changing conditions.
Reassess fraud detection against legitimate-customer patterns and measure the effects of changes.
questions.explanation: The guide links analytics, emerging patterns, adaptive controls and customer experience; seasonal spikes and new products warrant ongoing review.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Fraud Analytics and Detection Systems
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Fraud Analytics and Detection Systems

questions.stem: A digital wallet identifies legitimate customers incorrectly as fraud at high rates. A director wants to know how reliably the classifier recognizes transactions that genuinely are NOT fraudulent, because these errors trigger costly manual reviews. The model validation report provides true-negative and false-positive counts. Which metric most directly answers the question?
options: Precision, which examines valid fraud predictions as a share of fraud predictions.
Recall, which examines detected fraud as a share of all fraud.
Specificity, which examines true negatives as a share of all actual negatives.
Lift, which alone measures the rate of legitimate declines.
questions.explanation: Specificity is TN/(TN+FP), the true-negative rate. It is distinct from recall/sensitivity and precision.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 2 · Selection Metrics, p. 76
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 2 · Selection Metrics, p. 76

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The transfer is the third attempt to send funds to an account that has never previously appeared in the customer’s profile. A recent mobile-number change was properly authenticated, and a contact-center employee initially considered the transaction a family emergency. There is little time before the hold expires. The investigator has no authority to bypass escalation rules, and the institution has specialist victim-support arrangements for suspected coercion.

A minor is being extorted by a stranger who threatens to circulate a private photograph unless a payment is sent immediately. An automated anti-fraud system holds the unusually large transfer. The account holder has apparently authenticated correctly and the transaction amount alone falls below the bank’s ordinary high-value escalation threshold. The assigned investigator knows the customer is frightened but has not yet verified the relationship with the beneficiary or the nature of the messages. A supervisor suggests releasing the payment as “customer authorized” to avoid a complaint. What is the most appropriate FIRST action under the guide?
options: Release after documenting customer authentication because fraud has not yet been legally established.
Issue an immediate external police report with the customer named before internal fraud triage.
Contact the minor’s family first without reference to the bank’s internal escalation or victim protocols.
Escalate internally under the bank’s fraud procedures and investigate the suspected extortion before making irreversible decisions.
questions.explanation: The guide’s Diego case requires internal escalation of the suspicious transaction in accordance with policy; authorization and urgency do not eliminate possible manipulation.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Introduction to Fraud Investigations
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Introduction to Fraud Investigations

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The alleged diversion occurred during a system migration, when correction entries were common and ordinary approval paths were temporarily modified. A finance reconciliation lists several unexplained credits, but it does not identify who initiated each entry. Management would prefer a quick outcome before the quarterly board meeting. There are plausible innocent explanations as well as troubling indicators, and neither may be assumed without review.

A senior fraud investigator is assigned a report alleging a branch manager is diverting client payments. The reporter is credible, but the manager has an excellent service record and claims the transfers were legitimate corrections. An analyst wants to close the complaint because the manager is trusted; another wants to record fraud immediately because whistleblowers are rarely mistaken. The lead investigator must maintain objectivity and preserve the chance of uncovering a more complex explanation. Which actions fit the guide’s investigative mindset? Select THREE.
options: Maintain curiosity, healthy skepticism and a documented evidence-based approach.
Examine relevant records and inconsistencies without accepting either account at face value.
Treat the whistleblower report alone as proof sufficient for disciplinary sanction.
Presume senior staff are incapable of fraud when their prior performance was excellent.
Develop and test reasoned hypotheses while recognizing personal and institutional biases.
questions.explanation: The guide emphasizes objective critical thinking, curiosity, alertness to red flags and skepticism about any uncorroborated account.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Fraud Investigative Mindset
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Fraud Investigative Mindset

questions.stem: A bank historically flags every transfer exceeding a static amount, leading to thousands of benign salary-related alerts. During the same period, criminals move repeated small amounts to a new beneficiary, just below the limit, in rapid succession. A fraud investigator is asked to propose thresholds that would better reflect behavior without automatically turning every customer deviation into a criminal accusation. Which approach is most consistent with the guide?
options: Use policy, risk appetite, channel risk, transaction history and frequency/new-beneficiary indicators to set purposeful thresholds.
Use external legal-reporting thresholds as the principal alert trigger, with exceptional overrides for unusual customers.
Use customer-amount thresholds alone and reassess the false-positive population quarterly.
Turn off subthreshold payments until a loss-based case review identifies repeat offenders.
questions.explanation: Threshold design considers value, frequency, customer behavior, channels, risk appetite and applicable regulatory triggers; alerts generate review, not automatic guilt.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Fraud Program Thresholds
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Fraud Program Thresholds

questions.stem: A customer reports that their email and mobile number were changed after a suspicious help-desk call. Immediately afterward, a known device was used to add a payee and send funds. A call agent notes that the correct password and OTP were supplied, so the complaint must be unfounded. The customer insists they did not request the changes. Which investigative framing best avoids an evidential shortcut?
options: Investigate the help-desk interaction, credential compromise, profile changes, device/session activity and transfer history for possible account takeover.
Start with the authenticated payment record and give it presumptive priority over the customer’s unsupported denial.
Focus solely on whether the password was entered correctly rather than the antecedent identity-change events.
Investigate first-party misuse because the transaction occurred from a previously known device.
questions.explanation: Account takeover can involve social engineering and compromised credentials; tracing the full sequence of identity/access changes is necessary.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Account Takeover and Fraud Alert Response
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Account Takeover and Fraud Alert Response

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The attack records show that customers did not all experience the stages in the same order: some first received an email, while others were called after opening a text. The domain registrar supplies relevant technical information, and a subset of victims confirms having read out one-time codes. The fraud squad must select a response plan that addresses the full attack chain rather than a single communication format.

An investigation uncovers a campaign with three coordinated communications. Customers first receive an SMS claiming their payment cards are frozen; an email directs them to a copy of the bank’s sign-in page; and a caller impersonating fraud support asks for authentication codes. One manager insists the entire campaign is “email phishing,” so SMS and telephone evidence can be discarded. Which classifications or conclusions are appropriate? Select THREE.
options: The fake-email/login component is phishing and may combine with the others in a broader attack.
The SMS component is smishing.
The voice-call impersonation component is vishing.
Only the final payment transaction is evidence; solicitation and credential requests are irrelevant.
Because a customer receives all three methods, none qualifies as social engineering.
questions.explanation: The guide distinguishes channels used for social engineering and recognizes campaigns spanning multiple attack mechanisms.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Phishing, Vishing and Smishing
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Phishing, Vishing and Smishing

questions.stem: A customer uses genuine credentials to authorize a transfer to a “fraud-protection account” after a caller impersonating the bank’s security division urges immediate action. The customer is not hacked and knowingly presses the payment confirmation button, but believes the funds will remain theirs. An analyst says a fully authorized transaction cannot be a fraud scheme by definition. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: The bank must label it first-party fraud solely because the customer knew the amount.
It is necessarily account takeover even without any access by a stranger.
It is a failed fraud attempt because the customer personally initiated the transfer.
The pattern can constitute an APP scam because social engineering induced the customer to authorize payment under false pretenses.
questions.explanation: APP fraud arises where the customer personally authorizes a transfer after manipulation; authorization and genuine credentials do not make the representation honest.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Authorized Push Payment Fraud
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Authorized Push Payment Fraud

questions.stem: A fraud monitoring model raises an alert involving unusually high transfer velocity. The account holder is traveling for work and presents coherent invoices; device and payment records appear consistent, although further checks are still needed. The investigator states that unusual velocity, without corroboration or due process, conclusively proves intentional deception. This meets the guide’s evidence-based investigation standard.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A threshold breach is suspicion; investigators must collect, validate and analyze available evidence objectively before reaching a conclusion.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Fraud Investigator and Investigation Process
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Fraud Investigator and Investigation Process

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The sender uses a counterfeit lawyer’s letterhead and a convincing payment-status portal. Every time the victim pays, a new supposed customs or tax requirement appears. The victim never receives a statement identifying an owned investment, financial product or lawful estate disbursement. The case analyst is asked to classify the predominant method by which the offender induced the transfers, rather than by the victim’s expectation of receiving money.

A victim receives a professional-looking message about an alleged inheritance. The sender claims a large payment is already reserved but cannot be released until the victim pays a “processing and clearance” fee. The victim transfers several fees, but no genuine assets, trading returns or investment holdings are ever provided. The business describes the case as an investment fraud simply because the promised future payment is large. Which primary scheme classification is better supported?
options: Investment fraud, because the offender promised a substantial future financial gain in exchange for earlier payments.
Payment diversion fraud, because an actual payment to a third party is the primary mechanism.
Advance-fee fraud, because money is extracted in advance for a falsely promised future benefit.
Origination fraud, because the victim was told that an entitlement already existed.
questions.explanation: Advance-fee fraud solicits upfront payments as a condition of receiving a purported reward or benefit. A promise of money alone does not make it an investment account scheme.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Advance Fee Fraud
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Advance Fee Fraud

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The organization’s invoice validation team had recently approved the real supplier’s ordinary bank account, but this request names a new foreign beneficiary. The purported message arrives during an especially busy month-end close, and the sender discourages any discussion with treasury. Several transaction fields match genuine prior invoices. Those accurate details may have been copied from compromised correspondence, which complicates any reliance on surface-level authenticity.

A finance manager receives an email seemingly from the chief executive requesting immediate settlement of a confidential acquisition fee. The email uses the executive’s correct title, references a real project and forbids telephone verification because the deal is “market sensitive.” The bank details are not previously approved. A junior investigator focuses only on a spelling inconsistency in the sender address, while a senior investigator stresses a more complete control failure. Which is the most relevant fraud assessment?
options: The absence of an obvious malware attachment excludes financial fraud.
Only a confirmed loss, not an urgent instruction, can ever trigger a fraud review.
The payment is safe if the email contains a correct confidential project reference.
The urgent secrecy and impersonated authority, paired with changed payment details, are consistent with business-email-compromise red flags requiring independent verification.
questions.explanation: BEC exploits executive/vendor impersonation, urgency and payment redirection. Independent confirmation is required despite apparently authentic contextual details.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Social Engineering and BEC Scenarios
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Social Engineering and BEC Scenarios

questions.stem: A corporate fraud team receives three allegations about senior staff. A cashier allegedly diverted company assets for personal use; a finance officer may have deliberately manipulated earnings figures to mislead investors; and a procurement manager may have accepted payments from a supplier to favor a contract award. Senior managers propose grouping these as three examples of the same narrow “asset theft” offense. Which categorizations follow the guide? Select THREE.
options: Improper value received to influence a commercial decision can be bribery/corruption.
Financial statement manipulation is not fraud unless cash is physically stolen.
Deliberate manipulation of reported figures can be financial statement fraud.
Diversion of organizational funds can be asset misappropriation.
Any internal fraud is automatically first-party customer fraud.
questions.explanation: The guide differentiates asset misappropriation, financial-statement fraud, and bribery/corruption as internal fraud forms.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Internal Fraud
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Internal Fraud

questions.stem:
Case-file context. Review of the student’s bank statement shows rapid inflows from multiple unrelated senders followed by transfers that leave minimal account balances. The “employer” used a temporary email address and said taxes would be handled centrally. The student accepted a percentage of each transfer, but there is no direct admission of criminal knowledge. The investigative challenge is not simply proving movement of funds; it is assessing participation and the underlying deception.

A student responds to a social-media advertisement offering a commission for “payment processing.” They receive funds in their own genuine bank account and quickly forward the money to unrelated beneficiaries. When questioned, the student says they believed the service was legitimate and shows messages from a purported employer. Investigators have not established whether the student knew the money was criminal. Which case handling is strongest?
options: Exclude the activity as intentional fraud because the student’s own valid identity appears on the account.
Investigate the inducement, knowledge, transaction sequence and links before distinguishing knowing collaboration from unwitting mule exploitation.
Treat the purported employment offer as dispositive evidence that the student had no reason to suspect criminal proceeds.
Provisionally determine knowing collaboration based on rapid payment velocity and the receipt of commission alone.
questions.explanation: Intentional and unintentional muling are treated differently in the guide. The investigator must establish the participant’s knowledge and circumstances rather than infer intent from money movement alone.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Money Mules
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Money Mules

questions.stem: A customer disputes a digital purchase made from a household device. Their adult relative knows the access credentials, but investigators have not established whether the customer consented, whether the relative acted independently, or whether the claim is genuine. The analyst proposes automatically categorizing every such event as deliberate first-party chargeback abuse. This is a defensible conclusion under the guide.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Household or family involvement creates competing hypotheses and requires evidence of authorization, participation and intent.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Friend and Family Fraud, Chargebacks
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Friend and Family Fraud, Chargebacks

questions.stem: A fraud investigation identifies a possible shell entity used in a supplier scam. A public registry shows one director, a commercial database shows a second individual, and an anonymous social-media account alleges that both are nominees. An investigator wants to present the anonymous post as verified evidence of beneficial ownership and search a restricted intelligence repository without authorization. Which decision is strongest?
options: Give the anonymous post controlling weight if it is newer than the official registry entry.
Use only the commercial dataset to avoid having to reconcile inconsistent ownership details.
Confirm authorization for data access and corroborate public, commercial and other evidence before drawing conclusions.
Access the restricted repository when the compliance officer considers the investigation important, without checking formal access rules.
questions.explanation: The guide stresses lawful access, source reliability, ethical research and corroboration, particularly when combining nonpublic and public intelligence.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · OSINT and External Evidence Sources
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · OSINT and External Evidence Sources

questions.stem:
Case-file context. A payment processor confirms that one transfer was released less than an hour earlier, and a correspondent bank may be able to provide routing information under established procedures. A separate cyber incident has caused partial log loss elsewhere in the institution. Internal emails show that different teams are acting on different time assumptions, potentially jeopardizing an urgent recall opportunity and the reliability of later reconstruction.

An incident team learns that a fraudulent wire may have moved rapidly through several beneficiary accounts. Operations wants to request a recall; the investigations unit seeks account and payment logs; IT is about to overwrite session records under a routine retention schedule; and customer relations wants to reassure the victim that recovery is guaranteed. What actions should be prioritized? Select THREE.
options: Document investigative decisions and manage victim communications without unsupported promises.
Trace the payment route and coordinate authorized recovery/recall actions promptly where feasible.
Preserve transaction, communication and relevant technical records before they are lost.
Delay securing time-sensitive evidence until the receiving institution confirms full recovery.
Treat a payment recall request as definitive evidence the money has been returned.
questions.explanation: Effective investigation protects evidence, follows the funds and considers urgent recovery opportunities while keeping accurate documentation and realistic communication.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Evidence Gathering and Tracing Payments
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Evidence Gathering and Tracing Payments

questions.topic: Chain of events and root causes
questions.stem: A fraudulent international wire passes through a workflow requiring two approvals. The investigator establishes that the beneficiary was created by an account compromise, but discovers that the second approver ignored a name mismatch because the first approver had high seniority. The case report calls the “root cause” merely “a fraudster sent a payment.” A reviewer asks for a stronger analysis. What should it include?
options: The sequence of events and why the control failed in design or operation, leading to corrective measures for both immediate and longer-term weaknesses.
Only the amount recovered because any unrecovered amount establishes every other cause.
Only the recipient bank’s name because the sending institution’s internal processes are irrelevant.
A finding of human error without asking why staff disregarded an existing control.
questions.explanation: Root cause analysis asks how and why the incident occurred, including failure or absence of controls and corrective measures.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Fraud Root Cause Analysis
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Fraud Root Cause Analysis

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The victim’s records show a series of transfers from more than one account. Some were described as loans, others as payments for a fictional medical emergency, and the victim avoided telling relatives for fear of judgment. A junior investigator prepared a confrontational questionnaire built around the hypothesis that repeated payments prove complicity. The senior investigator needs both accurate evidence and a process that does not unnecessarily worsen the victim’s distress.

A victim of romance fraud appears distressed and changes details when recounting repeated payments over many months. The interviewer wants to confront the victim as dishonest and compare them immediately with a suspect’s confident explanation. The victim has also disclosed embarrassment and fear of family reactions. The investigation requires a reliable timeline and supporting evidence. What approach best supports a sound interview?
options: Use calm, structured, nonleading questions, build rapport, document the account accurately and corroborate discrepancies with independent records.
Conduct a discrepancy-focused challenge interview at the outset, because repeated transfers are inconsistent with victim status.
Use a structured statement that leads the witness through the investigator’s preferred chronology to reduce recall errors.
Prioritize a definitive claim about recovery during the interview to encourage disclosure of embarrassing details.
questions.explanation: The guide emphasizes careful interviews, clear statements, objectivity and sensitivity to victims. Discrepancies should be explored rather than pre-judged.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Interviewing Victims, Witnesses and Whistleblowers
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Interviewing Victims, Witnesses and Whistleblowers

questions.stem: A fraud team analyzing a possible merchant ring has records of dates, amounts, card-entry methods, transaction frequencies and geolocations. It also has employee interviews, customer descriptions of pressure tactics and unstructured correspondence from the merchant. The senior investigator wants to understand measurable patterns and the reasons people behaved as they did. Which approaches are appropriate? Select THREE.
options: Treat nonnumeric witness accounts as statistical proof without coding or corroboration.
Organize and code qualitative statements to identify themes, explanations and perceptions.
Ignore numerical outliers because qualitative impressions are always more persuasive.
Combine quantitative and qualitative insights while validating source reliability and investigating inconsistencies.
Use cross-tabulation or trend analysis for structured numeric patterns.
questions.explanation: The guide covers quantitative trend/cross-tabulation and qualitative thematic coding as complementary methods rather than mutually exclusive evidence.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Analyzing Customer Information
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Analyzing Customer Information

questions.topic: Payment networks and card scheme rules
questions.stem: A customer reports card-not-present transactions with an unfamiliar online merchant. Investigation confirms the transactions bypassed expected card authentication and identifies a chargeback window under the relevant payment network. A manager dismisses scheme rules as “commercial paperwork,” proposing to wait until a police investigation ends before any recovery review. Which action is most aligned with the guide?
options: Defer all dispute steps until law enforcement confirms the fraud offense, even where network deadlines are shorter.
Treat the card network’s general rules as a guarantee of reimbursement before reviewing dispute conditions.
Focus on merchant location and amount only because card-entry and authentication data are not material to a card dispute.
Examine payment scheme rulebooks and available dispute/recovery channels while preserving evidence and meeting applicable time limits.
questions.explanation: Card-payment rulebooks, authentication and dispute evidence can be material to recovery and case handling, alongside broader investigation.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Using Card Payment Scheme Rulebooks
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Using Card Payment Scheme Rulebooks

questions.stem: An investigator has completed required checks, documented the evidence, interviewed relevant parties and established no remaining actionable leads. The file contains a clear reasoned conclusion and has met the relevant legal and policy thresholds. The investigator nevertheless argues the case can never close unless the suspected offender confesses and every loss is fully recovered. That argument follows the guide’s case-closure criteria.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The guide’s closure criteria concern sufficient evidence, required procedures, lack of further actionable leads and appropriate legal/escalation requirements; confession or total recovery is not always necessary.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · When Do You Have Enough Evidence?
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · When Do You Have Enough Evidence?

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The case-management dashboard currently mixes attempted fraudulent payment instructions, transactions intercepted before settlement and funds later recovered from beneficiaries. Finance books losses only when value leaves the institution, but the threat-intelligence team tracks all attempted attacks to evaluate preventive controls. Both perspectives are legitimate for different metrics; the committee’s immediate question concerns the portion of disbursed value that remains unrecovered.

A fraud case involved attempted transfers totaling $500,000. Payment controls stopped $300,000 before disbursement. Of the remaining $200,000 sent, the bank recovered $120,000. A junior analyst lists $500,000 as the final net fraud loss because that was the attackers’ attempted amount. The committee asks for a defensible distinction among exposure, prevented amount, recovery and net loss. What is the net realized loss based on these facts?
options: $80,000, the amount successfully sent less recovered funds.
$300,000, the value prevented before disbursement.
$200,000, the amount successfully sent before recovery.
$500,000, the total attempted value.
questions.explanation: Net loss here is $200,000 paid less $120,000 recovered = $80,000. Attempted exposure, prevented value and gross paid value are distinct management measures.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Estimating Losses and Reporting
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Estimating Losses and Reporting

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The draft could be read by risk management, audit, legal advisers and potentially authorities through proper reporting channels. Several interview notes contradict an automated fraud alert, but the conclusion does not explain how those contradictions were resolved. The investigator has reliable transaction IDs and timestamps and is able to identify the control weakness. A concise summary is useful, but it cannot replace a reviewable evidentiary trail.

An investigation concludes that a series of improper card refunds involved a merchant employee and a compromised terminal. The draft report gives a single sentence: “Fraud happened; customer reimbursed.” It omits payment chronology, interviews, data sources, findings on failures, account treatment, reporting decisions, and corrective recommendations. The investigator says detail is unnecessary because operations already booked the loss. Which components are important in a decision-ready case report? Select THREE.
options: A transparent rationale for conclusions, dispositions, material loss calculations and reporting decisions.
A clear allegation/incident narrative supported by relevant evidence and investigative analysis.
Deletion of investigator notes once a management summary exists.
Every unverified rumor about suspects included as settled fact.
Findings on root causes, appropriate corrective steps, and documentation or retention of supporting records.
questions.explanation: The guide requires documented research, reasoned decisions, evidence, outcomes and a report structure sufficient for stakeholders and later scrutiny.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Documentation and Investigation Report Structure
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Documentation and Investigation Report Structure

questions.stem:
Case-file context. Customer A’s file shows evidence of deceptive conduct at application and repeated attempts to mislead the investigators. Customer B has assisted the investigation, provided available records, and asked whether a new card would make continued banking safe. The institution’s product agreements and regulatory duties may constrain the exact choices, while reputational and fraud risks differ sharply between the two relationships.

Two customers request closure after fraud investigations. Customer A deliberately misrepresented income to secure a loan and later attempted to destroy relevant records. Customer B was an unrelated victim whose debit card details were stolen and whose compromised card can be cancelled. A relationship manager proposes placing both on a prohibited-customer list because both accounts had fraud losses. Which approach best matches the guide?
options: Differentiate the intentional first-party perpetrator from the third-party victim, applying appropriate approvals, protections, restrictions and customer communication.
Use the same enhanced monitoring and exit process for both, then differentiate only if additional financial loss occurs.
Retain Customer A under ordinary terms because misrepresentation at onboarding is an origination rather than ongoing risk.
Terminate the victim relationship to eliminate future risk without considering narrower protective measures.
questions.explanation: Customer treatment depends on whether the customer perpetrated the fraud or was victimized. First-party confirmed fraud can warrant stringent exit; third-party victims call for proportionate, protective handling.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Customer Exit Following Investigation
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Customer Exit Following Investigation

questions.stem: A customer suffers unauthorized debit-card use, but their salary account and investment services are not compromised. The bank considers canceling the affected card, reimbursing the eligible loss after investigation, raising monitoring and continuing the broader relationship. A manager argues that any confirmed third-party fraud mandates the permanent closure of all of a victim’s accounts. Which assessment is strongest?
options: No enhanced monitoring can occur once the disputed transaction has been refunded.
Proportionate control restrictions and enhanced monitoring can support retention where allowed by law, contracts and risk appetite.
All accounts must be terminated after any card fraud regardless of the customer’s role.
The card should remain active to preserve potential future forensic evidence.
questions.explanation: The guide gives examples where banks maintain victims’ relationships while disabling compromised instruments or limiting future high-risk activity.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Maintaining an Account After Fraud
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Maintaining an Account After Fraud

questions.stem: A bank’s investigative team detects an emerging scheme in which altered contact details precede account takeover, but the information remains only in closed case notes. Fraud analytics has not been informed, the control owner has no remediation plan, and the risk team’s register still labels the threat as low. A quality reviewer asks what an effective post-investigation feedback loop requires. Select THREE.
options: Assume closing a case automatically proves the enterprise framework has learned from it.
Share analyzed case findings and emerging behavior indicators with relevant fraud analytics and risk functions.
Keep all findings permanently within the original investigator’s private notes.
Test and monitor whether changes improve detection and update fraud risk records as needed.
Translate root causes and missed red flags into feasible control actions with defined responsibilities and milestones.
questions.explanation: The feedback loop connects alerts, investigation, analysis, risk management and measurable corrective action rather than ending with case disposition.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Fraud Feedback Loop
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Fraud Feedback Loop

questions.stem: An employee provides original documents suggesting deliberate manipulation of payment records by a supervisor. The investigator properly preserves the records, separates allegation from verified fact, restricts disclosure to those with a need to know, and coordinates any interviews through the internal investigation plan. These measures are broadly compatible with the guide’s approach to investigations of insiders.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The guide stresses evidence preservation, confidentiality, objective assessment and controlled processes for potential internal fraud.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Investigating Someone Inside the Organization
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Investigating Someone Inside the Organization

questions.stem: A fraud investigation into repeated fake merchant refunds reveals linked transfers to newly created personal accounts and possible laundering of proceeds. The fraud team has records of refund manipulation, while the AML team has relevant transaction patterns and reporting responsibilities. The unit head insists that fraud cases and AML cases can never be worked together because the legal definitions differ. Which approach best reflects the guide?
options: Transfer all fraud responsibility to AML and discontinue customer-protection work.
Share complete customer records with every external bank without evaluating permissible legal gateways.
Ignore the laundering indicators because only the original merchant fraud is within scope.
Coordinate relevant fraud and AML expertise through authorized internal joint investigation and reporting channels while protecting confidentiality.
questions.explanation: The guide describes collaboration across fraud and AML to follow criminal flows, assess suspicious conduct and meet relevant reporting responsibilities.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Internal Joint AFC Investigations
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Internal Joint AFC Investigations

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The merchant’s proof-of-delivery package shows a recipient signature but contains no independent identity check. Customer contacts were routed through a newly registered email address, and some device records are retained by an external processor. An earlier examiner criticized the bank for treating authentication as equivalent to consent, while customer service worries about holding funds too long. The lead investigator must resolve meaningful contradictions before a defensible finding.

A suspected card fraud case has contradictory records. The customer denies a purchase, an OTP was used, the phone was reportedly stolen, and merchant evidence shows delivery to a new address linked to several other disputes. An analyst proposes closing the case as first-party fraud simply because the OTP was correct. Another wants to refund and erase the record immediately. The lead investigator reviews the closure standard. What should occur before a defensible disposition? Select THREE.
options: Treat correct OTP entry as conclusive proof of deliberate customer deception.
Determine whether relevant evidence and procedures are complete and whether actionable leads remain.
Avoid documenting contradictory material because it reduces confidence in the report.
Document the rationale, account treatment, loss impact and any required reporting or escalation.
Corroborate authentication, device, delivery and customer accounts rather than relying on one indicator.
questions.explanation: Contradictory indications call for corroboration, procedural completeness, open leads assessment and a transparent documented conclusion.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Evidence, Closure and Decision Documentation
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Evidence, Closure and Decision Documentation

questions.stem: An investigations team sees many fraud cases with high attempted amounts but relatively small final net losses after recovery. The board receives only case count and gross exposure. A regulatory liaison asks for reporting that distinguishes actual impact, status and systemic control gaps; investigators fear the additional reporting would overburden the team. Which approach best follows the guide?
options: Stop reporting control gaps if net loss was small.
Present all alerts as completed confirmed cases so the trend appears comprehensive.
Report exclusively gross attempted loss because recoveries cannot matter to risk appetite or regulators.
Include exposure and net loss, material case characteristics, trends and relevant control weaknesses in documented governance reporting.
questions.explanation: The guide calls for meaningful reporting on volume, exposure versus net loss, controls and relevant findings, with appropriate internal and external escalation.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Fraud Reporting Requirements
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Fraud Reporting Requirements

questions.stem: A fraud analyst finds that two customers use the same public Wi-Fi connection and labels them co-conspirators in a merchant fraud network. There are no shared payments, devices or other corroborated links. The analyst claims a single network connection establishes intentional collaboration under the guide’s evidence framework. This conclusion is justified.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A shared signal is a lead that needs corroboration; linkage is not sufficient proof of intent or fraud.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · Analyzing Patterns and Evidence
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · Analyzing Patterns and Evidence

questions.stem:
Case-file context. The bank has already submitted the reports required by its procedures and retained the relevant evidence. Investigators have no new transaction or account leads within their authority, although a future law-enforcement information request is possible. Finance continues to track any civil recovery separately. The decision concerns the status of the completed internal investigation, not whether the wider consequences of the crime have ended.

An internal fraud team has obtained sufficient evidence and completed its assigned investigation into a supplier diversion. A law-enforcement agency separately continues to examine suspects, and a civil recovery action remains unresolved. One manager argues the internal case must stay technically open forever until both external processes finish, even if all bank procedures and reporting steps are complete and no internal actionable lead remains. Which position best reflects the guide?
options: Close and destroy the original evidence once the external investigators confirm receipt of a summary.
Keep the case open for criminal adjudication in all circumstances, while marking every remaining internal task complete.
Determine internal closure according to policy, evidence sufficiency, outstanding actions and reporting obligations, while recording external follow-up where necessary.
Suspend closure until civil recovery concludes, because net loss is the sole determinant of evidential sufficiency.
questions.explanation: Case closure concerns the institution’s required investigation steps and actionable leads. External legal processes and follow-ups may continue under separate obligations.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Ch. 3 · When Evidence Is Sufficient and Case Closure
questions.sourceSection: Ch. 3 · When Evidence Is Sufficient and Case Closure

description: High-complexity control, detection and investigation questions with multi-select and True/False.

title: Fraud Threat Intelligence & Decision Quality · Form E
name: Fraud Threat Intelligence & Decision Quality · Form E
subtitle: Advanced cross-domain · Form E

questions.topic: Risk appetite during a new product launch
questions.stem:
A digital lender proposes an instant salary-advance service for first-time customers. Risk committees had approved the annual fraud risk assessment only six weeks earlier; however, that assessment assumed loans were funded one business day after identity verification. The proposed product will fund in under ninety seconds and allow funds to leave through a new wallet interface. The commercial director cites a competitor's impressive conversion rate and argues that annual approval means the fraud team cannot reopen its assessment. A vendor guarantees identity-document authenticity but has not evaluated customers' intent to repay. Operations estimates that a successful launch will triple the volume of origination decisions. The board wants a decision that preserves the launch opportunity without silently exceeding its fraud risk appetite.

What is the most defensible decision before launch?
options: Launch under the existing approved assessment and recalibrate once the first confirmed loss occurs.
Refresh the product-specific inherent and residual fraud assessment, test funding and cash-out controls, and decide launch conditions against appetite.
Treat the vendor identity guarantee as covering both synthetic identity and first-party intent to default.
Delay the entire company-wide fraud assessment until the next annual renewal to maintain consistency.
questions.explanation: A materially different funding speed and cash-out channel require a current product risk assessment; a verified document does not establish willingness to repay.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Risk-based approach to fraud prevention (pp. 39–40)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Risk-based approach to fraud prevention (pp. 39–40)

questions.topic: Risk appetite during a new product launch
questions.stem:
A digital lender proposes an instant salary-advance service for first-time customers. Risk committees had approved the annual fraud risk assessment only six weeks earlier; however, that assessment assumed loans were funded one business day after identity verification. The proposed product will fund in under ninety seconds and allow funds to leave through a new wallet interface. The commercial director cites a competitor's impressive conversion rate and argues that annual approval means the fraud team cannot reopen its assessment. A vendor guarantees identity-document authenticity but has not evaluated customers' intent to repay. Operations estimates that a successful launch will triple the volume of origination decisions. The board wants a decision that preserves the launch opportunity without silently exceeding its fraud risk appetite.

Which THREE elements belong in the immediate fraud assessment? Select THREE.
options: Change in exposure from near-instant funding and wallet withdrawals.
Whether the loan may attract first-party as well as identity-related origination fraud.
Whether last year’s low loss rate conclusively establishes low inherent risk.
Effectiveness of controls and remaining residual exposure relative to approved risk appetite.
Whether the marketing team can replace independent assurance with conversion data.
questions.explanation: The assessment must analyze new channel risks, party-risk typologies, existing mitigants and residual risk; historical loss and sales performance cannot substitute.
