questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Risk-based approach to fraud prevention (pp. 39–40)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Risk-based approach to fraud prevention (pp. 39–40)

questions.stem:
A private bank prohibits staff from initiating and approving their own wire transfers, but the chief operating officer can approve any payment after writing 'urgent' in a free-text field. The override was intended for disaster recovery and has never been independently sampled. During a quarterly review, four large payments to newly created beneficiaries appear immediately after an executive's calendar shows private meetings with a supplier. The payments were formally approved and therefore do not violate the computer system's programmed validation. Human Resources reports no prior disciplinary history, and the supplier has long provided legitimate services. A risk manager is asked whether compliance with the automated workflow proves effective fraud prevention.

Which control conclusion best follows?
options: The four payments are legitimate because the executive acted within technical access rights.
The historic vendor relationship demonstrates that bribery and procurement risks are remote.
Executive overrides create a control design or operating weakness requiring risk-based review, independent validation, and limited exception authority.
Only a confirmed criminal conviction permits a control deficiency to be recorded.
questions.explanation: Authority to bypass a preventive control can defeat segregation; exceptions should be constrained, monitored, and independently tested.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Common gaps in fraud prevention (p. 56)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Common gaps in fraud prevention (p. 56)

questions.stem:
A private bank prohibits staff from initiating and approving their own wire transfers, but the chief operating officer can approve any payment after writing 'urgent' in a free-text field. The override was intended for disaster recovery and has never been independently sampled. During a quarterly review, four large payments to newly created beneficiaries appear immediately after an executive's calendar shows private meetings with a supplier. The payments were formally approved and therefore do not violate the computer system's programmed validation. Human Resources reports no prior disciplinary history, and the supplier has long provided legitimate services. A risk manager is asked whether compliance with the automated workflow proves effective fraud prevention.

Because each payment had system-recorded authorization, the segregation-of-duties control can be judged effective without testing how the override privilege operated.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A technically authorized override can still leave effective preventive segregation absent.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Common gaps in fraud prevention (p. 56)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Common gaps in fraud prevention (p. 56)

questions.stem:
A university student receives a message offering payment for receiving transfers into her personal account and immediately sending the amounts to a digital-asset platform. She supplies her real documents and signs the bank's application herself. She tells investigators she believed she was assisting an overseas charity. Chat records retrieved later show that the recruiter offered a commission, demanded secrecy, and instructed her to split several transfers; the student did not reply to one message explaining the funds' suspected criminal origin. The recipient account is not owned by the recruiter. A supervisor proposes classifying every mule customer as a fully informed collaborator because using one's own genuine account is necessarily first-party fraud.

Which TWO findings would be consistent with the guide’s approach? Select TWO.
options: Money-mule arrangements may be intentional or unintentional depending on knowledge and manipulation.
Using genuine identity documents always proves the accountholder originated the underlying fraud.
Investigators should distinguish knowing collaboration from being manipulated by an unrelated offender.
An offered commission by itself establishes proof beyond doubt that the student knew the funds were criminal.
Second-party fraud never involves an account in the genuine name of a participant.
questions.explanation: The guide distinguishes intentional money muling/second-party involvement from unintentional muling through third-party manipulation.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • First-, second-, and third-party fraud (pp. 13–15)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • First-, second-, and third-party fraud (pp. 13–15)

questions.stem:
A university student receives a message offering payment for receiving transfers into her personal account and immediately sending the amounts to a digital-asset platform. She supplies her real documents and signs the bank's application herself. She tells investigators she believed she was assisting an overseas charity. Chat records retrieved later show that the recruiter offered a commission, demanded secrecy, and instructed her to split several transfers; the student did not reply to one message explaining the funds' suspected criminal origin. The recipient account is not owned by the recruiter. A supervisor proposes classifying every mule customer as a fully informed collaborator because using one's own genuine account is necessarily first-party fraud.

Which investigative classification is most appropriately supported at this stage?
options: Confirmed second-party intentional muling because secrecy was requested.
Confirmed first-party synthetic identity fraud because digital assets were involved.
Confirmed third-party account takeover because the recruiter gave directions.
Suspected money-mule activity with the participant’s knowledge and coercion or deception unresolved pending corroboration.
questions.explanation: Unusual transfers and instructions warrant concern, but intent cannot be inferred conclusively from the sparse evidence.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • First-, second-, and third-party fraud (pp. 13–15)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • First-, second-, and third-party fraud (pp. 13–15)

questions.stem:
An insurance business rates supplier payments as low residual fraud risk because its incident log shows no confirmed fraud. Its RCSA workpapers reveal that maker-checker approvals exist in policy but not during weekend settlement windows; an automated vendor-name match ignores bank-account changes; and the principal reviewer is also paid a bonus for timely invoice release. One controls analyst argues that the documented policy is sufficient. Another proposes rating the process high inherent risk while assessing whether actual controls adequately reduce it. Management fears that a higher score will damage the launch of a new claims product, although the risk taxonomy already includes invoice redirection and insider collusion.

What should the RCSA team do?
options: Conclude residual risk is low from the absence of reported losses.
Recognize operating exceptions, assess impact and likelihood, document residual risk and assign corrective actions.
Exclude weekend processing since it is not part of standard operations.
Replace control testing with a short employee awareness survey.
questions.explanation: RCSA considers likelihood, impact, actual control effectiveness and remediation, not just historic incidents or policies.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Line of business fraud risk self-assessment (pp. 42–43)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Line of business fraud risk self-assessment (pp. 42–43)

questions.stem:
An insurance business rates supplier payments as low residual fraud risk because its incident log shows no confirmed fraud. Its RCSA workpapers reveal that maker-checker approvals exist in policy but not during weekend settlement windows; an automated vendor-name match ignores bank-account changes; and the principal reviewer is also paid a bonus for timely invoice release. One controls analyst argues that the documented policy is sufficient. Another proposes rating the process high inherent risk while assessing whether actual controls adequately reduce it. Management fears that a higher score will damage the launch of a new claims product, although the risk taxonomy already includes invoice redirection and insider collusion.

A fraud risk can have substantial inherent exposure even where the firm has never recorded a confirmed incident of that typology.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Inherent risk measures exposure before controls, not the frequency of prior confirmed losses alone.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Line of business fraud risk self-assessment (pp. 42–43)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Line of business fraud risk self-assessment (pp. 42–43)

questions.stem:
A multinational payments company wants to pool mobile-device locations, voice recordings and customer identity documents in a single overseas analytics hub. Fraud analysts argue this would improve cross-border attack detection. The proposed workflow would copy all source records indefinitely for potential future retraining even when they are irrelevant to a particular investigation. Customer consent for location sharing has not been established for two regions, and local legal teams have raised data-transfer restrictions. An executive says the objective of fighting fraud makes otherwise applicable privacy rules less important. Security engineers propose encrypting the hub and allowing every analyst access because data will be used for a good purpose.

Which THREE safeguards are aligned with the guide? Select THREE.
options: Validate applicable lawful access and cross-border transfer conditions.
Retain data indefinitely because future anti-fraud innovation is a valid business objective.
Restrict access to authorized personnel and protect stored personal data.
Apply purpose-appropriate retention and secure destruction rules.
Treat encryption as a substitute for authorization and consent rules.

Fraud analysts argue this would improve cross-border attack detection. Use anonymized public news only, abandoning institution-held data completely.
Proceed if the fraud function alone signs a business-purpose waiver.
Design an effective analytics program within regional privacy, consent, access and retention requirements.

questions.stem:
A senior treasury analyst starts making unusually large personal payments after a medical emergency and requests an advance on salary. She also has unattended access to a dormant general-ledger suspense account and can approve corrections through an old administrative role. A colleague says she has complained that executives are rewarded while operations staff do all the work. An internal audit finds no confirmed unauthorized postings yet, but an access review shows the employee could move balances without a second approver. The head of compliance is asked whether the fraud triangle itself is evidence of misconduct and whether management can do anything before a crime has been proved.

Which statement best distinguishes red flags from substantiated fraud?
options: Financial pressure and grievance conclusively establish intentional criminal deception.
Only opportunity matters; pressure and rationalization are irrelevant to risk assessment.
The indicators suggest pressure, opportunity and potential rationalization; they justify proportionate controls and review but do not alone establish fraud.
Absence of losses means the risk triangle is inapplicable.
questions.explanation: The fraud triangle explains possible drivers, not proof; a known incompatible access configuration is a control weakness.

questions.stem:
An online retailer is about to begin a holiday promotion that doubles transaction volume. Its fraud team predicts a surge in returns and disputes after the promotion, but Finance wants all checks removed because the average purchase value will be small. Last year's chargeback loss peaked in January, not December, and merchant-service data show repeated claims from a narrow group of accounts. The customer-experience director is concerned that a blanket three-day hold will drive legitimate shoppers away. A proposed alternative is to tune targeted checks by device, abnormal returns and payment behavior while monitoring changes during and after the seasonal period.

What is the best fraud response?
options: Remove controls temporarily because the fraud amount per purchase is modest.
Apply an untargeted hold to every seasonal customer regardless of fraud indicators.
Ignore post-holiday claims because the principal selling period is over.
Adopt risk-based seasonal monitoring and customer-sensitive targeted controls, including post-promotion claims trends.
questions.explanation: Seasonal risk can peak after the original sales event, and the guide advocates tailored prevention balanced with customer experience.

questions.stem:
The chief risk officer asks the internal audit department to design fraud alert thresholds, execute day-to-day monitoring, own all fraud investigations and later independently audit its own work. The fraud operations leader wants the second line to approve every individual payment so that the first line has no accountability for fraud losses. The board has received no integrated reporting of risk appetite breaches, customer reimbursements or remediation actions for three quarters. Senior management proposes a streamlined governance matrix in which each line has distinct responsibilities and committees receive comparable information.

Which THREE allocations fit the guide’s framework? Select THREE.
options: The first line typically performs prevention, detection and fraud response.
The second line focuses on policies, oversight, monitoring and regulatory compliance.
Internal audit may implement the primary transaction controls and then self-certify its independence.
Internal audit supplies independent assurance and challenges the first two lines.
The second line must replace first-line ownership by authorizing all individual transactions.
questions.explanation: The three lines divide operational ownership, oversight and independent assurance; creating and auditing the same controls compromises independence.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Fraud risk management framework (pp. 32–38)

questions.stem:
A regional lender proposes outsourcing document verification and suspicious login detection to a startup offering superior benchmark performance. The vendor's security review is incomplete, its board members have not been screened and its service contract excludes access to error logs. The lender's product manager believes outsourced technology transfers fraud accountability to the supplier. An unrelated existing vendor was recently found to have employed an insider who sold customer contact information. Procurement has prepared a low-price comparison, but neither regulatory reporting obligations nor the new provider's integration limits were assessed.

Which procurement recommendation is most defensible?
options: Adopt the provider because competitive pricing offsets unknown control performance.
Require documented use-case, due diligence, cybersecurity and integration validation, monitoring rights and defined accountability before adoption.
Treat the provider’s benchmark slides as the replacement for independent control testing.
Waive staff screening because a software vendor cannot create bribery or insider risk.
questions.explanation: Vendor selection requires KYV, technology fit, controls and ongoing performance governance; outsourcing does not remove institutional accountability.

questions.stem:
A bank suffers two attacks in the same fortnight. In one, criminals use stolen credentials to sign in from new devices and make unauthorized payments. In the other, customers log in on their familiar devices and personally authorize transfers after a caller impersonating the bank's fraud unit warns that their money is unsafe. Authentication checks pass in the second attack. The fraud director proposes increasing the number of one-time passcodes for every outbound payment, assuming that this will fully address both typologies. Complaints show that customers disregard generic warnings but recognize targeted messages that explain the reason for a transaction concern.

Which THREE responses address the distinct control needs? Select THREE.
options: Strengthen device and account-change authentication for takeover risk.
Use behavioral deviation and tailored intervention for manipulated but authenticated customers.
Rely on a successful OTP to rule out social engineering in every case.
Expand customer education about impersonation and urgent safe-account transfers.
Classify every customer-authorized payment as legitimate and outside fraud management.
questions.explanation: Account takeover and APP scams involve different fraud pathways; consent obtained through deception needs behavioral and awareness controls.

questions.stem:
An institution learns that a malicious software update has redirected hundreds of small incoming payments. The fraud team is investigating, but rumors about the affected accounts spread through social media. The head of customer service proposes publishing a list of suspected accounts immediately. The media team wants to deny that an incident occurred until confirmed losses are fully quantified. The incident manual defines severity triggers, internal contacts, customer notices and legally required reporting paths; however, the last rehearsal was more than a year ago. A whistleblower also alleges that an employee ignored repeated vulnerability reports.

What should the incident leader do?
options: Withhold all communications until each individual fraud claim closes.
Publish the detailed customer list so the public can independently detect fraud.
Activate the response protocol, coordinate verified messaging and required notices, preserve evidence and document decisions.
Delegate all decisions to public relations because the immediate concern is reputational.
questions.explanation: Coordinated, controlled communication and evidence preservation follow the response plan and protect customers and legal obligations.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Fraud response roles; communication protocols (pp. 88–92)

questions.stem:
A customer reports an unauthorized card-not-present purchase while traveling. The merchant has a dispute mechanism, the payment processor can supply authorization evidence and the customer requests immediate reimbursement. Separately, a business client reports a completed international wire sent to an impostor vendor and insists the bank can simply reverse it at will. An executive combines these claims in a monthly financial report as 'fully recoverable' because both have a payment trail. Investigators are still assessing each event, applicable deadlines, and whether temporary customer credits are required.

Which statement correctly distinguishes the remedies?
options: Provisional credit is an investigative customer remedy, not proof that the bank has recovered funds; chargeback and wire recall depend on distinct processes.
All transfers with a bank reference can be unilaterally recalled by the sending institution.
A card dispute cannot be initiated unless police have convicted the fraudster.
Issuing provisional credit permanently closes the underlying fraud investigation.
questions.explanation: Provisional credit affects customer treatment, whereas recovery from merchants or other banks requires the applicable route and rules.

questions.topic: Assessing emerging fraud without data history
questions.stem:
A payments company enters a jurisdiction where it has no established customer base or validated fraud dataset. The launch includes a new high-value instant payment product and a distribution relationship with an agent that has not undergone independent vendor diligence. Management proposes assigning the lowest likelihood score because no historical losses appear in the internal database. An external industry warning describes a low-frequency scam with potentially catastrophic settlement exposure. Operational resilience and Legal disagree on the appropriate worst-case impact, and a product manager asks whether a qualitative scenario exercise would add value without statistically meaningful data.

Which THREE inputs can reasonably support the risk assessment? Select THREE.
options: Cross-functional scenario analysis for low-frequency high-impact threats.
Risk assessment of agent/vendor exposure and product design.
Use of external typology intelligence and process mapping to identify weaknesses.
Automatic classification as low risk solely because no internal fraud records exist.
Treat absence of a trained supervised model as proof that control testing is unnecessary.
questions.explanation: The guide describes scenario analysis, process mapping, collaboration and external intelligence when identifying risks beyond historical claims.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Common fraud risk assessment tools (pp. 39–42)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Common fraud risk assessment tools (pp. 39–42)

questions.stem:
An investment firm's vendor invoice control requires two separate approvals and an automated match of bank-account details. An internal test invoice with an altered beneficiary account passes because both reviewers rely on a common payment screen; neither validates against a trusted source. Audit finds that the automated check compares only the vendor name. The control owner says the test is invalid because no real money was lost and both reviewers clicked 'approve' as required. Management proposes adding a third reviewer who would use the same screen without independent evidence. A testing specialist questions whether that would genuinely strengthen prevention.

What is the most appropriate control improvement?
options: Count the test as a success because the approval boxes were checked.
Require additional clicks by a third reviewer using identical unverified data.
Replace approvals with automated acceptance of low-value invoices.
Independently validate beneficiary changes using trusted records, remediate automated matching and retest bypass scenarios.
questions.explanation: The flaw is ineffective independent validation and data matching; adding the same weak check may not reduce residual risk.

questions.stem:
Two credit-card applications originate from unrelated mobile devices. Applicant A uses accurate identity details, makes six months of on-time payments, secures incremental credit increases and then empties the available limit across several merchants before disappearing. Applicant B uses a real national identifier associated with a different person, supplies fabricated address and employment data, and builds a favorable credit profile before requesting a larger line. A senior underwriter argues both must be identity theft because neither will repay, and a separate analyst claims that any successful initial authentication excludes origination fraud.

Which classification is most accurate?
options: A is third-party account takeover; B is purely a legitimate credit default.
A is first-party bust-out; B is synthetic identity fraud in the origination channel.
A is second-party money muling; B is merchant chargeback abuse.
Both are exclusively internal fraud because the lender increased the credit limits.
questions.explanation: The first uses a genuine identity and repayment grooming before bust-out; the second blends real and fictitious identity components.

questions.topic: KYE, vendor conflicts and employee privacy
questions.stem:
A procurement manager has awarded a sequence of urgent technology contracts to a vendor whose beneficial owners are difficult to identify. A colleague anonymously reports that the manager's relative works for the supplier. A third party offers to provide full personal credit reports and private messages for every employee, regardless of role or local legal limitations. Legal advises that relevant employee screening and conflict checks may be permitted if conducted lawfully and proportionately. The fraud unit has no evidence of an actual bribe but notes unexplained invoice changes and the vendor's privileged access to customer information.

What is the best initial program response?
options: Obtain all employees’ private communications without legal review because fraud risk overrides privacy.
Ignore the report unless the vendor admits paying a bribe.
Use lawful, proportionate KYE and KYV due diligence, conflict checks, access review and documented escalation.
Terminate every vendor contract automatically where owners are not immediately known.
questions.explanation: KYE and KYV require proportionate verification, ongoing monitoring, lawful handling and assessment of insider and third-party risks.

questions.stem:
After a phishing campaign, a bank announces that 99% of employees completed mandatory training. Yet the help desk still accepts high-risk account changes after unverified calls, and customer complaints reveal confusion about bank impersonation warnings. A call-center supervisor explains that the training contains generic slides and no realistic scripted scenarios. Fraud operations noticed a surge in attempts to change mobile numbers immediately before instant-payments activity. Marketing wants to count the number of emails sent as sufficient evidence that the awareness program works. Senior management asks how to test whether learning has meaningfully changed behavior.

Which THREE measures would be informative? Select THREE.
options: Scenario exercises of caller authentication and escalation during account-change requests.
Evaluation of repeat account-change incidents and resulting fraud losses.
Tracking of customers’ responses and reports after tailored threat notifications.
Reliance solely on course completion percentage as evidence of effective behavior change.
Automatic classification of any help-desk complaint as malicious insider misconduct.
questions.explanation: Scenario performance and outcome feedback show whether training reinforces controls; completion and outreach counts alone are output metrics.

A retail bank boasts that the number of blocked suspicious payments increased by 35%. At the same time, fraud losses rose in the fastest-growing payment channel, genuine customers experienced more declined transactions, and complaints about account freezes doubled. The fraud dashboard presents one enterprise-level total without showing product or channel segments. Senior management proposes rewarding the fraud analytics team solely for the increase in alerts generated. An independent reviewer notes that the organization has not distinguished false positives, actual prevented fraud, loss severity or customer reimbursements.

Compare only the team staffing levels with the previous year.

questions.topic: Large incident response and internal reporting
questions.stem:
A mobile bank identifies a coordinated takeover incident involving customers in three jurisdictions. Analysts initially believe 80 accounts are affected, but the count increases to 600 after transaction reconciliation. The fraud department freezes certain high-risk payments while Legal reviews jurisdiction-specific reimbursement and reporting duties. Senior management learned about the event through social media because the fraud response manual's severity criteria were not applied consistently. A communications officer suggests sending detailed incident reports to all employees. Investigators worry that this could reveal confidential client information and compromise tracing efforts.

What should take priority in managing the incident?
options: Let public comments determine incident severity and notification rights.
Activate a cross-functional response with appetite-based escalation, defined contacts, evidence preservation and controlled communications.
Delay executive notification until the complete final loss figure is verified.
Share the full case evidence with every member of staff to establish transparency.
questions.explanation: The incident manual coordinates severity triggers, lawful escalation, confidentiality, immediate mitigation and progress reporting.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Fraud response plan (pp. 88–92)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Fraud response plan (pp. 88–92)

questions.topic: Continuous improvement after a recovered loss
questions.stem:
A corporate customer receives a forged invoice and transfers funds into a mule account. Both institutions cooperate quickly, and nearly all funds are recovered. Senior leadership argues that the absence of net loss means the matter should not feature in the risk register. The investigation nevertheless finds that confirmation-of-payee warnings were shown but badly worded, account-change verification was bypassed and staff misunderstood when to escalate warning overrides. A previous incident report had identified the same weaknesses, but nobody tracked whether the remediation actions were completed.

What should management do with the investigation?
options: Close the incident as low risk because the recovery outcome was favorable.
Avoid disclosing the root cause internally to prevent undue reputational attention.
Treat the recovered funds as proof the original control design was appropriate.
Use the incident and near-miss insights in a tracked corrective-action feedback loop, retest controls and update risk reporting.
questions.explanation: Recoveries do not erase the vulnerabilities that permitted fraud; lessons learned should improve policies, training and controls.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Fraud feedback loop; investigation closure
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Fraud feedback loop; investigation closure

questions.stem:
A fraud program has resources for one initiative this quarter. Project A addresses common low-value card disputes, easy to detect with current controls. Project B addresses a previously unobserved insider override pathway that could transfer far more than the firm's loss appetite in one event, though its likelihood is lower. Project C reduces call-center wait time but has no demonstrated connection to fraud losses. A regulatory examination has also flagged the override pathway for urgent remediation. The finance head proposes ranking purely by historical event frequency because it is the only objective number in the three business cases.

Which THREE criteria are particularly important for a defensible prioritization? Select THREE.
options: Potential severity and impact relative to fraud risk appetite.
Detectability and effectiveness of existing control measures.
Regulatory obligation and time sensitivity of remediation.
Only observed frequency, excluding potential catastrophic consequences.
The seniority of the project sponsor regardless of risk.
questions.explanation: The guide balances severity, likelihood, detectability, customer impact and mandated regulatory priorities.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Fraud risk prioritization criteria (p. 65)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Fraud risk prioritization criteria (p. 65)

questions.stem:
A mobile-wallet provider compares two models for screening instant outbound payments. On a holdout population of 10,000 payments containing 100 confirmed fraudulent transactions, Model A alerts on 200 payments, of which 80 are truly fraudulent. Model B alerts on 400 payments, of which 90 are fraudulent. The fraud team can manually review only 220 alerts a day, and the merchant network threatens penalties if legitimate transactions are repeatedly held. The data science director advertises Model B as 'better at finding fraud,' but Finance asks whether the alert stream will overwhelm operations. Both models have strong overall accuracy because almost every transaction is legitimate.

Which comparison best captures the operational trade-off?
options: Model A has higher recall and lower precision than B.
Model B has higher precision and lower recall than A.
Model B captures more fraud but with much lower precision and alert volume beyond the team’s capacity.
Both models perform identically because total accuracy will be very high.
questions.explanation: A: precision 80/200=40%, recall 80/100=80%; B: precision 90/400=22.5%, recall 90/100=90%; capacity and customer cost matter.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Fraud detection model selection and evaluation metrics (p. 76)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Detection and Analytics • Fraud detection model selection and evaluation metrics (p. 76)

questions.stem:
An institution's fraud analyst says a new detection system is 99.7% accurate. The test dataset comprises 100,000 transactions with 300 confirmed fraud events. A naïve model that labels every transaction legitimate would also produce 99.7% accuracy. The proposed system is evaluated using a random sample of customers from the same month, while several recently confirmed fraud events remain outside the reporting window. Fraud operations has not been shown a confusion matrix, and the model sponsor says the success rate is enough to authorize production. A senior analyst is concerned that the marketing metric offers no evidence of actually finding the minority fraud cases.

Which challenge most directly undermines the claimed success?
options: Accuracy is high because the dataset has a high share of legitimate transactions, and it does not show whether fraudulent events were detected.
Accuracy automatically proves every fraudulent payment was found.
A low fraud rate makes precision and recall mathematically impossible to calculate.
The only meaningful metric is the number of legitimate payments approved.
questions.explanation: A model predicting all payments genuine is 99.7% accurate here but has zero fraud recall.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Fraud detection model selection and evaluation metrics (p. 76)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Detection and Analytics • Fraud detection model selection and evaluation metrics (p. 76)

questions.stem:
A card-issuer data scientist identifies a feature named 'claim accepted after investigation' that correlates strongly with fraud labels. The field is updated six weeks after a transaction and is never available when a payment is authorized. Including it produces an impressive test score. The team also proposes combining device changes, time of day and transaction velocity as features computed from only information available before decision time. The product lead wants immediate release because the first feature's statistical significance is outstanding. The fraud operations lead says an authorization engine must score transactions before the later claim decision exists.

Which feature decision is most defensible?
options: Include the later claims outcome because its correlation makes the model predictive.
Replace all features with the claim disposition and tell the provider to infer it in real time.
Exclude the after-the-event outcome from real-time inputs and validate features available at authorization time.
Ignore timestamp alignment because fraud models are normally retrospective.
questions.explanation: Using the eventual investigation result in a live authorization model creates look-ahead leakage and invalidates the performance claim.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Feature engineering; model evaluation (pp. 78, 82)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Detection and Analytics • Feature engineering; model evaluation (pp. 78, 82)

questions.stem:
A new e-commerce marketplace has not accumulated enough confirmed fraud cases to train a reliable labeled fraud classifier. Customer support reports clusters of new sellers who post nearly identical product descriptions and route proceeds to a small number of beneficiary accounts. Some sellers have not generated any chargebacks yet, and others may be legitimate franchise operators using shared software. The analytics team proposes an unsupervised anomaly or cluster-detection technique as an initial screen and wants investigators to validate results before adding the patterns to production rules. A competing proposal is to fabricate a large fraud-labeled training dataset and claim a fully supervised accuracy score.

What is the most appropriate initial analytic approach?
options: Use unsupervised exploration to identify unusual clusters, then investigate and validate patterns before deciding controls.
Assume shared beneficiary accounts conclusively prove fraud in every seller cluster.
Treat unverified synthetic labels as confirmed fraud outcomes for supervised training.
Declare that no analytics are possible until one calendar year of chargeback outcomes exists.
questions.explanation: Unsupervised methods can identify patterns without reliable labels, but anomalies require contextual investigation.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Supervised versus unsupervised learning (pp. 65–68)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Detection and Analytics • Supervised versus unsupervised learning (pp. 65–68)

questions.stem:
A customer receives a phishing message requesting identity confirmation. Minutes later, the customer's mobile banking session registers a device change and a password reset. A caller purporting to be from the bank then persuades the customer to make a payment from a branch because the mobile transfer was temporarily blocked. The branch records only the final payment, while digital fraud analytics sees only the failed device activity. Each channel's independent rules remain below alert thresholds. After funds are lost, teams disagree about whether the event is an account takeover, social engineering or a completely normal in-person cash-transfer instruction.

Which THREE signals should be linked to reconstruct the customer journey? Select THREE.
options: Phishing interaction and subsequent credential or device change.
The sequence of mobile authentication attempts and cross-channel movement.
Branch payment and related customer-contact context.
Only the final channel because earlier steps cannot inform fraud detection.
The customer’s branch appointment time as definitive evidence of legitimate payment intent.
questions.explanation: Channel switching can defeat siloed controls; combined chronology links compromise, manipulation and payment execution.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Switching channels for fraud (pp. 21–24)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Detection and Analytics • Switching channels for fraud (pp. 21–24)

options: Add isolated alerts in each channel without sharing context.
Aggregate customer and device signals across channels and design interventions for the overall sequence.
Force all customers to use one branch permanently.
Remove digital logs when the final payment occurs in person.

questions.stem:
A lender has card transaction records, customer call transcripts, KYC files and device telemetry in separate systems. The call-center transcripts use free text, transaction IDs are occasionally truncated, and the address field is populated with different country abbreviations. The model team wants to blend these sources to detect suspicious new beneficiaries. An engineer proposes dropping all records with inconsistent identifiers, arguing that the remaining clean records will produce a sufficiently high-quality model. Investigators worry that discarded data might be disproportionately associated with compromised accounts and that some unstructured complaints contain early warnings of scams not captured in transaction codes.

Which THREE actions should form a sound preparation approach? Select THREE.
options: Standardize and validate identifier formats and field definitions.
Map unstructured complaint and call information into usable, traceable analytical features.
Assess missingness and coverage across affected fraud and legitimate segments before filtering.
Delete all unstructured records without checking whether they contain risk signals.
Treat perfectly formatted data as automatically accurate, complete and unbiased.
questions.explanation: Preparation requires extraction, transformation, matching, quality checks and careful treatment of missing or qualitative data.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Data collection and preparation (pp. 29–45)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Detection and Analytics • Data collection and preparation (pp. 29–45)

questions.stem:
A motor insurer investigates suspicious claims across 18 recently created policies. Several applicants share a repair shop, two telephone numbers and a small pool of vehicle photographs. A graph model highlights one address as a central node connecting nearly all claims, but the address turns out to be a shopping mall containing the repair shop and several unrelated businesses. The fraud head wants to automatically reject every linked claim. Investigators note that genuine customers may share service providers, and a photo similarity indicator might be stronger evidence than co-location alone. An analyst is asked to turn the visualization into defensible investigative leads.

What is the most appropriate use of the graph?
options: Treat every shared node as conclusive proof of collusion.
Use network relationships to prioritize corroboration of the suspicious connections, including claim documents and transaction details.
Remove all links because a shopping-mall address is legitimate.
Substitute graph centrality for any case-specific investigation.
questions.explanation: Network analysis identifies potential hidden relationships; investigators must validate whether specific links are meaningful.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Social network analysis and fraud graphs (pp. 56–57)

questions.stem:
A bank's card fraud model has performed well for years on domestic point-of-sale activity. Following a product launch, online transactions increase substantially while in-store purchases decline. Customer complaints show a new pattern of text-message delivery scams, but these are not represented in the original labeled training sample. Precision drops gradually, and several confirmed losses were never routed back to the model team due to a disconnected case-management feed. The model's original evaluation report remains formally valid, so a technology manager argues there is no reason to conduct additional testing until the next contractual renewal.

Which response addresses both observed and emerging risks?
options: Maintain the model unchanged because a historic test report is still signed.
Lower all thresholds until every payment alerts, irrespective of customer impact.
Update the feedback labels, monitor performance by channel and typology, and retrain or tune under controlled governance.
Discard monitoring metrics because fraud prevalence has changed.
questions.explanation: Evolving channels and typologies require monitoring, feedback, controlled tuning and further validation.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Training/tuning; challenges and limitations (pp. 81–82, 96)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Detection and Analytics • Training/tuning; challenges and limitations (pp. 81–82, 96)

questions.stem:
A digital bank's new fraud rules reduce successful card fraud, but a large group of legitimate customers face repeated login challenges and delayed merchant payments. Customer support reports rising abandonment among older users and expatriates whose devices frequently change location. The risk team argues that a lower fraud-loss ratio always means the control should remain unchanged. A product designer proposes context-aware step-up verification only for higher-risk sequences; risk analysts want to test whether those steps keep recall acceptable while reducing needless friction. The data protection team also requires appropriate handling of device data.

Which intervention best reflects the guide?
options: Keep maximum friction for every customer because false positives are harmless.
Disable all controls until complaints return to historic levels.
Use only customer age to reject transactions, without fairness review.
Pilot differentiated, risk-based interventions measuring fraud outcomes and the legitimate-customer impact.
questions.explanation: Fraud controls should strike a measured balance between risk reduction, false positives and customer experience.

questions.stem:
A payment provider notices that its fraud classifier disproportionately declines transactions from a region with limited historic banking data. The region was represented mainly by old confirmed-fraud samples because few legitimate transactions had been labeled there. The model team insists that all customers are scored using the same threshold, so the system is necessarily fair. The fraud operations team reports that legitimate customers in the affected region increasingly abandon the service. The head of model governance wants to preserve effective fraud interdiction while examining whether dataset representation and error rates differ systematically across customer groups.

Which THREE steps are appropriate? Select THREE.
options: Assess class balance, label quality and representativeness in the training population.
Compare false-positive outcomes across relevant segments and validate business impacts.
Test controlled changes for fairness and fraud effectiveness before release.
Assume identical numerical thresholds guarantee equivalent error rates for every segment.
Exclude all data from the region so that measured bias becomes zero.
questions.explanation: Fairness requires examining data representativeness, disparate errors and the effect of changes, not merely an identical threshold.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Bias and fairness in fraud detection models (pp. 98–99)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Detection and Analytics • Bias and fairness in fraud detection models (pp. 98–99)

questions.stem:
A data science team oversamples confirmed fraud cases so a classification model can learn minority-class patterns. The resulting training set contains 50% fraud, while live transactions contain less than 1% fraud. The director presents precision calculated only on the oversampled training population as evidence that the live system will produce few false alarms. Another analyst notes that class proportions and sampling conditions can strongly change the operational meaning of predictive scores. The bank has access to a recent, unmodified holdout sample of actual customer transactions but has not yet evaluated on it.

What is the strongest next test?
options: Use the oversampled training-set precision as the sole production estimate.
Evaluate on a representative untouched holdout with confusion-matrix metrics and operational thresholds.
Train and test on the same resampled records to maximize consistency.
Conclude precision is unrelated to fraud prevalence and alert workload.
questions.explanation: Representative evaluation is needed to estimate real-world alert quality when training data are intentionally rebalanced.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Model evaluation and training (pp. 81–82)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Detection and Analytics • Model evaluation and training (pp. 81–82)

questions.stem:
A card issuer's rule flags any international purchase above a fixed currency amount. Criminals discover the threshold and begin using many smaller purchases through a small number of merchants within minutes. Some legitimate corporate clients also make numerous cross-border payments, while ordinary retail customers rarely do. Fraud analysts want to add velocity and merchant-concentration signals without simply dropping the monetary threshold. The operations manager demands a decision that will identify attempted rule circumvention without producing an unmanageable number of false alerts from corporate travel accounts.

Which THREE enhancements are most appropriate? Select THREE.
options: Evaluate frequency, time-window and merchant concentration in addition to amount.
Consider expected customer or segment behavior when calibrating alert thresholds.
Back-test changes on confirmed events and monitor false-positive burden.
Raise the existing fixed amount indefinitely because smaller purchases never represent fraud.
Treat every international corporate purchase as automatically fraudulent.
questions.explanation: Fraud may be structured under static thresholds, so behavioral and contextual rules need testing and monitoring.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Fraud rules review; transaction monitoring (pp. 91–93)

questions.stem:
A bank sees suspicious digital wallet transfers but cannot confirm whether the same devices are attacking other institutions. Its internal model is strong for card-present patterns, yet the newest digital account-takeover technique appears rarely in its historical data. An industry consortium offers aggregated typology indicators from participating institutions under a defined data-sharing framework. The fraud analyst proposes using external insights alongside internal behavioral records, while Legal cautions that privacy and sharing permissions must be observed. A director argues consortium data should immediately replace all internal transaction history since the peer dataset is larger.

What is the best data strategy?
options: Use properly governed consortium intelligence to supplement institution-specific records and validate signals against local risk.
Replace internal behavioral evidence entirely with external aggregates.
Refuse all cross-institution intelligence even when lawfully obtained.
Assume every consortium indicator applies equally to every customer and channel.
questions.explanation: Consortium data broadens threat visibility but should complement local context, validation and lawful sharing.

questions.stem:
A customer calls a bank to change her registered contact number. The speaker passes a voice-biometric check, but real-time analysis detects an unusual acoustic signal and the call script resembles a recent deepfake impersonation series. The caller knows the customer's full name and date of birth, and a newly registered device attempts a large payment moments later. A staff member argues that passing the biometric match is definitive proof of legitimacy. Another analyst says that voice authentication is one layer and the suspicious pattern should be examined alongside account behavior and any additional verification measures.

Which TWO responses are best supported? Select TWO.
options: Consider deepfake risk and investigate conflicting biometric and behavioral indicators.
Treat the biometric pass as irrebuttable proof that no account takeover occurred.
Apply appropriate step-up checks and review device and account-change history.
Approve the payment solely because the caller knew personal information.
Permanently block all biometric authentication technology.
questions.explanation: Biometrics can help but should be combined with other controls, especially when impersonation and device anomalies appear.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Biometric analytical tools (pp. 69–70)

questions.stem:
A transaction-monitoring model is developed by the same analyst who approves its performance testing and can override fraud thresholds without recording a change ticket. The model performs well against a historic test sample but the company never tests whether large shifts in customer behavior are reflected in the assumptions. A business executive requests an immediate parameter change that would reduce declined payments ahead of a marketing campaign. Compliance has not reviewed model risks, and investigators are told not to document minor false-negative events because they would make monthly model statistics look worse.

What is the most serious governance concern?
options: The model contains more than one engineered feature.
A regulated business uses analytics rather than purely manual monitoring.
Customers may find some fraud controls inconvenient.
Model changes, testing and performance reporting lack independent challenge, auditability and reliable feedback.
questions.explanation: Governance depends on accountable change control, oversight, defensible validation and complete reporting.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Fraud compliance model governance (p. 86)

questions.stem:
An accounts-payable employee makes a protected internal report alleging that her manager approved duplicate invoices submitted by a company controlled by an undisclosed relative. The manager controls her performance assessment and has authority to delete old invoice attachments. An investigator has access to invoice metadata, access history and supplier onboarding documentation, but has not yet obtained a complete payment trail or independent evidence of the relationship. Human Resources is concerned that interviewing the manager without preparation may expose the whistleblower. An executive insists the fraud unit should immediately broadcast the allegation to all department heads for transparency, while another wants the case dismissed because the manager has an excellent disciplinary record.

What should lead the investigation response?
options: Publicly identify the reporter to discourage speculative internal complaints.
Protect confidentiality, secure potentially alterable records, coordinate authorized specialists and investigate independently.
Conclude the allegations are true because the manager can delete records.
Wait for the manager to resign before obtaining digital evidence.
questions.explanation: Insider cases call for careful escalation, preservation, confidentiality, independence and fair assessment.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Investigating someone inside the organization
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Investigating someone inside the organization

questions.stem:
A finance officer receives an apparently urgent email from the chief executive asking for a confidential acquisition-related wire. The message uses the chief executive's ordinary signature and refers accurately to a pending confidential transaction. The email address differs by a single character from the official domain, and the officer receives a follow-up call from a person who sounds like the executive. The officer releases the payment after the caller warns that confirming with colleagues will breach securities confidentiality. The legitimate chief executive later says no instruction was given. A fraud investigator must decide whether to treat the officer's documented approval as an indication that the payment was authorized and therefore non-fraudulent.

Which characterization fits the evidence best?
options: An unauthorized third party appears to have used impersonation and urgency to induce an employee-authorized transfer.
The recorded employee approval proves a legitimate underlying business instruction.
The payment is first-party chargeback abuse because the staff member used genuine credentials.
The acquisition reference means the source necessarily had legitimate authority.
questions.explanation: Business email compromise can cause an employee to authorize payment after deceptive impersonation; authentication of the approver does not validate the instruction.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Phishing, vishing and smishing; social engineering
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Phishing, vishing and smishing; social engineering

questions.stem:
A teenage customer makes a sequence of unusual payments from an account that has been quiet for months. A support agent learns that the customer sent an intimate image to a person contacted on social media and is now being threatened with public disclosure unless more funds are sent. The customer is distressed, asks the bank to keep the conversation secret from other people and says the next demand has a deadline that evening. A fraud analyst labels the activity 'self-authorized' and recommends closing the alert as non-fraud. A second investigator worries that a confrontational interview could cause the customer to stop cooperating and that the threats may continue after a single account block.

Which approach is best supported by an effective investigative mindset?
options: Focus only on whether login credentials were valid and dismiss the customer’s account of threats.
Assume the customer is a willing collaborator because transfers were personally authorized.
Use sensitive, nonjudgmental engagement, assess coercion and immediate safety/risk, preserve evidence and escalate appropriately.
Threaten account closure unless the customer identifies the perpetrator immediately.
questions.explanation: The guide addresses victim impact and interviews; a fraud investigation should distinguish genuine consent from payment under manipulation or coercion.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Fraud investigative mindset; effective communication for victims
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Fraud investigative mindset; effective communication for victims

questions.stem:
An elderly customer living alone reports that several payments were made after a relative began 'helping' with her banking. The relative had access to her phone and a signed mandate to assist with routine bills but the disputed transfers are to a newly formed business owned by the relative's acquaintance. The customer remembers approving a utility bill, not an investment. Records show normal device authentication, and the relative says all payments were gifts. A junior investigator proposes treating authentication as proof of consent, while a customer-service manager proposes automatically blocking every family member from future access without checking the mandate or local safeguards.

What is the most defensible investigative direction?
options: Close the case because a previously trusted device was used.
Assume family relationships categorically exclude fraud.
Immediate permanent closure of the customer account without investigation.
Review scope of authority, intent and destination evidence while applying proportionate safeguarding and respectful customer engagement.
questions.explanation: Family involvement can conceal misuse of authority; legitimate authentication and a general mandate do not establish authority for every transfer.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Friend and family fraud; victim communication

questions.stem:
A long-standing customer denies an online transfer made after a password reset and a registered-telephone-number change. A support agent handled the change request following a call from someone who knew the customer's previous address, birth date and recent card transaction. The bank's device system recorded the transfer from a device not previously seen on the account. A separate report indicates that customer data were exposed in a recent phishing campaign. The customer had independently visited a different city that week, and the fraud analyst is cautious about treating geolocation as conclusive proof of either guilt or innocence. The branch manager says knowledge-based responses to the phone agent establish that the caller must have been the customer.

What best explains the most concerning evidence?
options: A combination of compromised personal information, changed recovery credentials and new-device activity is consistent with possible takeover requiring corroboration.
A visit to another city proves the transfer must be genuine.
A correct answer to security questions means no independent check is needed.
A password reset automatically establishes first-party loan application fraud.
questions.explanation: Multiple linked indicators suggest potential account takeover even if individual attributes can have innocent explanations.

questions.stem:
A publicly listed manufacturer records unusually strong quarterly profits. Reviewers find three different anomalies: a finance manager accelerated revenue recognition without supporting delivery records; a procurement employee approved inflated invoices from a vendor with whom she exchanges undisclosed personal favors; and a warehouse staff member removed inventory that was later sold through an online marketplace. The chief executive argues these are all ordinary accounting errors because the journal entries were processed through standard systems. Audit workpapers show a pattern of post-period adjustments and inconsistencies between physical inventories and accounting records. Fraud investigators are asked to distinguish typologies before deciding whether incidents should be pursued separately or through a coordinated review.

Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: All three are external third-party identity theft by definition.
All three can be treated as the same type of honest ledger-estimation error.
The facts potentially indicate financial statement fraud, bribery/corruption and asset misappropriation, respectively.
The actions cannot qualify as fraud because the accounting system accepted the entries.
questions.explanation: The guide distinguishes deliberate statement manipulation, corrupt influence and theft/misuse of organizational assets.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Internal fraud: asset misappropriation, financial statement fraud, bribery
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Internal fraud: asset misappropriation, financial statement fraud, bribery

questions.stem:
An exporter authorizes a wire to a supplier after receiving a false bank-account amendment. Within hours the beneficiary account disburses funds through several linked entities in another jurisdiction. The sending bank's operational team has a wire message identifier and can request information from correspondent institutions, but the exporter's relationship manager wants to guarantee that every foreign intermediary will return the funds. Investigators are gathering an evidential timeline and have not yet established which accounts remain funded. Compliance is also considering suspicious activity reporting based on the payments and supporting communications.

What is the most appropriate operational position?
options: The original sending bank can reverse all international payments unilaterally after settlement.
A recall and institution-to-institution cooperation should be pursued promptly with complete information, but recovery is uncertain.
The customer should be guaranteed the funds before any tracing begins.
Wire identifiers alone establish which intermediary was complicit in the fraud.
questions.explanation: SWIFT and other networks can support tracing or recalls, but transferred funds may not be recoverable.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Tracing fraudulent transactions; global payment networks
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Tracing fraudulent transactions; global payment networks

questions.stem:
A fraud investigator identifies a social-media profile resembling the proprietor of a shell supplier. The profile mentions a luxury property and displays a photograph that appears elsewhere in a public image search. A company registry lists a director with a similar name, but the date of birth is inconsistent with the firm's onboarding record. A colleague suggests joining a private group under a fake identity to solicit confidential documents. Another proposes purchasing a hacked database because its contents may resolve the director discrepancy. Legal advises that sensitive data and nonpublic financial information require lawful access and that open sources should be independently corroborated.

Which use of OSINT is most defensible?
options: Treat a matching profile photograph as conclusive proof of beneficial ownership.
Acquire the hacked records because investigation necessity eliminates legal restrictions.
Exclude all internet sources because only financial records count as evidence.
Use lawful public registries and imagery as leads, verify identity discrepancies, and document source reliability.
questions.explanation: The guide emphasizes lawful access, ethical collection, source quality and corroboration.

questions.stem:
Three employees may have observed a suspicious beneficiary change before a high-value payment. The manager circulates a draft narrative saying that the payment was obviously fraudulent and requests that witnesses sign it without modification. One witness disagrees with the stated time sequence, while another says she only heard the story from a colleague after the transfer. The fraud investigator has logs that contradict the manager's version and knows separate interviews have not yet been conducted. Legal warns that a leading question or collectively drafted statement could reduce confidence in the evidence. The team is under pressure to complete the investigation report the same day.

What interview method best protects evidential quality?
options: Use a single group session to reach a unanimous narrative before any individual statements.
Ask open questions, interview witnesses separately where appropriate, preserve their own accounts and reconcile differences against records.
Require all witnesses to adopt the manager’s chronology because it was written first.
Discard accounts that differ from the automated logs without attempting clarification.
questions.explanation: Fair, structured interviews elicit independent accounts and document differences rather than imposing conclusions.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Interviewing victims, whistleblowers and witnesses; taking statements

questions.stem:
A newly opened account receives three inbound transfers followed by an attempt to send nearly the entire balance abroad. The customer profile states low-volume domestic activity, and a previous attempted transfer to a different beneficiary was declined after a mobile-device change. The latest transaction has not yet settled. The case management queue is overloaded, with investigators reviewing alerts by the amount of the most recent payment rather than cumulative activity or risk. A relationship manager says the account appears compliant with the numeric alert threshold because each single payment is below a fixed limit. The fraud manager must decide whether to investigate immediately or wait for the amount threshold to be exceeded.

Which triage decision is most defensible?
options: Ignore the alert until a single transaction exceeds the static threshold.
Automatically and permanently terminate the relationship without analyzing the transfers.
Prioritize review of linked velocity, new-account and device-change risk, using available interdiction and investigation procedures.
Close the alert because deposits into a new account always establish a genuine trading profile.
questions.explanation: The sequence and risk indicators can justify escalation despite individual amounts below a single rule threshold.

questions.topic: Sufficiency of evidence and investigation closure
questions.stem:
A customer denies a set of card-not-present payments. The case contains device records, payment logs and a merchant response but no preserved customer communication from the time of purchase. The device identifier had previously been used for legitimate transactions, yet forensic review suggests that the same browser could have been accessed remotely. A reviewer wants to deny the claim on the basis of that device match, while another investigator proposes postponing the conclusion forever because perfect proof is rarely available. The statutory response deadline is approaching and the organization must decide and notify the customer on the strength of reasonable, relevant evidence.

Which case-closure method is most defensible?
options: Deny solely because the historic device match is not zero.
Keep every disputed case open indefinitely until all hypothetical possibilities are eliminated.
Issue a customer-favorable decision automatically without considering relevant records or applicable rules.
Evaluate the full corroborated evidence against policy and legal requirements, document uncertainty and reasoning, and close within applicable deadlines.
questions.explanation: Case closure requires sufficient relevant evidence, fair analysis, documented reasoning and timely customer communication.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • When do you have enough evidence?; investigation case closure
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • When do you have enough evidence?; investigation case closure

What flaw is most significant in the device-only denial?
options: It uses technical evidence rather than a witness interview.
It mistakes a single nonexclusive indicator for conclusive proof of customer authorization.
It would allow a customer to receive a provisional credit.
It would require documentation of why the claim was denied.
questions.explanation: One previously known device identifier does not conclusively establish who performed or authorized the disputed transactions.

questions.stem:
A gig-economy worker's account receives fraudulent proceeds after the worker responded to a fake recruitment message. The worker promptly provides messages showing he was instructed to forward funds for 'payroll testing,' returns money remaining in the account and agrees to enhanced monitoring. A related account owned by another individual shows repeated similar inflows, deletion of contact records and attempts to recruit new account holders. The business wants to close both customers immediately under a zero-tolerance statement, while the fraud team notes that deliberate involvement and unwitting manipulation require different evidential assessments. The institution's policy permits proportionate controls while a case is reviewed.

Which approach is strongest?
options: Retain every account indefinitely because closing one could create customer complaints.
Close both automatically without assessing participation or future risk.
Apply evidence-led differentiation of the two cases, proportionate restrictions, reporting and exit decisions based on risk and policy.
Conclude that money-mule accounts are always first-party fraud carried out intentionally.
questions.explanation: Case closure and account decisions should distinguish knowledge, customer treatment, continuing risk and applicable requirements.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Maintaining an account after fraud activity; customer exit
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Maintaining an account after fraud activity; customer exit

Which factor most materially distinguishes the worker’s account from the related account?
options: Evidence of possible deception and cooperation compared with repeated suspicious patterns and concealment requiring independent assessment.
The worker’s employment title alone.
The number of letters in the beneficiary names.
Whether the account was opened on a weekday.
questions.explanation: Intent and cooperation are not decisive alone but relevant when evaluating potential unwitting and deliberate money muling.

questions.stem:
A commercial customer reports a supplier impersonation scam resulting in a completed payment. The fraud investigation substantiates deceptive beneficiary instructions but identifies no evidence that the customer's employees knowingly collaborated. The sending institution has initiated appropriate recovery efforts, and the recipient has already moved most funds onwards. An operational manager recommends filing no suspicious activity report because the customer is the victim, while another claims a report is mandatory solely because any customer says the word 'fraud.' The AML team wants to evaluate applicable suspicion thresholds, jurisdictional requirements and information needed in a coherent report.

What is the soundest reporting approach?
options: Automatically report every customer allegation without assessing information or legal criteria.
Never report schemes involving a victim because only criminal customers can be named.
Wait for a final criminal conviction before considering any regulatory suspicious activity report.
Assess applicable reporting obligations, suspicion evidence and escalation pathways, documenting whether a report is required.
questions.explanation: Regulatory reporting depends on jurisdictional rules and suspicion assessment; a victim case can involve reportable criminal activity.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Fraud reporting requirements; investigative outcomes
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Fraud reporting requirements; investigative outcomes

The AML team wants to evaluate applicable suspicion thresholds, jurisdictional requirements and information needed in a coherent report.

Which distinction must remain clear in the case record?
options: A bank’s attempted recall is identical to successful fund recovery.
The fraudulent payment outcome, customer treatment, potential criminal suspicion and recoverability are related but separate determinations.
Fraud reporting removes the need to conduct a case investigation.
Loss allocation decides whether the attempted impersonation actually occurred.
questions.explanation: An investigation should separately establish circumstances, reporting, restitution and recovery outcomes.

questions.stem:
A fraud investigator prepares to close a complex internal collusion case. Her draft conclusion is detailed but cites links to a shared drive that automatically purges call recordings in seven days. The evidence list omits time zones, source identifiers and the distinction between original files and the screenshots copied into an email. A line manager wants the draft sent to a regulatory liaison immediately because the fraud was financially immaterial. Another reviewer asks for a traceable decision chronology that explains why alternate interpretations were rejected and identifies which evidence and interviews supported the final conclusion. The investigator worries that saving comprehensive notes may slow closure.

What is the best preparation before issuing the final investigative report?
options: Retain only an executive summary and assume the original evidence remains accessible.
Delete interim notes to simplify the file and avoid contradictions.
Secure original evidence and meaningful records under retention requirements, document provenance and reasoning, then issue a supported conclusion.
Include screenshots without timestamps because a visual representation is self-verifying.
questions.explanation: Case files need preservation, provenance, relevant reasoning and support for conclusions under applicable retention standards.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Documenting research; retaining notes and supporting documents
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Documenting research; retaining notes and supporting documents

questions.topic: Acquisition and an obsolete fraud budget
questions.stem:
A mid-sized retail bank acquires an online marketplace lender whose fraud controls assume that applicants present documents at a branch. The acquired company now issues virtual credit cards within three minutes and permits immediate merchant refunds into linked wallets. During due diligence, business leaders noted a low historic loss rate, but the reporting taxonomy excluded unsuccessful attempts and reversals booked by merchants. The bank’s annual budget is fully committed to branch surveillance. The acquiring executive believes that keeping the inherited budget demonstrates disciplined governance. Fraud strategy identifies new opportunities for synthetic identity applications, cross-channel mule activity and first-party chargeback abuse. Several changes could be funded, but management has not estimated their residual risk reduction or customer friction.

Which decision best reflects risk-based program management?
options: Maintain the inherited allocation until the next annual review because historical confirmed losses remain low.
Adopt the lender’s vendor identity assurance and defer analysis of downstream wallet exposure until the launch reaches stable volume.
Reassess inherent risk, control effectiveness and residual exposure for the changed products, then reprioritize resources against risk appetite.
Pause only the merchant refund feature and retain prior underwriting controls, because that addresses the most recently identified risk.
questions.explanation: A major change in products and channels requires refreshed risk assessment and measured investment decisions. Historical low recorded losses may be incomplete and are not a substitute for exposure analysis.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Risk-based approach to fraud prevention (pp. 39–40)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Risk-based approach to fraud prevention (pp. 39–40)

Which THREE considerations should materially change the prioritization? Select THREE.
options: The comparative effectiveness and legitimate-customer impact of candidate mitigants.
The absence of losses from unrelated branch products as conclusive evidence of low exposure.
Rapid virtual-card origination and cash-out opportunities not addressed in old controls.
The commercial preference to avoid rewriting board reports regardless of risk.
Evidence that the prior loss taxonomy omitted some relevant risk events.
questions.explanation: Completeness of losses, new fraud vectors and the impact of proposed controls inform risk appetite and resource allocation. The other options do not establish that the changed business is safe.
