questions.stem:
A fraud operations director owns daily monitoring and has approved a process change that removes second review of small-value international payments. After several customers complain, the same director requests that internal audit formally certify the decision using a spreadsheet prepared by her own analysts. The second line has issued risk appetite parameters but was not told about the change. The third line has no staff trained in the new monitoring platform, and the director offers to select the test sample and draft the assurance conclusion herself. A board committee wants to understand whether the three lines of defense can all participate without losing the independence that makes assurance meaningful.

Which allocation of responsibilities is most defensible?
options: Request a management attestation plus a second-line compliance review as adequate replacement for independent audit testing.
Internal audit should own production thresholds and later audit its own decisions to ensure continuity.
The second line should perform all customer investigations and prevent the first line from seeing fraud trends.
The first line owns operational controls, the second oversees policy and risk appetite, and the third independently challenges effectiveness using suitable evidence and expertise.
questions.explanation: Operations is generally responsible for prevention and response; the second line establishes oversight; independent audit tests and challenges. The third line may obtain independent expertise when needed, rather than surrender sampling to the control owner.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Fraud risk management framework; three lines of defense (pp. 32–38)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Fraud risk management framework; three lines of defense (pp. 32–38)

The third line has no staff trained in the new monitoring platform, and the director offers to select the test sample and draft the assurance conclusion herself. A board committee wants to understand whether the three lines of defense can all participate without losing the independence that makes assurance meaningful.

Which TWO actions preserve meaningful assurance? Select TWO.
options: Treat the director’s seniority as evidence that the control could not fail.
Obtain competent independent testing and a representative sample not controlled by the person being assessed.
Let the first line define the audit population and remove suspected outliers before sampling.
Have the second line review whether the control change exceeded approved appetite and whether escalation operated.
Use first-line metrics solely because they are produced more quickly than source records.
questions.explanation: Independent validation and appropriate second-line oversight are necessary. The operational owner can provide records and explanations, but cannot determine the audit conclusion.

questions.stem:
A clearing house supports low-value retail payments as well as a rarely used emergency high-value settlement route. The route has not caused a loss during the last three years, and the risk matrix therefore assigns it the lowest probability score. A process map reveals that the route bypasses normal beneficiary verification after two senior employees invoke a crisis code. Technical staff cannot demonstrate whether the fraud monitoring engine receives these transfers in real time. The highest plausible loss could threaten the institution’s capital, although routine volume is small. One committee member insists that heat-map color alone should determine investment priority and another suggests a dedicated scenario exercise.

What assessment approach best captures this risk?
options: Test the crisis override with scenario analysis, examine detectability and controls, and assess catastrophic impact alongside likelihood.
Defer the control assessment until the emergency route is used more frequently, while applying the standard retail heat-map scoring.
Rate the residual risk as low by copying its transaction frequency.
Use average observed loss severity as the principal impact measure, while noting the potential extreme scenario qualitatively.
questions.explanation: The guide identifies scenario analysis as valuable for low-probability, severe-loss threats. Residual risk also depends on controls, detectability and potential consequences.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Common assessment tools and scenario analysis (pp. 39–42)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Common assessment tools and scenario analysis (pp. 39–42)

Technical staff cannot demonstrate whether the fraud monitoring engine receives these transfers in real time. One committee member insists that heat-map color alone should determine investment priority and another suggests a dedicated scenario exercise.

Which THREE findings deserve explicit inclusion in the risk register? Select THREE.
options: Possible very high loss severity despite low observed frequency.
A recommendation to ignore the risk because the channel serves few customers.
Named owners, mitigating actions and review triggers for the exceptional process.
A statement that no historic loss proves future fraud is impossible.
An unclear monitoring feed and emergency exception design that may reduce detection.
questions.explanation: Risk registers document impact, control vulnerabilities and remediation. Rare activity is not the same as immaterial exposure.

questions.stem:
Three regional business units report fraud independently. Card services records disputed merchant purchases as 'card claims,' lending records falsified applicants as 'credit quality,' and digital banking records takeover transfers as 'online security incidents.' Fraud operations discovers that one set of compromised identities was used to create accounts, add new cards and then transfer proceeds through a wallet. The board pack shows each unit below its loss limit because overlapping events are either split into different categories or omitted from the fraud dashboard. The finance team worries that harmonizing descriptions will break historic trend analysis. An investigator cautions that classification should capture both fraud type and the channel at which it occurred.

What should the governance team do first?
options: Introduce a consistent fraud taxonomy and mapping of historical data, allowing cross-product analysis without losing source-level lineage.
Exclude unconfirmed attempted fraud from every governance report without documenting the exclusion.
Retain the historic unit-specific definitions, but add a separate manually compiled table of cross-product events each quarter.
Use one enterprise category for all linked incidents, but remove the original product and channel details to reduce duplicate counting.
questions.explanation: A common taxonomy creates comparable reporting across business lines, while mapping and data lineage preserve the basis for trend assessment.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Fraud taxonomy and fraud reporting (pp. 32–35, 63–65)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Fraud taxonomy and fraud reporting (pp. 32–35, 63–65)

An investigator cautions that classification should capture both fraud type and the channel at which it occurred.

Which TWO consequences may arise from leaving the data fragmented? Select TWO.
options: Separate labels prove there are separate offenders and independent events.
Inconsistent classifications automatically prevent any fraud investigation from starting.
Linked multichannel attacks may be obscured by inconsistent labels.
A single taxonomy eliminates all false positives and investigation costs.
Different units may understate enterprise exposure and allocate controls ineffectively.
questions.explanation: Fragmented labels can obscure patterns and understate enterprise risk. Taxonomy improves analysis but does not independently establish criminal identity or eliminate control errors.

questions.stem:
A retail financial institution outsources customer voice authentication to a vendor. The contract permits vendor software updates but does not specify regression testing, reporting of model changes or secure retention of voice templates. Following an unannounced update, false rejections fall sharply. At the same time, several customers report a contact-number change they did not request; these cases all occurred after callers were authenticated by the revised tool. The vendor presents an attractive slide showing overall accuracy but refuses to share methodology or update logs. Procurement notes that replacing the platform would be expensive, while the bank’s fraud program remains accountable for responding to emerging losses.

Which response best addresses the bank’s responsibilities?
options: Reassess and test the changed control, obtain update evidence, enforce vendor oversight and add compensating authentication while exposures are investigated.
Rollback the update permanently without establishing whether the older configuration was susceptible to the same impersonation pattern.
Obtain a supplier attestation that the latest accuracy figures are calculated correctly and postpone independent control testing until contract renewal.
Hold only the call-center staff responsible because they used the vendor’s prescribed workflow.
questions.explanation: Outsourcing does not remove fraud risk ownership. Vendor changes require performance assessment, due diligence, governance and appropriate compensating controls.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Fraud vendor management; KYV (pp. 35, 61, 72–73)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Fraud vendor management; KYV (pp. 35, 61, 72–73)

Assurance that data security and handling meet applicable requirements.

An exemption from incident notification for improvements marketed as accuracy gains.
questions.explanation: Change control, genuine effectiveness measurement and data protection are necessary for an outsourced fraud control.

questions.stem:
An online furniture merchant records excellent conversion during a major holiday discount campaign, after temporarily waiving address checks and increasing instant refunds to improve customer satisfaction. Six weeks later it sees a concentrated wave of claims that goods were not delivered even when carrier records show signed delivery. Some genuine customers also report parcels sent to incorrect locations. The fraud committee argues the wave is unrelated to seasonal exposure because it occurred after the holiday. Customer support asks whether every disputed claim should be denied based on a matching signature, but the payment processor warns of varying chargeback evidence and network procedures.

Which analysis is best supported?
options: Classify the concentrated post-season disputes as presumptive first-party abuse and use the signed deliveries to close them in batches.
Classify every later dispute as an unrelated operational error because the calendar period ended.
Continue the lower-friction control settings for one more sales cycle, then retest once enough subsequent chargebacks have matured.
Treat post-season refund and chargeback abuse as potential seasonal fraud, examine claim patterns and delivery evidence individually, and retest temporary control relaxations.
questions.explanation: The guide notes that seasonal fraud risk may materialize after peaks through returns and chargebacks. Fair analysis and stronger targeted controls are preferable to automatic denials.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Seasonal fraud risk; first-party transaction fraud (pp. 47–49)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Seasonal fraud risk; first-party transaction fraud (pp. 47–49)

questions.topic: Authorized payment induced by emotional coercion
questions.stem:
A long-standing customer transfers the equivalent of two years’ savings to a new payee after an online acquaintance claims to need urgent medical treatment. The transaction passes multi-factor authentication and is entered by the customer on her trusted device. Before sending it, she has repeatedly returned to the payment screen and spent an unusually long time rereading warnings; a recorded contact with customer service reveals that an unknown person instructed her not to discuss the beneficiary. A supervisor says no fraud controls can apply because the customer knowingly pressed 'send.' The bank has an established escalation path for suspicious authorized payments, including customer education and enhanced verification.

What risk interpretation is most defensible?
options: Treat the transaction as standard customer-directed activity and issue a generic scam warning after settlement rather than intervening before release.
Rely on the trusted device and second-factor checks to exclude account takeover, while logging the unusual customer behavior for a future trend review.
Possible APP/social-engineering fraud warrants a proportionate intervention that considers behavioral anomalies and the customer’s circumstances.
The case is definitively an unauthorized account takeover despite the customer’s own entry.
questions.explanation: APP fraud involves a victim authorizing a payment due to manipulation. Authentication alone does not prove that the underlying purpose or recipient is genuine.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Fraud mitigation lifecycle; APP fraud (pp. 36, 57–58)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Fraud mitigation lifecycle; APP fraud (pp. 36, 57–58)

Which THREE mitigants align with the guide’s approach? Select THREE.

Reliance exclusively on the completed multi-factor authentication step.
Review of the new payee and payment circumstances before release where permitted.

questions.topic: Repeated false disputes or genuine compromise
questions.stem:
A customer reports a fifth card-not-present purchase as unauthorized. Two earlier disputes resulted in refunds, while a third merchant submitted signed delivery records and device records associated with the customer’s household. In the current event, the merchant’s shipping address matches the customer’s residence, but the customer says a former housemate retained access to the online account. The fraud team has evidence that some transactions were conducted using a familiar browser, yet no direct record identifies who placed the order. Marketing argues that refunds must be automatic for loyalty customers. Another manager wants to ban future claims because repeated disputes always prove dishonest first-party behavior.

What should the investigator conclude from the available pattern?
options: A delivery address matching the customer automatically proves who submitted the order.
Repeated claims justify enhanced evidence-led investigation but do not, on their own, establish deliberate first-party chargeback fraud.
Accept the latest dispute after an enhanced identity check because the authenticated claimant’s statement outweighs merchant evidence.
Treat the repeated disputes as likely first-party abuse and apply permanent card restrictions before determining the circumstances of each claim.
questions.explanation: Suspicious claims can indicate first-party abuse, but a fair decision requires corroboration and consideration of alternative explanations such as access by another person.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • First-party transaction fraud; payment disputes (pp. 48–49, 94–95)
questions.sourceSection: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • First-party transaction fraud; payment disputes (pp. 48–49, 94–95)

Marketing argues that refunds must be automatic for loyalty customers. Another manager wants to ban future claims because repeated disputes always prove dishonest first-party behavior.

Which TWO evidence sources should be weighed together? Select TWO.
options: Only the number of previous disputes, without their outcomes.
Authentication, account access and device history alongside the customer’s explanation.
Delivery and fulfillment evidence, including any contradictions or access limitations.
The investigator’s intuition without retained records.
The loyalty score as exclusive evidence of customer integrity.
questions.explanation: Shipment and technical records may support competing hypotheses; they should be considered with customer statements rather than treated as individually conclusive.

questions.topic: Fraud triangle under an executive incentive plan
questions.stem:
A finance head manages earnings recognition during a period in which senior bonuses depend on reaching a narrow quarterly profit target. An internal audit finds that the executive has unrestricted access to adjust manual journals and that no independent reviewer is required to approve end-of-period entries. The finance head tells a colleague that 'we can reverse anything next month, so investors are not really harmed.' No criminal conclusion has been reached, and the board is reluctant to investigate because the executive previously stabilized the firm during a crisis. A junior analyst is asked to identify the pressure, opportunity and rationalization dimensions without asserting that incentive alone proves fraud.

Which mapping best fits the fraud triangle?
options: Bonus targets indicate pressure, lack of oversight indicates opportunity, but a proposed reversal rules out any rationalization.
The finance head’s prior success is pressure; bonus targets are control effectiveness; journal access is rationalization.
Bonus targets are pressure; unrestricted journal adjustment is opportunity; the “no harm after reversal” claim is rationalization.
The opportunity and incentive elements are established, but a rationalization cannot be inferred from a statement minimizing the perceived harm.
questions.explanation: The guide distinguishes incentives or pressures, the opportunity from ineffective controls, and the offender’s justification. These indicate risk but do not independently establish guilt.

questions.topic: Fraud triangle under an executive incentive plan
questions.stem:
A finance head manages earnings recognition during a period in which senior bonuses depend on reaching a narrow quarterly profit target. An internal audit finds that the executive has unrestricted access to adjust manual journals and that no independent reviewer is required to approve end-of-period entries. The finance head tells a colleague that 'we can reverse anything next month, so investors are not really harmed.' No criminal conclusion has been reached, and the board is reluctant to investigate because the executive previously stabilized the firm during a crisis. A junior analyst is asked to identify the pressure, opportunity and rationalization dimensions without asserting that incentive alone proves fraud.

Which TWO prevention responses most directly reduce the identified opportunity? Select TWO.
options: Eliminate performance evaluation across the entire organization.
Limit privileged access and review executive overrides rather than granting personal exemptions.
Presume every quarterly adjustment was made with criminal intent.
Treat senior management reputation as an adequate preventive control.
Require independent approval and auditable evidence for exceptional journal entries.
questions.explanation: Effective segregation, limited overrides and independent oversight reduce the opportunity to manipulate records.

questions.topic: Data retention during a multi-country incident
questions.stem:
A fraud response team is investigating stolen customer identifiers across three countries. Investigators request full copies of every client’s passport images, call recordings and device data to be held indefinitely in an unrestricted shared folder. A jurisdiction-specific retention schedule requires destruction after designated periods and another location restricts transfers of personal information outside the territory. The incident commander notes that some records are material to the fraud event and need preservation, while many others are unrelated. Two subsidiaries propose using cloud storage without consulting their privacy and information security specialists to avoid delaying the investigation.

What is the most defensible evidence and privacy approach?
options: Preserve relevant evidence securely with lawful access, transfer and retention controls, while avoiding unnecessary indefinite duplication.
Preserve the entire dataset in a controlled central repository while deferring review of cross-border restrictions until the incident is closed.
Restrict the investigation exclusively to data stored in each original country, even if an authorized transfer could materially improve evidence gathering.
Release the entire dataset to all participating staff to maximize speed.
questions.explanation: The guide requires secure, need-to-know handling, lawful processing and retention while preserving evidence necessary to an investigation.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Data security and privacy (pp. 22–23); fraud response plan (pp. 88–92)

Which THREE safeguards should be applied? Select THREE.
options: Treat data needed for one case as permission to reuse it for unrelated marketing.
Assume any investigator’s personal device is an approved evidence repository.
Establish whether international transfers and collection purposes are permissible.
Restrict access to authorized individuals with a legitimate need.
Document secure retention and disposal rules applicable to each data class.
questions.explanation: Privacy and security requirements must be integrated with investigation preservation. Fraud objectives do not justify unrestricted access or unrelated use.

questions.topic: KYE and a privileged service provider
questions.stem:
A bank uses a small vendor to maintain its mobile authentication gateway. One contractor can modify production configuration and approve the change through a shared administrator account. Procurement performs sanctions screening of the vendor company at onboarding but never screens named directors or checks the contractor’s privileged access. A whistleblower reports that a bank employee is a relative of a person who controls the vendor, although no payment irregularity has yet been identified. The technology division says outsourced workers are outside the scope of employee and vendor fraud due diligence. The fraud risk team wants a proportionate plan consistent with employment and privacy rules.

Which program enhancement best addresses the combined exposure?
options: Conduct risk-based vendor and relevant individual due diligence, examine conflicts and secure privileged change controls with ongoing monitoring.
Keep existing access rights but introduce an annual vendor due diligence questionnaire to address the conflict allegation.
Screen only the vendor’s trade name because individuals cannot affect technical controls.
Obtain direct explanations from the potentially connected vendor personnel before protecting the reporting source or securing change logs.
questions.explanation: The guide recommends KYE/KYV checks and cybersecurity reviews for service providers with IT access. Conflicts and privileged access warrant controlled assessment, not unverified conclusions.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Know your employee and vendor (p. 61)

The lack of documented financial loss means due diligence is unnecessary.

questions.stem:
An investment manager tests its dual-authorization control with a simulated vendor payment that contains altered settlement instructions. The test succeeds because either approver could flag the change; however, a separate internal investigation reveals that two actual approvers routinely share passwords and sometimes approve each other’s drafts. Both report that the practice reduces customer processing delays. The head of operations presents the successful simulation as proof of sufficient controls, while internal audit suggests testing alternative fraud paths and validating beneficiaries independently. The firm has no documented procedure for handling intentionally collusive insiders.

Which conclusion best reflects residual risk?
options: Accept a password-sharing exception when the two approvers provide retrospective written confirmation that they acted independently.
Distinct login IDs are sufficient to demonstrate independence, even where password sharing is documented.
The tested control addresses some errors, but collusion and shared credentials require additional controls and bypass testing.
A successful test against one fraudulent invoice eliminates fraud opportunity from two-person collusion.
questions.explanation: Four-eyes mechanisms can be undermined by collusion or shared access. Testing must challenge realistic bypasses rather than rely on form-only approvals.

questions.stem:
A regional bank discovers a malware incident affecting forty customers. Confirmed direct losses total less than the numerical threshold for escalation to its enterprise crisis committee, but attack attempts continue against more accounts. Customer identification records may have been accessed, and reporters are asking for comment. The incident manual also includes nonfinancial triggers involving scope, ongoing threat, data exposure and potential public harm. A relationship manager suggests suppressing the event until recoveries are complete because the direct-loss amount is small. The communications department is preparing to publish a general statement without input from fraud, Legal or cybersecurity.

What is the best immediate response?
options: Assess all relevant escalation triggers, activate coordinated incident roles where triggered, protect evidence and direct communications through the approved plan.
Continue business-line incident management until the financial threshold is met, while notifying executives informally of the possible data exposure.
Issue a preliminary statement describing the suspected attack before confirming it with the technical and legal incident owners.
Delegate the entire risk assessment to customer service because confirmed loss is below appetite.
questions.explanation: The response manual and risk appetite may call for escalation based on affected customers, continuing incidents and data compromise, not loss alone.

questions.stem:
An electronic-payment customer reports an unauthorized debit. The institution issues temporary credit during the investigation and begins its relevant card-network recovery procedures. Finance books the entire credited amount as recovered fraud proceeds because the customer balance has been restored. A separate treasury employee proposes treating an international wire recall request as settled simply because a SWIFT message was transmitted. In fact, neither the merchant nor the receiving bank has returned funds. The fraud program must report gross customer losses, reimbursements, unresolved recoveries and operational costs to management without confusing a consumer remedy with a successful external funds return.

Which reporting treatment is most defensible?
options: Distinguish customer reimbursement or provisional credit from actual funds recovered through chargeback, recall, insurance or partner cooperation.
Count sent recall requests as probable recoveries and disclose the amount as an estimate without confirming receipt of returned funds.
Exclude unrecovered losses from monthly fraud monitoring because they are under dispute.
Classify provisional credits as recoveries if the customer does not immediately challenge the credit amount.
questions.explanation: Customer credit changes the customer’s balance, not necessarily the institution’s net recovery. Recovery efforts and outcomes must be recorded separately.

Sending an international payment-recall request establishes that the bank has already recovered the funds.

questions.topic: Training that looks complete but is ineffective
questions.stem:
An institution reports 100% employee fraud training completion. Its course is a generic ten-minute slideshow updated only once in four years. Customer service staff routinely transfer callers after requests to change registered telephone numbers, even when callers cite urgent security threats. Several fraud losses originated from impersonators who exploited that call flow, and the case review finds employees did not know where to escalate suspicious calls. Management celebrates the completion metric and proposes repeating the same slides monthly. An operations manager suggests designing realistic role-specific exercises, checking understanding and using incident feedback to update the content.

What action is most likely to improve training effectiveness?
options: Require the frontline team to complete the existing awareness slides twice per quarter, without updating the response simulations.
Repeat mandatory generic training more frequently and assume that greater exposure to the same material improves frontline escalation quality.
Discourage staff from raising uncertain cases so that escalation reports decline.
Replace a static completion-only approach with role-specific scenarios, assessment and updates based on new typologies and actual incidents.
questions.explanation: The guide favors relevant role-based, ongoing fraud education and feedback, not completion statistics without demonstrated understanding.

questions.topic: False assurance from a control simulation
questions.stem:
A wholesale payments company conducts a mystery-shopper exercise in which a trusted tester submits a modified supplier invoice. The automated control flags the new account number and two employees stop the payment. Leadership announces a 'zero fraud exposure' conclusion. However, the test used a large round-number invoice within business hours, whereas actual losses involved small alterations made late in the evening through an exception queue. The response team also learns that changes to approved vendor accounts are not always updated in the trusted master file before matching. Internal audit asks to revisit the testing design and relevant source records rather than simply repeat the same successful exercise.

What is the most justified conclusion?
options: A simulation is irrelevant unless the bank actually loses money during the test.
A control test cannot reveal operating weakness because testing is performed by employees.
Successful two-person approval proves vendor master-data integrity for all time.
Passing one control test supports control effectiveness, but exception-path exposures require separate assurance before a zero-residual-risk conclusion.
questions.explanation: Control testing should explore vulnerabilities and variable conditions. One successful path does not validate a separate exception queue or incorrect reference data.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Building a Fraud Risk Management Program • Fraud control tests (pp. 66–67)

Control tests should consider how assumptions, operating hours or exceptions change bypass risk even following an initial successful simulation.

questions.stem:
A group of job seekers is instructed by a supposed recruitment agency to open consumer credit accounts and hand over the access credentials as part of a paid 'identity verification assignment.' One applicant provides genuine personal information and claims a recruiter threatened to publish private messages if he refused. Another applicant admits that she received a share of every drawdown and knew the funds were being diverted. Investigators cannot determine whether the same recruiter controls both cases. Credit losses arise before lenders can contact the individuals. A program manager argues that genuine identity documentation means every account is first-party intentional fraud and that coercion can never affect how the roles of participants are evaluated.

Which classification approach is more defensible?
options: Investigate origination abuse and distinguish voluntary collaboration, coercion and unknowing participation based on corroborated evidence.
Treat all legitimate identity holders as deliberate fraudsters regardless of manipulation.
Classify both as intentional second-party actors based on the use of genuine identities and third-party instructions, leaving coercion for later review.
Assess both as first-party application fraud because their own identity details were used, but refer coercion to a separate customer-care process.
questions.explanation: The guide recognizes origination fraud involving coercion and differing roles of mule participants. Genuine documentation alone does not establish knowledge or consent.

questions.topic: Applying the guide’s UK offense categories
questions.stem:
A UK employee responsible for procurement withholds a required conflict-of-interest declaration while arranging for a connected supplier to receive a contract. A separate salesperson knowingly makes a false statement about the security of a product to convince a client to purchase it. A third manager abuses authority over corporate payment authorizations to direct a personal benefit. A workshop facilitator claims these behaviors fall outside the guide’s Fraud Act discussion unless a victim can already demonstrate a completed financial loss. Legal cautions that the study guide emphasizes dishonest conduct and intent to gain or cause loss or risk of loss, not merely the size of a final reimbursement.

Which set most accurately matches the principal Fraud Act categories described in the guide?
options: Negligent error, mistaken judgment and ordinary delay.
Phishing, ransomware and money laundering as the Act’s three statutory forms.
Bribery, tax evasion and insider dealing as the Act’s three exclusive categories.
False representation, dishonestly obtaining services and failure to prevent fraud.
questions.explanation: The guide identifies false representation, failure to disclose and abuse of position as the three main fraud offense categories, with dishonesty and relevant intent.

questions.stem:
A payment institution launches services in a new country through distribution agents. Product leadership identifies possible fake-merchant onboarding, vendor collusion and rapid outgoing transfers but lists the initiative as 'low risk' because the institution has not operated there before. The first-line assessment lacks a clear control owner and includes no analysis of the jurisdiction’s supervisory requirements. The second line has expressed concern that the proposed thresholds exceed the company’s usual residual risk appetite, and internal audit has never tested the agent process. A senior executive signs a one-page note saying that the business’s commercial value alone justifies accepting any fraud loss.

Which missing element most directly undermines the governance decision?
options: A formal board notation that the opportunity is strategically important, without a supporting product-level risk assessment.
A projection of distribution-agent sales that treats increased customer counts as evidence of reduced inherent risk.
The absence of a marketing campaign for the agents.
A documented cross-functional inherent/control/residual assessment with clear ownership, appetite alignment, relevant local requirements and independent challenge.
questions.explanation: Risk acceptance cannot be supported simply by commercial benefit. A risk-based, governed decision needs clear exposure, mitigations, residual risk, responsible stakeholders and relevant requirements.

questions.stem:
An account takeover attempt is stopped when a new-device alert causes a payment to be held. Investigators later link the event to a recent phishing campaign, but no money was lost and the customer did not formally complain. The fraud department records the case as 'no loss' and proposes destroying its notes after summarizing the operational success. Meanwhile, frontline staff have observed similar impersonation attempts against a different customer segment, and the technology team has not reviewed whether the same control works in the newly launched mobile app. Senior management wants to understand how a prevented incident could still shape the risk assessment and control-testing program.

Which approach best uses the attempted event?
options: Extend the identical rule to all new products without testing differences in their event data or customer behavior.
Capture the attempted typology, investigate the control and attack path, share the learning and evaluate coverage across affected channels.
Record the stopped transfer as successful control performance, but exclude its attack details from the annual risk assessment because it caused no loss.
Close the issue by increasing the number of reports without changing control rules.
questions.explanation: The mitigation lifecycle and feedback loop draw lessons from prevented events as well as confirmed losses. A successful stop may reveal transferable threats and untested gaps.

questions.topic: Call-center channel pivot before a wallet withdrawal
questions.stem:
A regional bank’s mobile app has strong login authentication, but fraud losses appear shortly after calls to a third-party help desk. Over five weeks, twenty customers called to dispute small fees, changed their registered phone numbers during the same contact and later sent high-value transfers from mobile sessions. The help-desk records show that several callers claimed to be traveling and knew the customers' recent balances, while device history shows the later payments were initiated through browsers not previously associated with those customers. The mobile fraud model evaluates each transfer but receives no record of recent call-center profile changes. Customer complaints are filed days later, after the fraud proceeds have left the bank.

What explains the detection failure most directly?
options: The users’ recent balances conclusively prove that every call was genuine.
An attacker may be pivoting from telephone-assisted profile changes to digital cash-out while critical signals remain siloed.
The bank used mobile authentication rather than branch controls.
Help-desk staff were outsourced, so no internal monitoring could apply.
questions.explanation: The guide highlights channel switching and combined signals from call logs, profile changes and device data. Reviewing only the final payment loses important context.

Over five weeks, twenty customers called to dispute small fees, changed their registered phone numbers during the same contact and later sent high-value transfers from mobile sessions. The help-desk records show that several callers claimed to be traveling and knew the customers' recent balances, while device history shows the later payments were initiated through browsers not previously associated with those customers. The mobile fraud model evaluates each transfer but receives no record of recent call-center profile changes. Customer complaints are filed days later, after the fraud proceeds have left the bank.

Which THREE signals should be combined in a risk-based rule? Select THREE.
options: Unusual timing or pattern of new-payee payments following the changes.
A default assumption that all travelers are committing fraud.
Use of a newly seen device or browser during a substantial transfer.
Recent sensitive profile changes made through the help desk.
Whether an employee describes the customer as polite on the telephone.
questions.explanation: Cross-channel linkage of meaningful behavioral changes, device novelty and payment activity improves detection while limiting unsupported generalizations.

questions.topic: Low-value velocity hidden by daily totals
questions.stem:
A payments platform monitors aggregate daily outgoing value and generates an alert when an account exceeds its historical monthly average. Criminals discover that each purchase below a small limit can be processed instantly without step-up authentication. They begin using the same merchant category and a shared cluster of devices to make many low-value payments across different customer accounts during a ten-minute period. Total daily activity for each account remains close to its normal level, and the existing monitoring dashboard shows an unremarkable average ticket size. A fraud analyst proposes comparing shorter time windows and inter-account relationships rather than increasing the amount threshold.

What is the primary weakness of the existing design?
options: The scoring system treats repeated device reuse as an account-level feature and therefore cannot establish whether a burst is abnormal.
The detection model is overly focused on merchant category and does not incorporate daily account totals, which should be prioritized instead.
It uses a known merchant category, which makes fraud analytics impossible.
Daily aggregation and account-level amounts can conceal coordinated short-window activity and shared-entity patterns.
questions.explanation: Fraud can be structured across short intervals or accounts so that coarse aggregates obscure the event. Velocity and linked-device patterns add relevant features.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Fraudulent behavioral patterns (pp. 12–17); identifying anomalies (pp. 51–52)

Which TWO new features are most directly relevant? Select TWO.
options: The full personal message history of every consumer without considering relevance or permission.
Customer age as a universal stand-alone reason to decline purchases.
Number of distinct accounts tied to a shared device or merchant cluster.
Count of purchases per short sliding window by account or device.
Average amount only across an entire calendar year.

questions.topic: Misaligned timestamps in the ETL pipeline
questions.stem:
Fraud analytics combines card transactions, digital logins and call-center activity into a feature store. Card records are stamped in UTC, call logs in a regional time zone, and the vendor’s mobile events are reported as local time without an offset. During a testing exercise, a device change recorded at 02:05 is treated as occurring after a payment that in fact happened twenty minutes later. A data engineer says source systems must be preserved exactly, while the analytics lead proposes translating timestamps to a common reference, retaining source values and recording transformations. The firm’s model appears to perform better after discarding records with missing offsets, but the exclusions disproportionately remove a new high-risk payment channel.

Which immediate corrective action is most defensible?
options: Discard temporally inconsistent records only for model training, without quantifying whether exclusions differ by channel.
Discard every transaction from the new channel and report improved model performance without qualification.
Normalize event time with auditable transformation and data-quality rules, preserving original records and investigating missing-offset bias.
Normalize only card-system time stamps and preserve other local times, reasoning that a consistent card clock will anchor the overall chronology.
questions.explanation: Data preparation must preserve correct sequencing and track missing or transformed information. Silent exclusions can distort model performance and attack visibility.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Data preparation; extraction, transformation and loading (pp. 39–42)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Detection and Analytics • Data preparation; extraction, transformation and loading (pp. 39–42)

Changing the outcome labels for difficult events so the validation score rises.
Suppressing data-quality incidents because they originate with a vendor.
Completeness checks for the newly launched channel and missing event fields.
Consistent time-zone representation and verifiable event ordering.

questions.topic: Few fraud labels, many unknown patterns
questions.stem:
A startup bank begins offering an instant payment product and has only forty confirmed fraud cases. Its transaction database contains many legitimate payments, a small set of cases under review and unlabeled events from new devices. The analytics lead suggests combining the small verified labels with unlabeled data and anomaly analysis to discover patterns not represented in the historic cases. Another developer proposes training a high-complexity supervised classifier using all disputed events as confirmed fraud. The chief risk officer asks which learning approach is justified by the actual label availability and how the institution should assess what the system discovers before automatically declining payments.

Which strategy most appropriately fits the data constraints?
options: Label all disputed events as confirmed fraud with a lower confidence weight until the investigation team can provide more outcomes.
Avoid monitoring until there are tens of thousands of confirmed losses.
Use unsupervised groupings as provisional fraud labels in production and confirm them only when customers later complain.
Explore semi-supervised or unsupervised approaches, carefully validate emerging anomalies and improve labels through investigation feedback.
questions.explanation: The guide differentiates supervised, semi-supervised and unsupervised learning by label availability. Novel anomalies require verification rather than being treated as confirmed fraud.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Supervised versus unsupervised learning; machine learning (pp. 65–68)

Which TWO statements correctly distinguish the approaches? Select TWO.
options: Unsupervised learning can identify unusual groups without requiring confirmed outcome labels.
Unsupervised analysis automatically determines whether the customer is guilty.
Semi-supervised learning means the data must be entirely labeled.
All models can be compared meaningfully without considering data quality or outcomes.
Supervised learning relies on labeled outcomes and is useful for known patterns.
questions.explanation: Supervised learning uses labels; unsupervised methods identify structures without them. Neither eliminates the need for meaningful assessment of results.

questions.topic: Misleading accuracy in a low-prevalence portfolio
questions.stem:
A digital bank evaluates 20,000 payments of which investigators confirmed 200 as fraudulent. Model A flags 160 of the actual frauds and wrongly flags 1,440 legitimate payments; it misses 40 frauds. Model B flags 120 actual frauds and wrongly flags 180 legitimate payments; it misses 80 frauds. A third proposal is a 'do nothing' classifier that approves every payment. The product owner argues the third approach is best because it is correct on 19,800 transactions and generates no false positives. The fraud director must consider investigators’ capacity, fraud loss appetite and the customer cost of unnecessary friction, not just accuracy.

Which statement correctly identifies the trade-off?
options: Model A should be preferred automatically because a higher number of detected frauds is more important than any operational burden.
Model B has higher recall because it produces fewer false positives.
Model B has lower precision because it detects fewer frauds, despite producing considerably fewer false alarms.
Model A has higher recall but substantially lower precision than Model B, so the preferred threshold depends on fraud cost and customer impact.
questions.explanation: Model A recall is 160/200=80% and precision 160/1600=10%; Model B recall is 120/200=60% and precision 120/300=40%. A high overall accuracy may hide failure to detect rare fraud.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Fraud detection model selection and evaluation metrics (pp. 75–77)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Detection and Analytics • Fraud detection model selection and evaluation metrics (pp. 75–77)

Model B precision is 40%.
Model A precision exceeds Model B precision.
The all-approve model has 99% overall accuracy yet 0% fraud recall.

questions.topic: Different error costs for two monitored products
questions.stem:
A bank has two fraud products: low-value transit micropayments and high-value business wire transfers. A common scoring rule would block the top two percent of both streams. In testing, transit riders experience many legitimate declines and queue at payment terminals, while a much smaller number of suspicious wire events show very high potential loss. The fraud analytics team can adjust action thresholds by segment; it can also apply additional verification rather than outright declines to intermediate scores. A business head argues that a single uniform threshold looks fairest on an executive dashboard, even though the products have materially different transaction sizes, fraud consequences and customer experiences.

Which design is most defensible?
options: Apply a uniform score threshold but allow relationship managers to reverse transit declines after a customer complaint.
Calibrate proportionate, risk-based interventions by product and compare detected losses, false positives and customer impact.
Choose the highest-volume payment stream for review staffing because incident count is a better proxy for risk than average severity.
Ignore transit false positives because avoiding fraud always outweighs customer friction.
questions.explanation: The guide emphasizes balancing fraud mitigation with positive customer outcomes. Product-specific consequences and thresholds may require different actions.

A business head argues that a single uniform threshold looks fairest on an executive dashboard, even though the products have materially different transaction sizes, fraud consequences and customer experiences.

Whether the threshold can be expressed as the same integer across all channels.

The cost and friction of intervening against legitimate customers.

questions.stem:
A development team builds a classifier to identify fraud before card authorization. During training, its strongest predictor is a variable labeled 'chargeback resolved as fraud,' which is created weeks after the transaction. Historical test performance appears almost perfect. The team also adds features available at authorization time, including recent device changes, velocity and payee novelty, but these contribute less to the training score. Operations asks whether the model can be deployed in real time without changing its feature list. A reviewer notices that the model’s training snapshots combine data recorded before authorization with post-investigation outcomes, making the predictive assessment unreliable for live decisions.

What is the decisive model-design problem?
options: Post-event outcome information is unavailable at decision time and creates misleading predictive performance.
Keep the post-event variable for model training but ensure it is excluded only from the production dashboard.
The bank used more than one feature.
Replace the leaked variable with a delayed merchant-dispute flag that is reported more consistently but also arrives after authorization.
questions.explanation: A feature must be available when a live decision is made. Using a later fraud conclusion as an input leaks the answer and invalidates apparent predictive ability.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Fraud detection model feature engineering; evaluation (pp. 78–82)

questions.stem:
A fraud model performs extremely well on two years of data collected before a mobile-wallet launch. After launch, customers adopt new payment patterns and criminals shift from bulk counterfeit-card payments to account takeover through help-desk profile changes. The vendor says the model does not need review because its back-test accuracy remains unchanged. Fraud operations reports rising confirmed misses in the new wallet channel, while investigators have also noticed that frontline staff stopped entering certain confirmed cases into the training repository. Senior management asks whether historical validation, current monitoring and proper label capture are interchangeable controls.

What is the strongest governance response?
options: Raise thresholds automatically until the new fraud misses disappear from the dashboard.
Eliminate model monitoring once a vendor certifies its platform.
Rely on the historic back-test without updating data because it has stable metrics.
Validate current performance by segment and unseen data, restore complete outcome feedback, and assess drift and retraining under controlled change procedures.
questions.explanation: The guide emphasizes retraining, data quality, out-of-sample testing and model-drift monitoring. A stable historical metric does not establish current effectiveness.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Model training, model evaluation and governance (pp. 81–86)

Which TWO conditions can contribute to misleading model assurance? Select TWO.
options: Keeping a documented model-change history.
Ignoring shifts in product and customer behavior since the training period.

Omitting confirmed missed frauds from the feedback dataset.

questions.explanation: Distribution shift and incomplete outcome labels can make performance reporting unreliable despite excellent historic back-tests.

questions.stem:
A customer phones a bank about a legitimate mortgage payment while a fraudster, pretending to be technical support, convinces him to install a remote-access tool on his computer. The customer logs in using valid credentials and a second factor. The bank’s behavioral biometric system observes unfamiliar cursor trajectories, long periods without keyboard input, and repeated switching away from the payment window. A newly created payee is then selected for a large transfer. Investigators cannot yet establish whether the customer personally initiated the payment or the remote operator controlled the session. The fraud model has historically weighted successful login authentication far more heavily than behavioral anomalies.

What is the most justified immediate interpretation?
options: A possible remote-access/social-engineering attack warrants layered review of session behavior, payee context and customer verification.
Classify the remote-control signal as confirmed account takeover before asking whether the customer was intentionally or deceptively involved.
Treat authenticated login as stronger evidence than behavioral anomalies and route the payment for manual review only after settlement.
The bank should permanently stop use of all remote-access software by every customer.
questions.explanation: Behavioral biometrics can identify deviations even where credentials were correctly supplied. They support investigation and real-time intervention, not conclusive attribution by themselves.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Biometric analytical tools (pp. 69–70)

questions.topic: Common IP addresses and weak network links
questions.stem:
An insurer creates a network graph for a cluster of suspicious claims. Fifteen unrelated claimants share a public internet address associated with a busy hospital; a subset also share the same bank account, identical repair invoices and a common contact telephone number. A junior analyst argues every claimant linked through the hospital IP must be in a criminal ring. Another analyst suggests weighting connections by specificity and verifying whether common nodes have innocent explanations. The business wants to rapidly suspend all related claims but has not interviewed patients or obtained original invoice records. External claim data may be incomplete for events occurring before a system migration.

Which analytical conclusion is most defensible?
options: Only transaction amounts can identify fraud networks.
Use shared IP address as the strongest network feature, even where a high-volume public endpoint explains repeated matches.
Graph links help prioritize investigation; common public infrastructure is weaker evidence than repeated unique financial and document connections.
Suspend all parties sharing the public network because graph size increases confidence in each individual link.
questions.explanation: Network analytics can reveal hidden relationships, but the meaning of a shared link requires context and corroboration. Public infrastructure is often a weak identifying signal.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Social network analysis and fraud graphs (pp. 56–57)

questions.stem:
A card issuer constructs a training set from customer disputes. Every disputed purchase is labeled fraud and every undisputed purchase is labeled legitimate. The fraud team learns that some customers are unaware of unauthorized charges, some disputes reflect merchant-service problems and some confirmed first-party abuse occurs in the disputes themselves. The data-science group has already trained a classifier that assigns unusually high fraud risk to a product used disproportionately by customers who file complaints promptly. A product manager argues that complaint status is objective and therefore requires no additional label-quality checks.

What is the core dataset problem?
options: The issuer is treating disputes as a balanced random sample of fraud outcomes, even though complaining customers may not represent all victims.
Dispute status is an imperfect proxy for confirmed fraudulent outcomes and can introduce systematic labeling errors and misleading features.
Customer disputes are always irrelevant to fraud analytics.
The issuer has not included a confirmed subset of merchant disputes, but the complaint labels can still be treated as reliable proxies.
questions.explanation: Dispute status, completed investigation outcomes and first-party abuse are not equivalent. Training requires reliable and consistently defined labels.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Fraud datasets; data preparation and quality (pp. 36–45)

questions.stem:
A bank’s board receives a monthly report showing the number of confirmed account-takeover cases, channels involved and losses over the preceding twelve months. Analysts also build a risk score from device novelty, recent password resets and short-window transaction patterns to estimate the likelihood that a pending payment is fraudulent. The fraud committee wants to use these outputs together but the reporting team calls both products 'descriptive analysis' because both rely on historical information. An operations executive is concerned that any predictive score should be treated as a final fraud determination rather than a decision aid whose accuracy must be measured.

Which distinction is accurate?
options: The live risk score is equivalent to an investigative verdict if it uses sufficiently many previously confirmed cases.
The historical dashboard is predictive because it contains a trend line, whereas the live risk score is descriptive because it uses known features.
The live score is descriptive because it has more than three variables.
The monthly breakdown describes observed events; the live score estimates risk for new events and must be validated against outcomes.
questions.explanation: Descriptive analytics summarizes past patterns; predictive methods estimate future or unseen outcomes. Neither establishes guilt without appropriate context and review.

questions.stem:
A fraud analytics unit proposes collecting precise GPS data continuously for all mobile banking customers to detect unusual locations. The vendor notes that device intelligence can help recognize account takeover, but users in several jurisdictions have not provided consent for the proposed collection. A branch customer who lives near an international border frequently appears in two countries on the same day. The project lead wants to block every cross-border location change automatically. Legal advises that location data is subject to relevant permission and privacy obligations, and the fraud team can combine less intrusive signals while it resolves the consent design.

Which control design best reflects the guide?
options: Implement geolocation with a legitimate fraud-prevention objective but postpone user permission checks until device telemetry is collected.
Use location only as a categorical country flag and automatically decline cross-border activity without comparing expected customer travel.
Use appropriately authorized geolocation as one contextual signal in a layered model and evaluate travel patterns and customer experience.
Treat border-crossing by a legitimate commuter as proof of impersonation.
questions.explanation: The guide describes geolocation as useful but notes explicit consent where required. A signal should be interpreted against known behavior rather than used indiscriminately.

questions.stem:
An analytics team compares a single decision tree with a random forest and a gradient boosting model on a labeled card-fraud dataset. The single tree is easy to explain but overfits several unusual training events. The random forest averages across many trees and performs more consistently on an unseen test sample. The gradient boosting model sequentially corrects the errors of previous learners but demands careful tuning to avoid unstable results. A director argues all ensembles are interchangeable and that testing on the training sample alone demonstrates production resilience. A data scientist cautions that feature quality, validation and drift monitoring remain important regardless of algorithm choice.

Which description best reflects the algorithms in the guide?
options: A random forest combines multiple decision trees; gradient boosting builds learners sequentially to correct earlier errors.
All ensembles are identical to a single manually fixed payment threshold.
A random forest uses sequential correction of prior predictions, while a gradient boosted model averages unrelated tree outputs.
An ensemble model eliminates the need to inspect individual input variables, although its test results should be retained.
questions.explanation: The guide describes random forests as aggregations of decision trees and gradient boosting as sequential correction. Different methods still need appropriate evaluation.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Basics of machine learning; ensemble methods (pp. 68, 79)

questions.stem:
A fraud analytics team tests two threshold strategies on an unseen portfolio. Strategy X produces 900 alerts per day, 90 of which are verified fraud; Strategy Y produces 250 alerts, 75 of which are verified fraud. Fraud operations can reliably investigate 300 alerts daily, and overflow cases are not reviewed in time to prevent transfers. Mean loss for fraud not identified before settlement is much higher than the cost of a legitimate customer being asked for one additional verification step. The chief analytics officer proposes choosing X because it detects fifteen more fraud events on the test set, while operations warns that X may be impossible to implement at current staffing.

Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: Neither strategy may be compared until every legitimate customer is surveyed.
Deploy X and use a first-in-first-out queue, assuming historical higher gross detection will translate into better real-time prevention.
Y has a higher observed alert precision and fits current capacity; a final choice should jointly consider missed-fraud cost, intervention options and achievable review throughput.
Choose Y solely from its higher precision without considering the marginal losses represented by the fifteen extra detected cases.
questions.explanation: X precision is 90/900=10%; Y precision is 75/250=30%. Operational capacity and loss trade-offs affect effective detection, not just laboratory counts.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Detection and Analytics • Fraud detection model: evaluation metrics; business impact (pp. 60–61, 75–77)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Detection and Analytics • Fraud detection model: evaluation metrics; business impact (pp. 60–61, 75–77)

questions.topic: Extortion alert involving a vulnerable young customer
questions.stem:
A 17-year-old account holder initiates an urgent transfer to a newly created beneficiary shortly after midnight. The bank’s fraud engine has held the transaction because the amount and payee differ sharply from his normal spending. During a short call, the customer appears distressed and says that someone online will release private photographs unless he pays immediately. He begs the investigator not to contact his school or family. A teammate argues the customer knowingly initiated the payment and therefore there is nothing to investigate. Another suggests identifying him publicly to deter other victims from making similar choices. The investigator has a fraud-escalation procedure but does not yet know the criminal’s identity, whether other payments occurred, or what legal safeguards apply to a minor.

What is the most defensible first operational action?
options: Release the payment after reiterating generic online safety advice because the young customer voluntarily instructed it.
Contact the beneficiary bank and customer’s school before the internal escalation because this could stop the extortion rapidly.
Conclude the beneficiary committed a particular offense before reviewing any evidence.
Follow internal policy to escalate the suspected extortion and investigate promptly while protecting the customer’s safety, dignity and confidential information.
questions.explanation: The guide’s extortion scenario emphasizes internal escalation before unrelated disclosures or automatic release. Emotional urgency and apparent authorization do not remove fraud concerns.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Importance of fraud detection; investigative mindset (pp. 6–11)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Importance of fraud detection; investigative mindset (pp. 6–11)

questions.topic: Disappearing webpages and an incomplete evidence trail
questions.stem:
A fraud investigator examines a website advertising a fictitious investment scheme and notices that the landing page changes every few hours. A victim has supplied screenshots from a phone, but the captures show neither the web address nor the date and time. The investigator saves the page through an authorized method and records the source location, download time, collecting employee and a secure evidence reference. Another team member proposes overwriting the original file after adding explanatory highlights to simplify the case. The investigation may later be referred to law enforcement, and the bank does not have authority to seize unrelated private documents from the promoter. Management wants a defensible trail of what was observed and how the records were preserved.

Which evidence practice is best?
options: Collect the promoter’s private devices through informal seizure to avoid law enforcement delays.
Preserve original digital captures and source metadata, separately annotate working copies, and maintain an auditable record of custody and access.
Rely on victim screenshots after securing them, but omit fresh capture of the live changing site because later versions might differ.
Prepare an annotated master exhibit by inserting comments into the only preserved original, rather than maintaining separate working copies.
questions.explanation: The guide stresses credible relevant evidence, preservation of originals, secure storage and chain of custody; dynamic websites should be saved while available.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Evidence gathering and chain of custody (pp. 62–64)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Evidence gathering and chain of custody (pp. 62–64)

questions.topic: Witness interview shaped by a leading question
questions.stem:
An employee reports that a regional manager may have diverted vendor rebates to a related company. Before obtaining invoices, a junior investigator asks a witness, 'You saw the manager steal the funds last Tuesday, did you not?' The witness agrees but later clarifies that she only saw a bank-account change request and has no direct knowledge of where the money went. A second witness claims to have heard the manager boast about the scheme, but cannot give an exact date. Human Resources wants the two statements merged into one narrative for efficiency. An experienced investigator recommends beginning with broad questions, separating firsthand observations from inferences and recording each witness’s confirmed account.

Which interviewing change most improves the evidence?
options: Interview the suspected manager first to establish an official version that others must adopt.
Begin by explaining the suspected diversion and asking witnesses to confirm which details they remember, then invite broader comments.
Prioritize the most incriminating witness account and address differences only if the alleged manager disputes it.
Begin with open, non-leading questions, clarify source and chronology of observations, and obtain an accurate verified statement from each person.
questions.explanation: The guide emphasizes planned open-ended questioning, attentive listening and accurate attestations. Leading questions can contaminate testimony and confuse observations with beliefs.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Effective interviewing techniques; taking statements (pp. 73–75)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Effective interviewing techniques; taking statements (pp. 73–75)

questions.topic: Interview sequencing with an influential suspect
questions.stem:
A bank receives an anonymous allegation that a senior account manager redirected small client reimbursements into a personal account. Three clients describe missing credits, a neutral settlement specialist understands the reconciliation workflow, and two direct reports might have witnessed exceptions. The suspect has access to their schedules and performance evaluations. An executive suggests interviewing the suspect immediately and then asking all other witnesses to confirm the explanation. The investigator is concerned that early contact could lead to altered records or coordinated accounts. The case team can preserve internal system records now and arrange controlled interviews with two investigators, one asking questions and one taking notes.

Which interview plan best follows the guide?
options: Interview the suspect with the direct reports present to minimize conflicting recollections, even though this may influence their answers.
Skip interviews because transaction records are always self-explanatory.
Interview the suspect first to obtain a baseline account and then compare it with witnesses, before preserving potentially alterable internal records.
Secure relevant records, gather victim and neutral contextual accounts first, then interview associated witnesses and the suspect with prepared questions.
questions.explanation: The guide favors gathering evidence and broader accounts before confronting a suspect, helping investigators evaluate competing explanations without premature contamination.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Interviews of victims, neutral witnesses and suspected offenders (pp. 73–75)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Interviews of victims, neutral witnesses and suspected offenders (pp. 73–75)

questions.topic: Tracing funds through an international payment chain
questions.stem:
A corporate client sends a large wire to an apparently familiar supplier after receiving a forged account-change notice. The funds travel through a correspondent bank to a foreign beneficiary and are soon divided into several onward payments. The customer supplies its invoice, email chain and transfer confirmation. The originator’s bank has the SWIFT message references but lacks visibility into final beneficiaries after onward movement. A relationship manager claims the transfer can simply be pulled back because its message remains in the bank’s system; another proposes waiting for a criminal conviction before contacting the recipient institution. The case is being investigated under the bank’s fraud response and recovery policies.

Which combined action is most defensible?
options: Start prompt authorized tracing and recall/recovery requests with supporting records, while recognizing that a reference number does not guarantee return of funds.
Treat the case as closed as soon as an initial recall request is sent.
Prepare the customer claim and trace internally, but defer contact with receiving institutions until the final investigative report is approved.
Give the customer a provisional estimate of a full return on the basis that network payment references are available for tracing.
questions.explanation: The guide describes payment tracing, SWIFT-related inquiry and collaboration. Completed transfers may not be recoverable, so attempts and outcomes must be tracked separately.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Tracing fraudulent transactions; global payment networks (pp. 67–69)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Tracing fraudulent transactions; global payment networks (pp. 67–69)

questions.topic: Card scheme evidence and dispute windows
questions.stem:
An issuer receives several customer complaints about card-not-present transactions made at a new online merchant. A customer insists that the issuer must win a chargeback because the cardholder says the order was unauthorized. The merchant has submitted order details and a delivery confirmation to an address that the cardholder previously used, while the device evidence is inconclusive. The issuer’s dispute team knows that scheme rulebooks govern the claim category, time limits, required documentation and allocation of liability. A fraud investigator proposes treating the rulebook as a substitute for interviewing the claimant or investigating suspicious merchant patterns. The bank’s filing deadline for a potentially eligible dispute is approaching.

What is the most defensible case strategy?
options: Document and investigate relevant facts while promptly pursuing any appropriate chargeback within the governing network rules and deadlines.
Wait until all criminal proceedings finish before examining the card scheme’s requirements.
Submit a broad dispute without verifying reason code and evidence because the issuer’s first priority is preserving time.
Accept the merchant’s delivery evidence as sufficient to reject the claim unless the cardholder supplies definitive proof of impersonation.
questions.explanation: A scheme rulebook determines dispute paths and evidence requirements, but facts still require fair assessment. Timeliness is critical for available recovery routes.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Using card payment scheme rulebooks (p. 69); fraud remediation (pp. 94–97 of Domain 1)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Using card payment scheme rulebooks (p. 69); fraud remediation (pp. 94–97 of Domain 1)

questions.topic: Financial loss calculation beyond stolen principal
questions.stem:
A procurement fraud diverts 1.8 million in company funds. Finance proposes reporting only this principal amount, even though the institution has spent money on forensic specialists, customer reimbursements and emergency system repairs. A small amount of diverted money has been recovered but may later be subject to a competing claim. The investigation also identifies lost future revenue after several corporate customers terminate their contracts; management cannot confidently quantify the entire reputational effect. Separately, process mapping reveals one employee could amend beneficiary details and suppress the exception alert. A board committee asks for one report showing both financial impact and the control deficiencies that enabled the scheme.

Which report best meets the objective?
options: Present both principal losses and forecast recoveries as realized net loss because management needs one decision-ready number.
Classify every future revenue estimate as an already realized cash loss.
Distinguish direct loss, verified related costs, recoveries and uncertain reputational impact; analyze control causes and document assumptions.
Report the diverted principal and incurred forensic fees, but exclude customer reimbursements and unresolved recovery status to avoid double counting.
questions.explanation: The guide discusses financial loss estimation and root cause analysis, requiring clear loss definitions, documented recovery treatment and consideration of broader consequences.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Fraud root cause analysis; estimating financial losses (pp. 70–72)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Fraud root cause analysis; estimating financial losses (pp. 70–72)

questions.topic: Public registry conflicts with internal customer records
questions.stem:
An investigator examines a business that opened several payment accounts and quickly received transfers from unrelated victims. The bank’s onboarding file names one director, while a public corporate registry lists another individual and an ownership change six months earlier. A commercial data vendor gives a third ownership name without showing a source or update date. A social media profile associated with the business displays images of lavish property, but the investigator cannot establish who manages the profile. The account holder claims all transactions relate to legitimate e-commerce shipments and offers invoices that contain repeated formatting errors. The lead investigator is asked which information should be trusted before attributing control of the accounts.

Which approach best reflects investigative use of external data?
options: Interpret the account-linked social media profile as strong ownership evidence and use it to resolve the conflict between registration dates.
Use the paid data vendor’s ownership record as primary evidence and reconcile the official registry only if the account holder disputes it.
Ignore corporate registries and rely solely on account-opening names.
Evaluate source reliability and dates, reconcile internal and official records, and corroborate assertions with independent transaction and business evidence.
questions.explanation: OSINT and third-party data can support inquiries, but differences in reliability, timing and provenance require corroboration before reaching conclusions.
questions.source: ACAMS CAFS v1.03 · Fraud Investigations • Sources of evidence; OSINT (pp. 62–66)
questions.sourceSection: Fraud Investigations • Sources of evidence; OSINT (pp. 62–66)
